issues.title: Stop the December shared ChatGPT/Codex limits: protect paying users and address rising usage costs

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: rate-limits
labels.description: Issues related to rate limits, quotas, and token usage reporting

issues.body:
## Enough is enough

I am a paying ChatGPT Pro subscriber. I am opening this as a **separate customer-impact issue**, not just adding another comment to existing discussions.

OpenAI plans to combine ChatGPT and Codex usage into one token-based allowance starting in December 2026. That means advanced ChatGPT conversations and Codex/Work tasks will draw on the same pool. OpenAI says Instant chat is excluded, but that does not resolve the concerns of subscribers who pay for advanced capabilities.

**Paying users should not have to accept less usable access, less predictability, or additional charges for the same subscription.**

## The announced change

OpenAI's official Help Center says that starting in December, Plus, Pro, and Business usage will be shared across ChatGPT and Codex, measured in tokens. Model choice and task complexity affect consumption. When the allowance runs out, users may need to wait, upgrade, or buy credits.

Official source: https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001625-understanding-chatgpt-and-codex-usage-limits

This is a confirmed *planned* change, not a claim that the December limits are already in force.

## Why I am raising this

- **ChatGPT is not just a coding tool.** Many subscribers use it mainly to talk, learn, research, create, and solve personal problems. They should not need to know what Codex or Work is to understand or retain the value of their paid subscription.
- **Separate activities would compete for one allowance.** Using advanced chat could reduce capacity for Codex/Work, and vice versa. That is a meaningful loss of independence unless the new allowance fully preserves existing practical usage.
- **Subscribers lack a usable before-and-after comparison.** Publish the actual included tokens, model/task consumption rules, reset windows, and realistic examples *before* implementation, not after we have paid.
- **My recent experience has already been frustrating.** I have encountered slower execution and what feels like faster usage/quota consumption during intensive tasks. This is a first-hand report, not a claim that I have proved a global performance regression. Those concerns should be measured and investigated instead of placing yet more quota uncertainty on users.
- **This follows another round of disruption.** OpenAI's October 29 release notes say it canceled the previously announced Pro 200 reduction. Subscribers should not face another round of uncertainty the very next month. Source: https://help.openai.com/en/articles/6825453-chatgpt-release-notes

## What I am asking OpenAI to do

1. **Cancel the compulsory December shared-limit change** and preserve independent ChatGPT advanced-reasoning and Codex/Work allowances.
2. If consolidation is still proposed, provide an **opt-in alternative or guaranteed protected allowances** that ensure no existing paid subscriber loses practical access for the same price.
3. Publish transparent per-plan limits, token consumption rates, reset rules, and before-and-after comparisons in advance.
4. Investigate reports of slower tasks and unexpectedly rapid allowance consumption, and provide detailed per-task usage records so customers can verify what they are charged for.
5. Avoid charging users' allowances or credits for avoidable failed and repeated work caused by service-side problems.

This is not a demand for unlimited compute. It is a demand for stable value, transparent accounting, and respect for existing customers.

**Stop making paying users absorb every new restriction. Enough is enough.**

## Public petition

I have also launched a Change.org petition so everyday ChatGPT users, not just developers on GitHub, can add their voices:

**OpenAI, Stop Punishing Your Paying Users!**  
https://c.org/YDxqchYg6T

Related discussion: #58742. This issue additionally requests an investigation into apparent slowing/usage cost concerns and documents the broader customer-impact and petition campaign.

issues.body:
## Summary

After an update on November 21, 2026 (Europe/Berlin), the user can no longer find the "On your computer" / "Auf deinem Computer" execution-location selector in ChatGPT Work on Windows. The user reports that selecting local execution had restored SSH access previously and still worked earlier the same morning, before the update. That workaround is now unavailable.

The user supplied an About ChatGPT screenshot confirming version **26.1117.41037**, labeled "Powered by Codex & OWL", with release date **November 20, 2026**. The user reports installing the update on November 21, 2026. The timing suggests a regression, but the update has not been independently established as the cause.

## Environment

- ChatGPT desktop / Work interface on Windows, German UI.
- User reports all relevant access/network settings are enabled.
- The supplied screenshot visibly shows the orange "Uneingeschränkter Zugriff" (Full access) control.
- The former location of the execution selector, at the lower right beneath the composer, is empty in the supplied screenshot. Full access is present; it is the execution-location selector that is missing in this report.
- Screenshots were inspected in the reporting conversation but are not attached to this issue.

## Observed behavior and diagnostics

PowerShell commands execute. Get-Location returned the configured project directory on an approved NAS share. This confirms shell execution and a configured working directory, not a full file-access or write test.

A read-only SSH test to an authorized private-LAN host was run repeatedly from the affected session (username/address redacted below):

```powershell
ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=6 -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes <user>@<private-LAN-host> hostname
```

The command tool returned exit code 1, with:

```text
Attempting to perform the InitializeDefaultDrives operation on the 'FileSystem' provider failed.
ssh: connect to host <private-LAN-host> port 22: Permission denied
```

The connection failed before authentication or remote command execution. The session's effective execution configuration reports restricted network access despite the visible Full access setting. The exact enforcing layer has not been identified; no claim is made that server credentials or host keys are faulty.

The user reports already fully restarting the app, with no recovery. No settings, SSH keys, host-key checks, or server configuration were changed during these diagnostics.

## Expected behavior

An authorized user should have a supported way to select local execution, or a clear replacement for the previous selector. The UI should accurately reflect the effective permissions, and explain why SSH is denied when Full access and network access are enabled.

## Impact

Existing infrastructure and development workflows requiring SSH to a private-LAN Docker host are blocked. The previously working local-execution workaround is no longer accessible.

## Related reports

- #60058 — related restricted-network/SSH behavior, with comments reporting that selecting local execution restored access.
- #61501 — missing permission controls and blocked SSH. This report differs: Full access remains visible, while the local/cloud execution selector is missing.
- #61120 — related Windows permission-selector/SSH report.

Please consolidate if appropriate. Is the missing execution-location selector intentional in the current rollout, and is there a supported recovery path or replacement control for affected users?

issues.title: [Desktop] Built-in automation restriction blocks monitoring tasks in external web systems, conflicting with Scheduled tasks docs

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

issues.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1029.61003 (build 24614), verified from the installed app Info.plist

### What subscription do you have?

Not collected for this report

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 26.6; uname -mprs: Darwin 25.6.0 arm64 arm

### What issue are you seeing?

The desktop app's built-in instructions cause the assistant to decline Schedule-based monitoring of a task running in an external web system, even though the official documentation explicitly describes checking long-running operations until they finish.

**Scope: the monitored task belongs to an external web system. It is not a Codex session, thread, subagent, or Codex task.** Codex would only periodically check its status and report or continue the user's authorized follow-up when the external operation finishes.

The app-provided Automations instructions include:

> Do not create an automation to track a specific job or task through a milestone, failure, or completion.

The following sentence directs the assistant to keep checking in the current task when asked to watch a run or task to completion. Neither sentence explicitly limits the restriction to Codex's own tasks.

In a fresh local chat, the assistant discovered the native automation_update tool (including thread-attached heartbeat support), but declined to create this kind of schedule because it interpreted the built-in restriction as also covering external-system tasks. Clarifying that the task is external did not resolve that interpretation.

This is an instruction/documentation conflict observed before scheduling, not evidence of a scheduler backend rejection or a missed scheduled execution. No tracking schedule was created during this investigation.

Official documentation, checked on November 5, 2026:
https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/automations?surface=app#schedule-a-task-inside-a-chat

It explicitly lists “checking a long-running operation until it finishes” as a use case for a schedule in an existing chat. It also describes minute-based follow-up intervals, preserved chat context, and prompts with reporting and stopping conditions. The documented deployment-follow-up example appears to fit this external-system use case.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Observed sequence on one installation; not independently reproduced on another installation:

1. Ask a local Codex chat whether it can use Schedule to follow a task running in an external web system until it completes.
2. In a fresh chat, check whether automation_update is available. It is discoverable here.
3. The assistant declines to create the monitoring schedule, citing the built-in prohibition on tracking a specific job or task to completion.
4. Clarify that the monitored task is external, not a Codex session/thread/task. The assistant still interprets the generic wording as applying to it.
5. Compare the built-in instruction with the linked official Scheduled tasks documentation.

Suggested minimal prompt for maintainers (a generalized example, not a verbatim transcript):
“Every five minutes, return to this chat and check the status of the task in the external web system. Notify me on completion or failure and stop the schedule. This is not a Codex task or session.”

The relevant tool was discovered, but its create operation was not called. This report does not establish whether the backend would accept that schedule.

### What is the expected behavior?

Please clarify and align the runtime instructions, tool guidance, and public documentation for external-system monitoring.

- If the prohibition is intended only for tracking Codex's own running tasks, explicitly scope it that way and allow user-requested monitoring of tasks in external web systems through the documented existing-chat Schedule flow.
- If external-system tasks are also intentionally prohibited, explain that boundary in the documentation and provide the supported alternative for periodic checks without keeping one conversational turn continuously active.
- Ensure a fresh chat does not refuse a documented use case merely because “job or task” is ambiguous.

A useful regression case would request monitoring of a harmless external task with an explicit completion/stop condition, separately from any test involving Codex's own task lifecycle.

### Additional information


The conversation then displays:

Allow should resume the pending action and return command output and an exit code, or a specific execution error. A successful approval interaction should not become an inactive request or be labeled user cancellation without evidence.

Approved development operations remain blocked. The successful ordinary execution and failed escalated execution narrow the observed problem to the escalation/approval path, but do not establish the underlying cause.

Related reports: #57436 and #60139. A shared root cause has not been confirmed.

Please investigate whether the UI approval state and backend request lifecycle diverge.

issues.body:
## Summary

On macOS 26.1 (Apple Silicon), selecting **Full Access** for a **fresh Local session** in the ChatGPT desktop app does not propagate to tool execution. The effective session profile is **managed / workspace-write / restricted**, with restricted network access and the repository's real `.git` directory protected as read-only.

A **personal Codex CLI 0.170.0** session on the *same Mac*, with the *same personal ChatGPT subscription* and local corporate VPN connection, can successfully run with `danger-full-access` / `on-request`, resolve a private Git host, and use SSH `git ls-remote`. This suggests a desktop-specific permission propagation / session-initialization discrepancy, though the exact layer is **not established**.

## Environment

- macOS 26.1, Apple Silicon
- ChatGPT desktop Local session, personal subscription
- Desktop tool execution originates from the Codex binary bundled inside ChatGPT.app
- Standalone personal Codex CLI: 0.170.0
- Observed/reproduced in a newly created Local session on November 22, 2026 (UTC+8)
- This is an independently reproduced issue; not simply an old thread inheriting permissions.

## Expected

Choosing Full Access in the desktop UI should deliver an effective Full Access execution profile for the new Local session, or clearly explain any policy restriction. Local repository metadata and network access should not be blocked when Full Access is actually allowed.

## Actual (desktop Local)

- UI selection: **Full Access**
- Effective `sandbox_mode = workspace-write`
- `permission_profile = managed` (filesystem restricted; `.git` explicitly read-only)
- `approval_policy = granular`; elevation unavailable according to supplied session metadata
- Network policy restricted; tool subprocess has `CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED=1`
- DNS lookup of a private, VPN-reachable Git hostname fails with `socket.gaierror`
- SSH `git ls-remote` fails at hostname resolution (exit 128)
- Earlier desktop attempts to `git fetch` also failed trying to write `.git/FETCH_HEAD` (Operation not permitted). The fresh-session reproduction was read-only and did not attempt a write.

Here `managed` refers to the Codex sandbox profile, **not evidence of MDM or corporate policy**.

## Control test: standalone personal CLI on the same Mac

- OpenAI provider, personal ChatGPT account; model request succeeded
- Effective permissions shown as `danger-full-access`, approval `on-request`
- Corporate VPN active, private Git hostname resolves
- Non-interactive SSH `git ls-remote` succeeds
- The Git metadata path passed access checks; no actual write-test was performed.

The CLI and desktop tests were **not simultaneous** and were performed in **two different local Git checkout paths**; no claim is made that the paths or exact runtime environments were identical. Nonetheless DNS was tested directly inside each tool environment, and the UI/runtime permission discrepancy is independently observed.

## Reproduction

1. Open the personal ChatGPT desktop application on macOS.
2. Create a new **Local** session for a local Git checkout and explicitly select **Full Access**.
3. Ask the session to report actual runtime permission metadata and execute a read-only DNS lookup and `git ls-remote` for a private Git host accessible to the native terminal.
4. Observe that the effective tool policy is managed `workspace-write`, network restricted, and `CODEX_SANDBOX_NETWORK_DISABLED=1`, despite UI Full Access.

## Requested investigation

Please correlate, for the same request:
1. Permission selection submitted by desktop UI.
2. Permission values accepted at session initialization / restoration.
3. Effective permission profile delivered to the first tool call, and the source of any override.

We have **not** established whether the mismatch comes from UI transmission, initialization, or runtime policy merge. No evidence has established contamination by a separate enterprise login, either.

## Related reports

- #55922 (similar macOS desktop Full Access vs managed workspace-write discrepancy)
- #62408 (similar Windows desktop symptom)

prs.title: Prevent MCP reply POSTs from resolving pending requests
prs.body:
Prevent MCP reply POSTs from resolving pending requests

## Why

Codex and an MCP server assign JSON-RPC request IDs independently. If
both use the same ID, a server message returned in response to Codex's
reply POST can incorrectly resolve Codex's own pending request.

## What changed

In the MCP Streamable HTTP client, accept HTTP `202` and `204` as
acknowledgements for outgoing JSON-RPC results and errors. After handling
authentication challenges, reject other statuses for reply POSTs before
decoding their bodies as JSON or server-sent events.

## Testing

Add a regression test that uses the same ID for a request and a reply.
It checks that the request still receives its JSON-RPC error, reply
POSTs reject HTTP `409` JSON and HTTP `200` JSON or SSE, and both
acknowledgement statuses are accepted.

prs.title: Keep Cloud reply stream recovery retryable after transient failures
prs.body:
Keep Cloud reply stream recovery retryable after transient failures

## Why

Repeated disconnects could exhaust the active recovery attempt limit. A
shared deadline also let time spent in the worker queue or waiting to
reattach cut into the time available to fetch history and install the
replacement stream.

## What changed

- Replace the active recovery attempt limit with exponential backoff
  capped at 30 seconds.
- Give worker dispatch, reattachment, recovery history reads, and stream
  installation separate timeout budgets. Wait for the caller to release
  the held stream before starting the installation timeout.
- Surface transient failures and timeouts as transport errors so callers
  can retry recovery. Continue to enforce sign-in and network policy
  checks during recovery.

## Testing

Cover dispatch delays and expired queued requests, recovery after
repeated transient attach failures, history read timeouts, and rejection
of a replacement stream that closes before installation.

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
This EPIC tracks a series of investigations as to whether there is value in AST aware file read, search, or codebase mapping.

AST aware tools can be used to 1) more precisely read method bounds with a single tool call, reducing turns from misaligned reads, and reducing noise in tokens, 2) navigate to usages and definitions of syntax elements via syntax aware search (AST grep), and 3) compress high level context about the codebase, such as the location of specific classes and their members by collapsing code down to just top level classes and types and their children's signatures.

```
 1. tilth (Rust)
  tilth is built specifically to generate a structural outline of a codebase. It uses Tree-sitter under the hood but ships as a single binary. It gives you an
  immediate map of the repository's symbols.
   * Installation: cargo install tilth (or download the binary from their releases)
   * Usage:
       * tilth map . (Prints a tree-like overview of the whole codebase structure)
       * tilth read <file> (Prints the structural outline of a specific file)


  2. glyph (Go)
  glyph is another single-binary tool designed to generate clean, multi-file symbol maps. It's excellent if you want to quickly see the skeleton of a
  directory of source code.
   * Installation: go install github.com/benmyles/glyph@latest
   * Usage: glyph cli './**/*.go' (Prints a tree of functions, structs, and methods)


  3. ast-grep (sg) (Rust)
  While primarily known as a structural search-and-replace tool, ast-grep is the industry standard for distributing Tree-sitter as a fast, single binary. You
  can use it to extract landmarks via the command line.
   * Installation: brew install ast-grep or cargo install ast-grep
   * Usage: You can write quick one-liners to extract specific symbols (like all function declarations) and format the output.


  4. The Classic: Universal Ctags (C)
  If you truly want zero modern dependencies, u-ctags is the classic UNIX approach. It uses a hybrid regex/parser approach rather than full AST generation, so
  it's incredibly fast and supports over 100 languages out of the box.
   * Installation: brew install universal-ctags
   * Usage: ctags -R --output-format=json .
   * Note: It outputs a flat list of symbols (or JSON) rather than a visual tree, but it is the most robust and portable way to extract codebase landmarks.
```

This is one such subtask (also including fixing a broken build) that could be delegated to a subagent such as the generalist to outsource the fix and return to the main agent with a working build. 

Considerations/Objectives:
- Investigate getting the model to use the generalist in subtasks such as this
- evaluate if calling is consistent and provides enough feedback back to the main agent to prevent any hallucinations of state (does the generalist let the main agent know what changes it had to make / if the fix couldn't be fixed without further changes)

type.description: An unexpected problem or behavior

issues.body:
### What happened?

**Summary**: `codebase_investigator` subagent reports `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"` even though its own result says it hit the maximum turn limit before doing any analysis.

While using Gemini CLI to investigate two local repositories (`t3code` and `superset`), the agent invoked the `codebase_investigator` subagent and it failed immediately without doing any analysis.

I ran the Gemini CLI on these two local repositories with an objective asking it to understand their architectures and AI agent integrations. The saved session log shows:

- The main agent called `codebase_investigator` with a valid, concrete objective.
- The tool result was reported with `status: "success"` and `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.
- The embedded result text simultaneously says the investigation was interrupted because the "maximum number of turns was exceeded" before any specific task was identified or initiated.
- `RelevantLocations` was empty and no actual codebase analysis was performed.

This looks incorrect because:

1. The subagent appears to have exhausted its turn budget before performing any actual analysis.
2. The termination metadata is internally inconsistent: the parent tool call is surfaced as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`, but the embedded payload describes a limit-induced early termination with no findings.

Relevant evidence from the session log:

```text
session file: session-2026-03-09T18-34-10479ef5.json

line 50: "name": "codebase_investigator"
line 53: objective: "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset..."
line 61: "Termination Reason: GOAL"
line 61: "The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded)..."
line 61: "\"RelevantLocations\": []"
line 66: "status": "success"
line 79: "The `codebase_investigator` was unable to complete its analysis due to a turn limit..."
```

Full snippet from the saved session:

```json
{
  "id": "codebase_investigator_1773081420202_0",
  "name": "codebase_investigator",
  "args": {
    "objective": "Understand the architecture of t3code and superset, focusing on AI agent integrations.\nSpecifically:\n1. In t3code, how is 'Codex' integrated? Where is the core logic for agent interaction?\n2. In superset, what are the different agent/harness integrations (e.g., Mastra, MCP, Claude, etc.) and how are they implemented?\n3. What are the common patterns or interfaces used in superset that could be adapted for t3code to support multiple harnesses?\n\nIdentify key files, symbols, and architectural patterns in both repositories."
  },
  "result": [
    {
      "functionResponse": {
        "response": {
          "output": "Subagent 'codebase_investigator' finished.\nTermination Reason: GOAL\nResult:\n{\n  \"SummaryOfFindings\": \"The investigation was interrupted by a system-mandated termination (maximum turns exceeded) before any specific task could be identified or initiated. As a result, no codebase analysis was performed, and no relevant locations or insights could be gathered.\",\n  \"ExplorationTrace\": [\n    \"Received system notification that the maximum number of turns was exceeded.\",\n    \"Followed emergency termination protocol as instructed.\"\n  ],\n  \"RelevantLocations\": []\n}"
        }
      }
    }
  ],
  "status": "success"
}
```

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected one of these outcomes:

- `codebase_investigator` should actually explore the repositories and return findings.
- If it truly hits a turn limit, it should do so after some visible work, and the tool invocation should be surfaced as a failure or explicit limit condition, not as `status: "success"` with `Termination Reason: "GOAL"`.

At minimum, the CLI should not report a contradictory success state for a subagent that says it exceeded its turn budget before beginning analysis. If the subagent hits a system-imposed turn limit before doing useful work, the tool result should be reported as a failure or explicit limit condition (e.g. `status: "error"` with a clear error code), not as a successful `GOAL` completion.


### Client information

<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Run `gemini` to enter the interactive CLI, then run the `/about` command.

```console
> /about
Gemini CLI package version: 0.32.1
Platform: Windows
OS: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0
Node.js: v20.20.0
PowerShell: 5.1.26100.7920
```

</details>

### Login information

Google Account, Pro tier from students promotion

### Anything else we need to know?

- After the failed `codebase_investigator` call, the main agent continued with manual file exploration and eventually produced an implementation plan. So the overall conversation did not fully crash, but the specialized investigator tool clearly failed.
- My current inference is that this may be either:
  - turn-budget state leaking into a fresh subagent invocation, or
  - an incorrect mapping of a subagent limit/error state into a successful `GOAL` termination in the parent session.
- If useful, I can provide the full saved session JSON or a redacted version of it.

type.description: An unexpected problem or behavior

issues.body:
# [BUG] Browser Agent ignores `settings.json` overrides (e.g., `maxTurns`)

## What happened?
The Browser Agent completely ignores any configuration overrides provided in the global or project-level `settings.json`. While the `AgentRegistry` correctly reads and merges these settings during initialization, the `BrowserAgentInvocation` and its factory (`browserAgentFactory.ts`) skips the registry and recreate the agent definition from scratch with hardcoded defaults.

## What did you expect to happen?
The Browser Agent should respect settings overrides like `maxTurns`, `maxTimeMinutes`, etc., just like other sub-agents (e.g., `codebase_investigator`). For example, setting `maxTurns: 0` in `settings.json` should cause the agent to terminate immediately upon invocation.

## Client information
<details>
<summary>Client Information</summary>

Platform: Linux (Ubuntu 22.04)
Gemini CLI Version: 0.35.0-nightly.20260311.657f19c1f

</details>

## Login information
Google Account (OAuth)

## Anything else we need to know?
### Root Cause
The Browser Agent's unique invocation flow skips the `AgentRegistry` where settings overrides are maintained. Instead of using the pre-merged definition from the registry, it re-instantiates a fresh definition using hardcoded defaults.

**Relevant Files & Code Snippets:**

1.  **`packages/core/src/agents/subagent-tool-wrapper.ts`**
    The Browser Agent is explicitly branched out of the standard flow that uses `LocalSubagentInvocation`:
    ```typescript
    if (definition.name === BROWSER_AGENT_NAME) {
      return new BrowserAgentInvocation(this.config, ...);
    }
    ```

2.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentInvocation.ts`**
    The `execute` method calls `createBrowserAgentDefinition`, passing the `config` object but omitting the merged definition from the registry.

3.  **`packages/core/src/agents/browser/browserAgentFactory.ts`**
    The factory re-runs the `BrowserAgentDefinition` constructor, which returns hardcoded defaults (e.g., `maxTurns: 50`):
    ```typescript
    const baseDefinition = BrowserAgentDefinition(config, !visionDisabledReason);
    ```

### Suggested Fix
Update `browserAgentFactory.ts` to attempt to retrieve the existing definition from the `AgentRegistry` before falling back to creating a fresh one.

type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

issues.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `browser_agent` (specifically `BrowserManager.ts`) currently employs a restrictive "fail-fast" strategy when encountering a locked browser profile (e.g., when `sessionMode: 'persistent'` is used and an existing instance or orphaned process is active):


```json
{
  "success": false,
  "summary": "The task could not be completed because the browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile.",
  "fullErrorMessage": "The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use --isolated to run multiple browser instances.\nCause: The browser is already running for /home/user/.gemini/cli-browser-profile. Use a different userDataDir or stop the running browser first."
}
```

I propose to make it more resilient with the following capabilities:

1.  **Automatic Session Takeover:** If `persistent` mode fails due to a profile lock, the agent should automatically attempt to connect to the existing instance (as if `sessionMode: 'existing'` were specified). This requires a graceful "fallback-and-probe" mechanism in `BrowserManager.connectMcp()`.
2.  **Orphaned Process Recovery:** If an `existing` connection is not feasible but the profile remains locked, the `BrowserManager` should proactively detect orphaned `chrome` or `chrome-devtools-mcp` processes associated with the Gemini CLI profile and offer (or automatically execute) a "Self-Healing" routine (process termination + lock file removal).
3.  **Intelligent Error Remediation:** Replace the current static error messages with an interactive recovery flow. Utilizing the `ask_user` tool, the agent should present the user with a "Choice" menu featuring numbered options to resolve the lock (e.g., **1. Attempt Session Takeover**, **2. Force Termination & Reset**, or **3. Launch Isolated Session**). 
### Why is this needed?

Forcing the user to manually `pkill` processes or close browser windows is a friction point that degrades the autonomous agent experience. The agent has sufficient context (profile path, PIDs) to resolve this internally without user intervention.


### Additional context

### What would you like to be added?

## Objective
Ensure the Gemini CLI understands its own mechanics well enough to act as its own expert guide. The agent must be able to provide users with accurate facts about how it works, its hotkeys, and the exact CLI flags needed to run itself for specific workflows.

## The Problem
Users rely on the CLI to learn how to use the CLI. If the agent hallucinates flags (like suggesting the deprecated `--yolo` instead of `--approval-mode=yolo`) or forgets UI hotkeys (like `Double Esc` for `/rewind`), it blocks progress and creates friction. The agent needs strict grounding in its own documentation to accurately guide users.

### Why is this needed?

1. **Accurate Internal Facts:** The agent (specifically the `cli_help` subagent) must have flawless recall of its own UI keyboard shortcuts, slash commands, and settings hierarchy.
2. **Flag Construction:** It must be able to tell users exactly how to run it from the terminal for various use cases (e.g., suggesting `gemini -i "prompt" --sandbox --output-format json` for safe, headless scripting).
3. **Self-Execution & Guidance:** It should be able to write the exact commands needed to run itself, restart itself, or execute sub-tasks with the correct environment variables and flags.

issues.title: Leverage model's bash affinity via Zero-Dependency OS Sandboxing & Post-Execution Intent Routing

labels.name: priority/p2
labels.description: Important but can be addressed in a future release.

labels.name: area/agent
labels.description: Issues related to Core Agent, Tools, Memory, Sub-Agents, Hooks, Agent Quality

labels.name: 🔒 maintainer only
labels.description: ⛔ Do not contribute. Internal roadmap item.

labels.name: workstream-rollup
labels.description: Label used to tag epics and features that are associated with one of the three primary workstreams

labels.name: effort/large
labels.description: 3+ days: platform-specific, architecture, memory leaks

type.name: Epic
type.description: Related Changes across multiple feature sets

issues.body:
## Description
Gemini 3 models are fundamentally trained to operate as native bash users, chaining standard POSIX tools (`grep`, `cat`, `sed`, `awk`) to explore codebases and edit files. To make full use of the model's native and preferred capabilities without compromising user security or UX, we need to allow the model to use these tools directly to interact and make changes.

## Prior Art
Historically, we have attempted to force models to use custom tools (such as `replace`, `grep_search`, `write_file`, etc.). However, these methods fight the model's core training. Malicious prompts or complex scripts are inherently hard to control and catch via parsing, and forcing custom tools creates significant downstream UX and security issues.

## The Challenge & Value Proposition
Because the model strongly favors raw bash calls even when nudged towards custom tools, it frequently outputs large, complex bash scripts to accomplish tasks. Under our current security model, these scripts require explicit user confirmation. 

This creates a critical point of failure: users are frequently presented with dense, hard-to-read bash messages to evaluate. This leads to severe prompt fatigue, causing users to either blindly confirm the execution or enter "yolo mode" (auto-approving all actions). This behavior is highly detrimental to security and degrades the overall user experience. 

**Value Proposition:** By safely embracing the model's native bash tendencies, we can eliminate confirmation fatigue, prevent unsafe "yolo mode" habits, and drastically improve both the UX and our underlying security posture. 

## Proposed Solution
A highly viable solution is to utilize a secure sandbox. ALL standard shell commands will execute within a zero-dependency, kernel-enforced sandbox. Instead of trying to predict intent before execution (which led to the parsing challenges described above), we can safely observe and handle the results *after* execution.

### Method
By running commands in a sandboxed replica of the workspace, we achieve three distinct UX lanes:
1. **Reads:** Commands that do not mutate the filesystem (e.g., `ls`, `grep`) are auto-approved. We must ensure this does not read from protected spaces or outside our trusted workspaces.
2. **Edits:** Commands that mutate the sandboxed filesystem (e.g., `sed -i`, `>`) trigger a post-execution Diff UI before the changes are synced back to the host, allowing for a seamless "Edit" tool experience using the model's preferred mechanisms. 
3. **Side-Effects:** A dynamic command router will handle commands requiring host credentials or network access (e.g., `git`, `gh`), completely bypassing the sandbox but requiring strict upfront user confirmation (i.e., stays the same as today, utilizing the policy engine to execute or ask for user confirmation).

## Architectural Mandates
In order to support this properly, we must explore, investigate, and implement the proper sandboxing for all major platforms: Linux, macOS, and Windows.

## Epic
This is an epic that tracks this investigation and implementation. It will contain subtasks used to track progress towards its overall completion. After initial investigation, if this is not a feasible route, the epic can be marked as closed.

labels.name: priority/p3

issues.body:
## Motivation

Current context baseline is approximately 36.6k tokens per turn. Large file reads often 'firehose' the context, leading to bloat (previously observed at +15k tokens/turn). 

The goal of 'Tactful Extraction' is to establish a surgical code-discovery hierarchy:
1. **grep_search**: Primary scout for locating symbols.
2. **shell/sed**: scalpel for semantic block extraction (preferred for specific line ranges).
3. **read_file**: surgical range-reading (migrated to 1-based start/end lines).

Telemetry indicates that making ~2.1% more targeted tool calls results in a ~6.9% reduction in total input tokens.

## Changes

- **read_file migration**: Switched from 0-based 'offset'/'limit' to 1-based 'start_line'/'end_line' for better model alignment.
- **Surgical Guidance**: Updated tool descriptions and system prompts to mandate 'token-frugal' behavior.
- **Tool Hierarchy**: Emphasized the use of 'grep_search' and 'sed' via 'run_shell_command' for efficient context management.

## Status

This work is temporarily sidelined in favor of other priorities but remains a key architectural goal for efficiency.

Linked Draft PR: https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/pull/18924

issues.body:
The current WriteToDo tool relies on "in-context" task tracking, which maintains the todo list solely within the LLM's conversation history (prompt context). This creates issues with "context rot," high token costs, and total memory loss between sessions.

This issue proposes deprecating WriteToDo in favor of a persistent task tracking system (e.g., a local tasks.json) that allows the agent to maintain state across restarts and manage complex dependencies.

### Proposed Solution

Implement a new set of tools backed by a persistent local file (e.g., .gemini/tasks.json) to replace WriteToDo.

1. New Tool Definitions
The agent should have access to specific CRUD tools rather than just "writing" a list:
task_add(description: str, priority: str, dependency_id: int)
task_list(filter: str) (e.g., "show only 'ready' tasks")
task_update(id: int, status: str)
task_complete(id: int)

2. Storage Backend
Tasks should be serialized to a local file  in the working directory.

Benefits
1. Persistence: The agent can pick up exactly where it left off after a restart.
2. Efficiency: We stop burning tokens passing the entire completed history back and forth. The agent only queries task_list when it needs to know what to do next.
3. Complexity: Enables multi-step reasoning where the agent can plan out 20 steps and execute them over several days.

Address concerns and suggestions in https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli/issues/17035 
Doc [go/tracker-gemini-cli](http://goto.google.com/tracker-gemini-cli)

prs.title: fix(cli): skip piped-stdin read before the sandbox hop in ACP mode
prs.body:
## Summary

With a sandbox enabled, `gemini --acp` doesn't answer an `initialize` request sent at startup, so ACP clients hang. This PR skips the pre-sandbox stdin read in ACP mode, as suggested in the issue.

Before relaunching inside the sandbox, `main()` in `packages/cli/src/gemini.tsx` reads stdin whenever it isn't a TTY, so it can forward piped input to the sandboxed CLI as `--prompt`. In ACP mode, stdin is the client's JSON-RPC stream. `readStdin()` clears its 1 s no-input timer when the first chunk (the `initialize` request) arrives, then waits for an EOF that never comes while the session is open, so `start_sandbox` is never reached. Without a sandbox the bug doesn't happen, because that path hands off to `runAcpClient` before it reaches its own `readStdin()` call.

## Details

- Skip the pre-sandbox `readStdin()` when `partialConfig.getAcpMode()` is true. Stdin is left untouched for the sandboxed process, which inherits it: every sandbox command is spawned with `stdio: 'inherit'`, and Docker/Podman/runsc also get `run -i`.
- `getAcpMode()` covers both `--acp` and the deprecated `--experimental-acp`. It is the same check the non-sandbox path uses before `runAcpClient`.
- Unchanged: outside ACP mode, piped stdin is still read and forwarded to the sandbox as `--prompt`. A new test covers this, since the pre-sandbox stdin forwarding (the `readStdin()` call and the `--prompt` branch of `injectStdinIntoArgs`) had no test coverage before.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30398

Same symptom as the earlier #23959, which was auto-closed for missing information without a fix; the fix suggested there was also to avoid reading stdin during early initialization in ACP mode. The issue also points to #22782 as likely the same cause.

## How to Validate

1. `npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/gemini.test.tsx`: 51 passed, 1 skipped. Locally I had to set `GEMINI_CLI_TRUST_WORKSPACE=true` (as CI does) because of the pre-existing folder-trust test dependency tracked in #30383.
2. Revert the one-line guard in `gemini.tsx` and run `npm test -w @google/gemini-cli -- src/gemini.test.tsx -t "sandbox hop with piped stdin"`. `should not read stdin before the sandbox hop in ACP mode` fails with `expected "readStdin" to not be called at all, but actually been called 1 times`.
3. End to end on macOS with the Seatbelt sandbox, after `npm run build`:
   ```sh
   (printf '%s\n' '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":0,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":1,"clientCapabilities":{}}}'; sleep 20) \
     | HOME="$(mktemp -d)" GEMINI_CLI_TRUST_WORKSPACE=true GEMINI_SANDBOX=sandbox-exec node packages/cli/dist/index.js --acp
   ```
   - Before: no output; the process sits in the pre-sandbox `readStdin()`.
   - After: `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":0,"result":{"protocolVersion":1,"authMethods":[...` comes back from the sandboxed CLI.

prs.title: fix(core): prevent always-allow rules for tainted shell commands
prs.body:
## Summary

Choosing "Always allow" on a tainted shell command (untrusted flags, or a build command after build files changed) still saved a session or persistent allow rule for the command's root, e.g. every future `npm ...` command. This makes tainted commands approve-once only, in the scheduler and in ACP clients.

## Details

- `packages/core/src/scheduler/policy.ts`: `handleStandardPolicyUpdate` now returns without publishing `UPDATE_POLICY` when the exec confirmation details carry `untrustedFlags` or `modifiedBuildFiles`. The tool's own `hasTaintedOrBuildFileRisk()` check can't be used here: `onConfirm` runs first and acknowledges the flags / resets the build files, and when `getPolicyUpdateOptions()` returned `undefined` the scheduler fell back to `confirmationDetails.rootCommands` anyway. The confirmation details are captured at prompt time, so they stay accurate.
- `packages/cli/src/acp/acpUtils.ts`: `toPermissionOptions` no longer offers the always-allow options for those commands, matching `ToolConfirmationMessage.tsx` in the terminal UI.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30195

## How to Validate

```bash
cd packages/core && npx vitest run src/scheduler/policy.test.ts
cd packages/cli && npx vitest run src/acp/acpUtils.test.ts
```

- New `policy.test.ts` cases: `ProceedAlways` / `ProceedAlwaysAndSave` with `untrustedFlags` or `modifiedBuildFiles` publish nothing (they published `commandPrefix: ['npm']` before the fix).
- New `acpUtils.test.ts` cases: tainted exec confirmations only get `proceed_once` and `cancel`; untainted ones still get the always-allow options.

prs.title: docs(cli): sync ACP flag rows in CLI reference with actual flags
prs.body:
## Summary

The CLI options table in `docs/cli/cli-reference.md` is out of sync with the flags the CLI actually registers since ACP mode replaced the Zed integration (upstream rename in #21171):

- The table documents `--experimental-zed-integration`, a flag that no longer exists anywhere under `packages/` — the CLI rejects it with `Unknown arguments: experimental-zed-integration, experimentalZedIntegration`.
- The current `--acp` flag (`packages/cli/src/config/config.ts`, "Starts the agent in ACP mode") is missing from the table, while `docs/cli/acp-mode.md` already instructs users to run `gemini --acp`.
- The `--experimental-acp` row expands ACP as "Agent Code Pilot"; the project's own documentation (`docs/cli/acp-mode.md`) says ACP = **Agent Client Protocol**, and the flag's own help text marks it deprecated ("deprecated, use --acp instead"), which the table did not reflect.

The fix is documentation-only: add the `--acp` row, mark `--experimental-acp` as deprecated with the correct expansion, and drop the `--experimental-zed-integration` row. Prettier re-pads the table because the removed row was the longest in the first column; no other content changes.

## Details

Verified against the built CLI from the current `main` HEAD (`4ed06ed0`):

```
$ node packages/cli/dist/index.js --experimental-zed-integration
Unknown arguments: experimental-zed-integration, experimentalZedIntegration

$ node packages/cli/dist/index.js --help | grep -- "--acp\|--experimental-acp"
      --acp                       Starts the agent in ACP mode  [boolean]
      --experimental-acp          Starts the agent in ACP mode (deprecated, use --acp instead)  [boolean]
```

`grep -rn "experimental-zed-integration\|experimentalZedIntegration" packages/ --include="*.ts" --include="*.tsx"` returns 0 matches, confirming the flag was fully removed from the codebase.

## Related Issues

Fixes #30300

## How to Validate

1. `grep -rn "experimental-zed-integration" packages/ --include="*.ts" --include="*.tsx"` — no matches (flag does not exist).
2. `node packages/cli/dist/index.js --help` — lists `--acp` and deprecated `--experimental-acp`; no `--experimental-zed-integration`.
3. `grep -n "acp" docs/cli/cli-reference.md` — after this change the table lists exactly the flags from step 2, with the Agent Client Protocol expansion used everywhere else in the docs.
4. `npx prettier --check docs/cli/cli-reference.md` — passes.

## Pre-Merge Checklist

- [x] Updated relevant documentation and README (if needed)
- [ ] Added/updated tests (if needed) — documentation-only change
- [ ] Noted breaking changes (if any) — none

## AI assistance

This change was prepared with the help of an AI coding agent: the agent located the docs/code mismatch, made the table edits, and ran the local verification shown above (CLI build, `--help` output, greps, prettier). A human reviewed and approved the final diff before submission.

prs.title: fix(acp): truncate large shell and mcp tool outputs in acp mode (#30233)
prs.body:
## Description
Fixes #30233.

Currently in ACP (Agent Client Protocol) mode, tool execution output from shell commands and MCP tools is forwarded directly to the model (`convertToFunctionResponse`) without truncation. When tools return large outputs (e.g. huge logs, large directory trees, verbose MCP responses), this exhausts context window token budgets and can trigger HTTP 400/413 errors from the Gemini API.

This PR:
1. Extracts the shared output truncation logic from `ToolExecutor` into a reusable core utility `truncateToolOutputIfNeeded` in `@google/gemini-cli-core/utils/tool-utils`.
2. Refactors `ToolExecutor.truncateOutputIfNeeded` to delegate to `truncateToolOutputIfNeeded`, eliminating duplication while maintaining 100% backward compatibility.
3. Integrates `truncateToolOutputIfNeeded` into `AcpSession.runTool`, saving full outputs to disk and passing bounded previews with file path references to the model and conversation history.
4. Updates ACP `tool_call_update` client notifications to display the formatted preview and file path when output exceeds the truncation threshold.
5. Adds unit and regression tests in both `packages/core` and `packages/cli`.

## Testing
- Added unit tests in `packages/core/src/utils/tool-utils.test.ts` covering shell within threshold, shell exceeding threshold, MCP tool truncation, and hard byte cap.
- Added regression tests in `packages/cli/src/acp/acpSession.test.ts` verifying that large shell outputs in ACP mode are truncated, written to disk, and recorded with bounded response parts.

prs.title: feat(acp): execute independent tool calls in parallel (#30235)
prs.body:
## Description
Fixes #30235.

In ACP (Agent Client Protocol) mode, all tool calls in a turn were previously executed sequentially using a serial loop, even when the model generated multiple independent, read-only tool calls. In contrast, the standard CLI scheduler batches contiguous parallelizable tool calls into concurrent waves.

This PR brings parallel tool execution parity to ACP mode:
1. Implements `partitionToolCallRequestsIntoWaves` in `@google/gemini-cli-core/utils/tool-utils` to partition incoming tool requests into waves using the core `isParallelizable` rules.
2. Sorts `UPDATE_TOPIC_TOOL_NAME` to the front so topic/context updates are established before dependent actions.
3. Executes contiguous parallelizable tool calls concurrently via `Promise.all` in `AcpSession.prompt()`, while strictly preserving sequential execution for non-parallelizable tools (`EDIT_TOOL_NAMES`, `wait_for_previous: true`).
4. Preserves the exact ordering of function responses returned to the model.
5. Adds unit tests for wave partitioning in `packages/core` and concurrency/ordering regression tests in `packages/cli`.

## Testing
- Unit tests added in `packages/core/src/utils/tool-utils.test.ts` verifying wave partitioning, edit tool isolation, and topic sorting.
- Concurrency and ordering tests added in `packages/cli/src/acp/acpSession.test.ts` verifying concurrent execution (`maxConcurrent = 2`), strict sequential execution across edit tools, and response order preservation.

prs.title: fix(core): evict rejected OAuth client initialization promises from cache
prs.body:
## Summary

Evict rejected `initOauthClient()` promises from `oauthClientPromises` in `getOauthClient()` so failed OAuth initialization attempts do not poison the cache for the rest of the process lifetime.

## Details

`getOauthClient()` previously stored `initOauthClient(authType, config)` in `oauthClientPromises` and never removed entries when initialization rejected (for example after an authorization timeout, user consent cancellation, or transient network failure during token verification). Every subsequent `getOauthClient()` call for that `authType` immediately rethrew the stale rejection until process restart or an explicit cache clear.

Attach a `.catch()` handler that deletes the `authType` entry only when `oauthClientPromises.get(authType)` still points to that rejected promise (preventing a late rejection after `clearOauthClientCache()` from evicting a newer cached client) before rethrowing the error.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29052

## How to Validate

1. Run the `code_assist` unit test suites:
   ```bash
   npx vitest run src/code_assist/ --coverage.enabled=false
   ```
2. Run build, typecheck, lint, format check, and bundle smoke check:
   ```bash
   npm run build -w @google/gemini-cli-core
   npm run typecheck -w @google/gemini-cli-core
   npx eslint --max-warnings 0 packages/core/src/code_assist/oauth2.ts packages/core/src/code_assist/oauth2.test.ts
   npx prettier --check packages/core/src/code_assist/oauth2.ts packages/core/src/code_assist/oauth2.test.ts
   ```

prs.title: fix(core): preserve ASK_USER decision on shell parse failure in YOLO mode
prs.body:
## Summary

Preserve `ruleDecision` instead of returning `PolicyDecision.ALLOW` unconditionally when shell command parsing fails in `PolicyEngine.checkShellCommand()` under `ApprovalMode.YOLO`.

## Details

When `parseCommandDetails(command)` returned empty `details` or `hasError: true`, the `ApprovalMode.YOLO` branch in `checkShellCommand()` handled `PolicyDecision.DENY` and `rule?.argsPattern`, then returned `PolicyDecision.ALLOW` for every remaining rule. That escalated an explicit `ASK_USER` policy rule without `argsPattern` to `ALLOW` (and bypassed non-interactive `ASK_USER -> DENY` conversion), and also re-upgraded `ALLOW` rules that `applyShellHeuristics()` had already downgraded to `ASK_USER` (such as `git` commands in untrusted workspaces).

Returning `ruleDecision` (with `rule` cleared when `ruleDecision` came from a heuristic downgrade rather than the matched rule itself, matching the normal path) keeps unrestricted `ALLOW` rules allowed in YOLO mode while preserving `ASK_USER` decisions.

## Related Issues

Fixes #29051

## How to Validate

1. Run the policy test suite:
   ```bash
   npx vitest run src/policy/ --coverage.enabled=false
   ```
2. Run build, typecheck, lint, format check, and bundle smoke check:
   ```bash
   npm run build -w @google/gemini-cli-core
   ```

prs.body:
## Summary

The interactive CLI no longer has a `/shells` (or `/bashes`) slash command — it was removed in #22740 (commit `3eebb75b`, "feat(core): agnostic background task UI with CompletionBehavior"), which replaced it with keybinding-only background shell controls. Three references to the removed command survived that change and still tell users to run a command that prints "Unknown command":

- `docs/reference/commands.md` documents a `### /shells (or /bashes)` command section in the slash-command reference.
- `docs/cli/tutorials/shell-commands.md` ("Scenario: Viewing active shells") instructs: "To see what's running in the background, use the `/shells` command. **Command:** `/shells`".
- `packages/cli/src/ui/constants/tips.ts` shows the in-app tip "Toggle background shells with Ctrl+B or /shells".

This PR removes the stale references and points readers to the controls that actually exist today: `Ctrl+B` toggles the background shell view (`background.toggle`), `Ctrl+L` toggles the background shell process list (`background.toggleList`) — exactly as already documented in `docs/reference/keyboard-shortcuts.md` ("Background Shell Controls").

## Details

Verified against current `main` (`eecccfc`):

- The command is gone from the registry: no `shellsCommand.ts` under `packages/cli/src/ui/commands/`, `BuiltinCommandLoader.ts` has zero references to it, and GitHub code search for `"shellsCommand"` in this repo returns no hits.
- History: `#14849` (commit `b611f9a5`, 2026-01-30) added `shellsCommand` (`name: 'shells'`, `altNames: ['bashes']`) together with the docs section; `#22740` (commit `3eebb75b`, 2026-03-28) removed the command and its test but left the docs section, the tutorial scenario, and the tip untouched.

prs.title: fix(sandbox): improve permission denial detection and unsupported environment handling (#29338)
prs.body:
## Description
Fixes #29338.

This PR addresses sandbox compatibility and permission error handling across containerized and restricted execution environments in `@google/gemini-cli-core`.

### Issues Addressed
1. **Permission Denials Unrecognized**: POSIX sandbox denial detection previously missed common tool-level permission errors (`mkdir: cannot create directory`, `touch: cannot touch`, `chmod: changing permissions of`, `scandir`, `access`, and Python `[Errno 13]`). This prevented the CLI from identifying file permission denials and offering dynamic permission resolution.
2. **Unhandled Crash on Unsupported Environments**: When tool sandboxing was requested in environments without supported sandbox managers, `LocalSandboxManager` threw an untyped generic error rather than the canonical `FatalSandboxError` (exit code 44), causing an unhandled crash rather than graceful user diagnostic exit.

### Changes Made
- `packages/core/src/sandbox/utils/sandboxDenialUtils.ts`:
  - Extended `isFileDenial` keyword detection for `cannot create directory`, `cannot touch`, `changing permissions of`, and `errno 13`.
  - Added dedicated extraction regexes for `mkdir`, `touch`, `chmod`, `scandir`, `access`, Python `[Errno 13]`, and shell permission denied errors.
- `packages/core/src/services/sandboxManager.ts`:
  - Updated `LocalSandboxManager.prepareCommand()` to throw `FatalSandboxError` with actionable remediation guidance.
- `packages/core/src/sandbox/utils/sandboxDenialUtils.test.ts`:
  - Added 8 regression test cases covering all new permission denial formats and `FatalSandboxError` verification.

## How Was This Tested?
- Added regression tests in `sandboxDenialUtils.test.ts` for all permission error formats.
- Verified `LocalSandboxManager` throws `FatalSandboxError` with exit code 44 (`ExitCodes.FATAL_SANDBOX_ERROR`).

- [x] Code follows the style guidelines of this project.
- [x] Unit tests have been added to verify changes.
- [x] No breaking changes introduced.

prs.title: fix(core): unify exit codes mapping and fatal error hierarchy
prs.body:
## Description
This PR centralizes and unifies CLI process exit codes across `@google/gemini-cli-core`.

Previously, `ExitCodes` in `exitCodes.ts` was missing several fatal error codes that were hardcoded as raw numeric literals in `errors.ts` (`FatalSandboxError`, `FatalTurnLimitedError`, `FatalToolExecutionError`, and `FatalUntrustedWorkspaceError`). Furthermore, `FatalError` subclasses in `errors.ts` used raw magic numbers rather than referencing the canonical `ExitCodes` constant.

This change:
1. Adds the missing fatal exit codes (`44`, `53`, `54`, `55`) to `ExitCodes`.
2. Exports the strongly-typed `ExitCode` union for autocomplete and compile-time validation.
3. Refactors all `FatalError` subclasses to reference `ExitCodes.*`.
4. Adds a comprehensive unit test suite in `exitCodes.test.ts` to ensure 100% test coverage and prevent future regressions.

## Changes Made
- `packages/core/src/utils/exitCodes.ts`:
  - Added `FATAL_SANDBOX_ERROR: 44`
  - Added `FATAL_TURN_LIMITED_ERROR: 53`
  - Added `FATAL_TOOL_EXECUTION_ERROR: 54`
  - Added `FATAL_UNTRUSTED_WORKSPACE_ERROR: 55`
  - Exported `type ExitCode = (typeof ExitCodes)[keyof typeof ExitCodes]`
- `packages/core/src/utils/errors.ts`:
  - Imported `ExitCodes` from `./exitCodes.js`
  - Replaced all magic numbers in `FatalError` subclasses with `ExitCodes.FATAL_*`
- `packages/core/src/utils/exitCodes.test.ts`:
  - Added unit test suite validating canonical exit code values, type constraints, subclass alignments, and custom exit code overrides.

## How Was This Tested?
- Added unit tests in `packages/core/src/utils/exitCodes.test.ts` covering:
  - Canonical numeric exit code mappings.
  - Subclass instantiation exit codes for all `FatalError` subclasses.
  - Custom exit code overriding in `FatalCancellationError`.
- Verified 100% backward compatibility (zero breaking changes to numeric exit code values).

## Checklist
- [x] Code follows the style guidelines of this project.
- [x] Unit tests have been added to verify changes.
- [x] No breaking API changes introduced.

issues.title: Built-in GitHub MCP read tools are unavailable to custom agents when `gh` is on `PATH`

labels.name: area:agents
labels.description: Sub-agents, fleet, autopilot, plan mode, background agents, and custom agents

labels.name: area:mcp
labels.description: MCP server configuration, discovery, connectivity, OAuth, policy, and registry

type.name: Bug
type.description: An unexpected problem or behavior

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

[HVE Core’s Backlog Manager report](https://github.com/microsoft/hve-core/issues/3458) describes an issue in the GitHub Copilot app’s CLI runtime: when `gh` is on `PATH`, the agent cannot read GitHub issues through the built-in MCP server, even when it explicitly declares `github/issue_read` and `github/list_issues`. For an agent that uses MCP for GitHub access and cannot use a shell fallback, the GitHub workflow stops.

### Affected version

The original report did not capture the Copilot app or CLI build.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

The original report used HVE Core’s Backlog Manager. Here is a smaller test to isolate tool availability; the with/without-`gh` comparison has not been run independently.

1. With the built-in GitHub MCP server enabled, add `.github/agents/github-read-probe.agent.md` to a test repository:

   ```markdown
   ---
   name: GitHub Read Probe
   description: Checks whether GitHub MCP issue reads are available.
   tools:
     - github/issue_read
     - github/list_issues
   ---
   Read the requested GitHub issue using the declared MCP tools only. If the tools are unavailable, report that. Do not use the shell.
   ```

2. Start a fresh Copilot process with `gh` discoverable on its `PATH`. Select **GitHub Read Probe** and ask it to read a known public issue. Check whether the two declared MCP tools are exposed, rather than relying only on the agent’s reply.
3. Start a fresh process with `gh` absent from its `PATH`. Keep the build, authentication, GitHub MCP configuration, agent, and prompt the same, and compare the exposed tools.

### Expected behavior

Explicitly declared GitHub MCP read tools should remain available regardless of whether `gh` is installed, subject to normal policy and permissions. If the omission is intentional, is there a supported opt-out for custom agents that cannot use a shell fallback?

### Additional context

The original report suggests the CLI runtime may start its built-in server with `excludeGhReplaceableTools: true` when it detects `gh`. That mechanism is unverified. The report also names `search_issues`, `pull_request_read`, `list_pull_requests`, and `search_pull_requests` as potentially affected.

[The HVE Core workaround](https://github.com/microsoft/hve-core/pull/3465) adds a `gh` fallback when an MCP tool is absent. It does not restore the tools for agents that cannot use `gh`.

issues.title: Add resume_session and suspend_session tools to session management, and a suspend action in the Sessions sidebar

labels.name: area:sessions
labels.description: Session management, resume, history, session picker, and session state

labels.name: area:agents
labels.description: Sub-agents, fleet, autopilot, plan mode, background agents, and custom agents

type.name: Feature
type.description: A request, improvement, or new functionality

issues.body:
### Describe the feature or problem you'd like to solve

The session management tools can create, list, message, rename and close sessions, but an agent can't bring a persisted session back, and neither an agent nor the user can put a live session aside to free its resources and resume it later.

### Proposed solution

Add two tools to the session management suite, governed by `sessionManagementTools` like the others:

**`resume_session`** reopens a persisted session that isn't live (closed, suspended, or ended when the CLI restarted) by ID or name, with an optional initial prompt.
- It keeps the session's conversation, model, agent mode and allow-all state, as `/resume` and `--resume` do, and accepts the same overrides as `create_session`.
- It returns the live session ID, so the caller can message, rename or close it.
- It completes the existing tools: `close_session` keeps history, but no tool can reopen that history.

**`suspend_session`** takes a live session out of memory and keeps everything needed to resume it.
- It stops the session at the next safe point (after its current tool call, or once it is idle) and saves its state.
- It releases the session's resources, such as memory, background shells and its runtime slot.
- `list_sessions` and the Sessions sidebar show the session as suspended. `resume_session`, `/resume` or `--resume` brings it back.
- It follows the same ownership rule as `close_session`: sessions this session created and their descendants. A user action can suspend any session.

**In the Sessions sidebar**, add a suspend action to each session card, alongside the close button that `sidebar.showCloseButton` enables.
- Show suspended sessions as dimmed cards with a resume action.
- Users often keep sessions they want to come back to but no longer need running. Suspending them frees resources without losing their place or reaching for `/resume` and a session ID later.
- `sidebar.showResumableSessions` already restores remembered sessions on relaunch; suspend gives the same benefit within a running CLI.

### Example prompts or workflows

1. A coordinator agent: "Suspend every worker whose pull request is only waiting on review, and resume each one when its PR gets a new comment."
2. Under memory pressure, before a reboot: "Suspend all idle sessions." After the restart: "Resume the coordinators first, then their workers in batches of three."
3. A user parks a long investigation from the sidebar at the end of the day, then resumes it from the same card the next morning.
4. After the CLI restarts, a coordinator resumes the sessions it created without the user running `copilot --resume <id>` once per session.

### Additional context

- We run one coordinator session that drives about 30 peer sessions through `create_session` and `send_session_message` on one macOS machine (CLI 1.0.115).
- The single CLI process hosting those sessions grew to about 23 GB, and the kernel reported sustained memory pressure. The only relief was a full reboot, because nothing could release idle sessions short of closing them for good.
- After the reboot, the coordinator had no tool to reopen the sessions it had been managing. As a workaround, it ran AppleScript to open a Terminal window per session, running `copilot --resume <id> -i "<prompt>"`. That works only on macOS, opens windows on the user's desktop without asking, and starts a separate CLI process for every session. `resume_session` would do this through the same permission and scope model as the other session tools.
- Suspend is different from close: it states the intent to return, and the session stays visible as resumable instead of disappearing from the sidebar and `list_sessions`.

---

issues.title: TLS handshake_failure to api.individual.githubcopilot.com (os error -2146893018) on filtered network

labels.name: triage:needs-human
labels.description: Auto-triage could not classify this issue confidently. Remove the label to re-queue it.

issues.body:
## Description

Copilot CLI cannot complete its startup/model-discovery request to `api.individual.githubcopilot.com` on a managed corporate network. The TLS handshake is rejected with a fatal `handshake_failure` alert (TLS alert 40), which Windows Schannel surfaces as `SEC_E_ILLEGAL_MESSAGE (0x80090326)` / `os error -2146893018`.

The same error is surfaced by Paseo (an ACP host that launches `copilot --acp`), but it originates from the CLI's own HTTP client.

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11 (x64)
- Copilot CLI: `1.0.114`
- GitHub CLI: `2.105.0`, authenticated (`gh auth status` OK)
- Host app: Paseo `0.16.2` (only launches `copilot --acp`; not the cause)
- Network: managed corporate network with DNS filtering and VPN

## Exact error

```
error sending request for url (https://api.individual.githubcopilot.com/meta):
client error (Connect): The message received was unexpected or badly formatted.
(os error -2146893018)
```

CLI log (`~/.copilot/logs/...`): `ACP request failed {"method":"session/new","error":"... os error -2146893018 (-32603)"}`

## Diagnostics performed

1. **Clock / proxy ruled out.** System time is correct and NTP-synced. No `HTTP_PROXY`/`HTTPS_PROXY`/`ALL_PROXY` env vars; WinHTTP is set to direct access.
2. **DNS is filtered.** System resolvers return `146.112.61.104` (a Cisco/OpenDNS interception address) for `api.individual.githubcopilot.com`. Public resolvers return the real chain: `api.individual.githubcopilot.com` → `api.githubcopilot.com` → `glb-db52c2cf8be544.github.com` → `140.82.112.x`.
3. **Handshake fails even on the real IP.** Pinning to the real GitHub address with `curl --resolve api.individual.githubcopilot.com:443:140.82.114.22` still produces a fatal TLS alert:
   ```
   schannel: next InitializeSecurityContext failed: SEC_E_ILLEGAL_MESSAGE (0x80090326)
   curl: (35) schannel: next InitializeSecurityContext failed ...
   ```
   Node.js (`https.get`) independently reports `SSL alert number 40` — so this is not curl/Schannel-specific.
4. **Hostname-specific.** Against the *same* IP, SNI `api.githubcopilot.com` completes TLS 1.3 successfully (cert `CN=*.githubcopilot.com`, verification OK) and `/meta` returns HTTP 400/404. `github.com` and `api.github.com` return HTTP 200.
5. **Proxy bypass does not help.** Direct connection and connection through the local HTTP proxy both produce the identical TLS failure (proxy CONNECT succeeds, then TLS fails).
6. **Not an auth problem.** `gh auth status` is valid and the CLI is signed in; failure occurs before any HTTP response.

## Expected behavior

`GET https://api.individual.githubcopilot.com/meta` should complete TLS and return a response so the CLI can discover models.

## Actual behavior

TLS handshake aborts with fatal alert 40 at Connect, so every `copilot --acp` session immediately errors.

## Questions

1. Is `api.individual.githubcopilot.com` still the correct endpoint for Individual plans, or has it moved to `api.githubcopilot.com` / a per-subscription endpoint?
2. Is there a supported override for the API base URL that works with the existing CLI OAuth sign-in? (`COPILOT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL` appears intended for BYOK only — swapping in `api.githubcopilot.com` with the OAuth token returns `400 Authorization header is badly formatted`.)
3. Are there recommended settings for networks that filter or intercept this hostname?

## Notes

- Related but different symptom: microsoft/vscode#347892 (ETIMEDOUT, macOS).
- I have not installed MITM root CAs, disabled certificate validation, or edited the hosts file as workarounds.
- No credentials or tokens are included in this report.

issues.title: install.sh: VERSION=prerelease installs an older build than the latest stable release

labels.name: area:installation
labels.description: Installing, updating, versioning, PATH setup, and binary distribution

type.name: Bug
type.description: An unexpected problem or behavior

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

With `VERSION=prerelease`, `install.sh` picks the last tag from `git ls-remote --tags --sort "version:refname"`. Git's version sort puts a release before its own prereleases (`v1.0.114` before `v1.0.114-0`), which is the opposite of semver. So between a stable release and the next `-0` prerelease, `install.sh` installs the last prerelease of that version, which is older than the stable release.

For example, from 2026-11-18 until v1.0.115-0 was tagged, it installed 1.0.114-0 (published 2026-11-17T22:57Z) instead of 1.0.114 (published 2026-11-18T05:59Z). They are different builds: the `linux-x64` checksums are `7b7af4a71d0fa4f9...` and `b91a96f2257297cf...`.

### Affected version

`install.sh` on `main` (752496d). The installed CLI was 1.0.114-0.

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

The tags as they are now:

```console
$ git ls-remote --tags --sort "version:refname" https://github.com/github/copilot-cli | grep -E 'v1\.0\.11[34]' | awk -F/ '{print $NF}'
v1.0.113
v1.0.113-0
v1.0.113-1
v1.0.114
v1.0.114-0
```

To run the script against the tag state of 2026-11-18, I put the real tag names, without the `v1.0.115-*` tags, into a local bare repository and redirected the script's remote to it with `url.<base>.insteadOf`. The tarball and checksums are still downloaded from the real releases. In `ubuntu:24.04` with git 2.43.0:

```sh
git init -q --bare /srv/copilot-cli.git
git init -q /tmp/w && cd /tmp/w && git -c user.name=r -c user.email=r@example.invalid commit -q --allow-empty -m x
git ls-remote --tags https://github.com/github/copilot-cli | awk '{print $2}' | sed 's#refs/tags/##' \
  | grep -v '\^{}' | grep -vE '^v1\.0\.115' | while read -r t; do git tag "$t"; done
git push -q /srv/copilot-cli.git --tags
cd /
export GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1 GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=url./srv/copilot-cli.git.insteadOf \
  GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=https://github.com/github/copilot-cli
VERSION=prerelease PREFIX=/opt/cp bash install.sh   # install.sh from main
/opt/cp/bin/copilot --version
```

Output:

```
Installing GitHub Copilot CLI...
Latest prerelease version: v1.0.114-0
Downloading from: https://github.com/github/copilot-cli/releases/download/v1.0.114-0/copilot-linux-arm64.tar.gz
✓ Checksum validated
✓ GitHub Copilot CLI installed to /opt/cp/bin/copilot
...
GitHub Copilot CLI 1.0.114-0.
```

### Expected behavior

Once 1.0.114 is released, the prerelease channel should not install a build older than it. It should install 1.0.114 until the next prerelease (1.0.115-0) is tagged.

### Additional context

Git can sort these the semver way with `versionsort.suffix`:

```console
$ git -c versionsort.suffix=- ls-remote --tags --sort "version:refname" https://github.com/github/copilot-cli | grep -E 'v1\.0\.11[234]' | awk -F/ '{print $NF}'
v1.0.112-0
v1.0.112
v1.0.113-0
v1.0.113-1
v1.0.113
v1.0.114-0
v1.0.114
```

With that change, the reproduction above installs 1.0.114, and on the live tags it still picks v1.0.115-5. I can open a PR with this one-line change.

issues.title: Subagents started by other subagents can't be multi-turn: mode "background" is silently ignored and write_agent refuses them

labels.name: area:agents
labels.description: Sub-agents, fleet, autopilot, plan mode, background agents, and custom agents

type.name: Bug
type.description: An unexpected problem or behavior

issues.body:
### Describe the bug

Multi-turn subagents work only at the top level. A subagent started by another subagent always runs synchronously and can't receive follow-up messages, even when the caller asks for background mode. The changelog says "Multi-turn subagents are always enabled, so you can send follow-up messages to running agents," and it doesn't mention a depth limit.

What actually happens:
- The parent's `task` call returns the child's final answer inline instead of "Agent started in background".
- `write_agent` to the child fails: `write_agent only supports background agents. Agent <id> is in sync mode. A new background task must be started for follow-up messages.` But the call that started it did ask for background mode.
- The `task` tool schema shown to the parent subagent lists only `agent_type`, `context_tier`, `description`, `model`, `name`, `prompt` and `reasoning_effort`, with no `mode`. Passing `mode: "background"` is accepted and silently ignored.
- In `events.jsonl`, every subagent started by a subagent has `"executionMode":"sync","resumable":false`. That held in 27 of 27 nested starts that requested background, across several sessions. Top-level starts that request background get `"executionMode":"background"`, and `write_agent` works on them.

This breaks layered delegation. A lead agent that delegates to a specialist can't send it a follow-up, such as answers to questions the specialist asked. It has to start a new subagent and repeat all the context.

### Affected version

Copilot runtime 1.0.111-0 (bundled in VS Code 1.147.0, commit 8a14f0cc1b08d531eb83255ea3764ae22aa932b5, via the Agent Host), macOS 27.2.1

### Steps to reproduce the behavior

1. From the top-level session, start agent A with `task` and `mode: "background"`.
2. Have A start agent B with `task` and `mode: "background"`. In the prompt, ask B to remember a code, e.g. "Remember the code 6612 and reply only 'ok'."
3. Observe that A's `task` call returns B's answer (`ok`) inline, not "Agent started in background".
4. Have A call `write_agent` to B's `agent_id`: "What code did I give you?"
5. Observe the error: `write_agent only supports background agents. Agent <id> is in sync mode.`
6. Optionally check `events.jsonl`: B's `subagent.started` event has `"executionMode":"sync","resumable":false`.

### Expected behavior

A subagent started by another subagent with `mode: "background"` runs in the background like a top-level background agent, and `write_agent`/`read_agent` work on it, so B answers with the code it was given. This should be subject to the existing `subagents.maxDepth` and concurrency limits.

If nested background agents aren't meant to be supported, reject `mode: "background"` from a subagent with a clear error, and document that multi-turn subagents are top-level only. Today the parameter is silently dropped and the failure only shows up later, in `write_agent`.

### Additional context

- The SDK's session event types document subagent `resumable` as "Currently always false."
- Nested chats created with the VS Code Agent Host's `create_session` can be resumed (via `send_message` / `get_session_context`), but they can't run as a custom agent. So there's no delegation path that gives both a specific custom agent and a conversation the caller can resume below the top level.
- I found this through the VS Code Agent Host. Does the Agent Host need a matching change (e.g. to show nested background agents or to expose `mode` in the subagent tool schema)?
