prs.title: fix(engine): compact diagnostic late-usage receipts at the ledger bound (#6842)
prs.body:
## What and why

The `.late-usage/<id>.json` ledger keeps a 1 MiB bound and refused the whole write when adding a record would cross it. Diagnostic-only receipts — the route-decision evidence written by `persist_late_decision_receipt` — carry no spend, but they count toward that bound and can fill it on their own.

This makes the write compact instead of refusing: when a candidate would exceed 1 MiB, drop the oldest diagnostic-only records until it fits, and keep every spend-bearing record (settled or unresolved) unchanged. Replay still dedupes by `source_fingerprint`, so no spend is forgotten or double-counted.

## Where this came from

Refs #6842. This is the sidecar half of the issue; bounding the unordered replay index (`usage_source_fingerprints`) and the retained journal archive policy remain open there.

## How I tested it

- `cargo test -p codewhale-engine --lib oversized_ledger_compacts_diagnostic_receipts_before_failing` — 1 passed (the new fixture builds a ledger over 1 MiB with diagnostic + spend records; after the write, all spend records survive, the diagnostic count shrinks, and the file is within the bound)
- The existing bound tests still pass: a ledger made only of spend-bearing records still returns `InvalidData` rather than silently truncating a receipt.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — passed
- The `Behaviour:` line is in the commit body; `scripts/check-behaviour-line.py` arrives with #7445 and is not on this branch yet.

prs.title: test(tui): guard all four paste-burst chunk-flush sites
prs.body:
﻿## What and why

This closes the gap I flagged in #7403 and in #7422's review thread: the suite catches chunking stopping entirely, but not a *single* chunk check going away.

oversized_raw_and_bracketed_pastes_preserve_every_char_and_newline drives a mixed payload, and mixed is exactly what hides the problem — each CJK or emoji character re-enters the separate !c.is_ascii() branch in handle_paste_burst_key, whose own 	ake_chunk_if_full() flushes the same buffer. Delete the ASCII-path check and that test stays green.

Two new fixtures, one per append path, both with the same 60% progress probe:

- `ascii_only_raw_paste_over_the_chunk_cap_lands_complete` — pure ASCII, no newline, so every character takes on_plain_char → handle_paste_burst_decision and nothing else.
- `cjk_only_raw_paste_over_the_chunk_cap_lands_complete` — CJK plus an astral-plane emoji, no newline, so every character stays in the !c.is_ascii() branch.

No newline in either: an Enter reaches ppend_newline_if_active, whose own chunk check would flush the buffer and stand in for the path under test.

## Where this came from

Refs #7403

## How I tested it

Mutation matrix on a scratch copy. M = that fixture fails and catches the regression; every injection reverted afterwards.

| injected regression | ascii_only | cjk_only | mixed |
|---|---|---|---|
| ASCII-path 	ake_chunk_if_full removed | **M** | — | — |
| non-ASCII-path 	ake_chunk_if_full removed | — | **M** | — |
| push_bounded drop rule restored (#7403 itself) | — | **M** | **M** |
| 	ake_chunk_if_full always returns None | — | — | **M** |

The probe messages are the evidence: `the composer holds 0 of 273000 bytes` for the ASCII path, `3 of 342000` for the non-ASCII one.

**Why scii_only does not catch the original drop rule** — this is arithmetic, not a hole. Its bytes are one UTF-8 byte wide, so the buffer fills to exactly the cap every cycle and a `len + ch.len_utf8() <= cap` guard always admits the character: injecting the rule loses 0 bytes there. The CJK fixture is 3–4 bytes wide, so the buffer stops short of the cap, the crossing character is rejected, and the tail is lost. Both facts are written into the test docs so nobody later reads scii_only as coverage it does not have.

**Deliberately not covered:** the third 	ake_chunk_if_full, after ppend_newline_if_active. It fires only when a pasted newline pushes the buffer past the cap, and the next plain character flushes the same buffer one keystroke later — deleting it leaves the text complete (verified: all three tests green). It bounds peak memory, not correctness, so no content assertion can observe it. Noted in  eed_raw_paste's doc comment rather than faked with an assertion that cannot fail.

```
cargo fmt --all -- --check
  -> clean

cargo test -p codewhale-tui --lib paste -- --skip credential_paste_content
  -> test result: ok. 62 passed; 0 failed
```

- [x] cargo fmt --all passes, and tests cover the behavior
- [ ] Tests only, so no docs/features.toml row

prs.title: perf(engine): cache the item index across processes
prs.body:
## What and why

The first thread a process opens pays a pass over the whole items directory: an item's filename carries only its item id, never its turn, so the only way to learn which items a turn owns is to open the item records. The in-memory index made that a one-time cost per process, and the server already warms it at startup — but nothing about the answer outlived the process, so a restarted engine (or any other client process) paid it again. Against a 55,572-item store that is the entire open time of the first conversation.

The index is now cached beside the directories it describes (`item-index.json` at the store root) and rebuilt from a directory listing plus only the entries the cache does not hold. The listing decides membership, so the cache cannot make an answer wrong: an entry that names a deleted item is simply not consulted, and a missing, unreadable or out-of-date file costs one full read — exactly what every process used to pay.

Measured on the same 55,572-item store, first index build in a process:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| before | 3.9s |
| after | 93ms |

Three deliberate choices:

- **Reading never writes.** Caching is `RuntimeThreadStore::cache_item_index`, called only by the startup warm-up. A `GET` that created a file would break what those routes promise, and the existing tests that snapshot a store to prove a route is read-only cover it.
- **The cache is not fsynced.** Losing it to a crash costs the next process one full read, which is the state every process was in before it existed. The write is a rename over a per-process temporary, so a reader never sees a partial file.
- **The cold pass no longer materializes records.** Deserializing into a one-field reference instead of `TurnItemRecord` avoids allocating a tool result's `detail` and `metadata` to learn an id.

## Where this came from

A bug fix with no issue: reopening a long conversation after a restart sat on the previous conversation for seconds, with the delay growing with the store. Diagnosis and measurements are in the commit message.

## How I tested it

```
cargo fmt --all --check                                   # clean
cargo clippy -p codewhale-engine --lib                    # no new warnings
cargo test -p codewhale-engine --lib -- runtime_threads::tests
                                                          # 346 passed
cargo test -p codewhale-app-server --lib -- \
  thread_summary_search_does_not_scan_the_whole_store_per_thread \
  thread_summary_listing_never_walks_the_items_directory \
  turn_operation_lookup_is_authenticated_read_only_and_survives_restart
                                                          # 3 passed
```

New tests cover the cache surviving a process, learning items written while it was closed, forgetting a deleted item, falling back from a damaged or foreign-version file, a read-only handle never writing, and — the invariant above — a read leaving the store byte-identical.

One pre-existing failure, unrelated: `runtime_threads::tests::engine_withdrawal_retires_approval_and_unblocks_queued_events` is flaky on `main` (it fails 2 of 3 runs there and 1 of 3 here; it passes when run alone). The same module needs `RUST_MIN_STACK` raised in a debug build for two other cases to fit, also on `main`.

## Checklist

- [x] One focused change, started from current `main`
- [x] `cargo fmt --all` passes, and tests cover new or changed behavior
- [x] No user-facing docs or `docs/features.toml` row: this changes how fast a thread opens, not what it does

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

Automations whose delivery is `{"mode":"announce","target":"owner"}` never deliver over Nostr when the runner's fallback announce does the sending. The owner target resolves to the session-route form `nostr:<hex>`. The Nostr outbound `sendText` passes that string unchanged to `normalizePubkey`, which throws `Pubkey must be 64 hex characters or npub format`.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Configure the Nostr channel with `dmPolicy: "allowlist"` and the owner's npub in `channels.nostr.allowFrom`.
2. Set up an automation whose delivery is `{"mode":"announce","target":"owner"}`. We observed this on the `heartbeat-<agent>` automations, which have exactly this delivery.
3. Let it run to completion without the agent sending anything through the message tool, so the runner's fallback announce delivers the result.
4. Run `openclaw cron runs --id <job-id> --json` and `openclaw cron show <job-id>`.

### Expected behavior

The owner receives the announce as a Nostr DM.

For comparison:
- The same job with an explicit target (`openclaw cron edit <job-id> --clear-delivery-target --channel nostr --to <owner-npub>`) resolves `to` to the bare hex pubkey, and its fallback announce is delivered. `cron show` then prints `announce -> nostr:<owner-hex>`. After we switched the affected jobs this way, 3 of 3 fallback announces were delivered, each with `fallbackUsed: true`, `delivered: true` and `resolved.to: "<owner-hex>"`.
- Message-tool sends to the same owner are delivered.

### Actual behavior

Every fallback announce fails before anything is published, and the run itself still reports `status: ok`.

- Run record: `delivery.resolved.to` is `"nostr:<owner-hex>"`, with `fallbackUsed: true`, `delivered: false` and `deliveryError: "Pubkey must be 64 hex characters or npub format"`.
- `openclaw cron show <job-id>` prints `delivery: announce -> nostr:nostr:<owner-hex>` and `last delivery error: Pubkey must be 64 hex characters or npub format`.
- Each run writes two lines to the gateway log: a `[delivery-recovery] … send_attempt_started; refusing blind replay without adapter reconciliation` line, then `[cron:<job-id>] notification failed: Pubkey must be 64 hex characters or npub format`.

We saw this on 10 of 10 fallback announces across 4 agents, between 2026-11-21 21:48Z and 2026-11-22 02:05Z. Runs in which the agent sent the message itself through the message tool, which targets the bare hex, were delivered.

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.6 (06afb10), with `@openclaw/nostr` 2026.11.6. The same code is still on main at ae8155cf5f.

### Operating system

macOS 27.0.1

### Install method

npm global (Node 26.13.1)

### Model

ollama/qwen3:30b. The model isn't involved: the failure happens in delivery, after a successful run.

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw -> ollama (local)

### Logs

```shell
[delivery-recovery] Delivery entry cron-direct-delivery:v1:cron:<job-id>:<ms>:nostr::<owner-hex>: delivery state is send_attempt_started; refusing blind replay without adapter reconciliation
[delivery-recovery] Outbound delivery retry: retry failed for entry cron-direct-delivery:v1:cron:<job-id>:<ms>:nostr::<owner-hex>:: delivery state is send_attempt_started; refusing blind replay without adapter reconciliation
[cron:<job-id>] notification failed: Pubkey must be 64 hex characters or npub format
```

Run record from `openclaw cron runs --id <job-id> --json` (redacted):

```json
{"status":"ok","delivery":{"intended":{"channel":"last","to":null,"source":"last"},"resolved":{"ok":true,"channel":"nostr","to":"nostr:<owner-hex>","source":"explicit"},"fallbackUsed":true,"delivered":false},"deliveryError":"Pubkey must be 64 hex characters or npub format"}
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

The code path, with line numbers from main at ae8155cf5f:

1. `src/cron/isolated-agent/delivery-target.ts:232-250`: for `target: "owner"`, it returns `to: resolved.to` from `resolveProactiveDeliveryTargetWithSessionRoute` and never strips the provider prefix.
2. `src/infra/outbound/targets.ts:516-522`, in `resolveDeliveryTargetWithPolicyAndSessionRoute`: the plugin-resolved target is replaced by the outbound session route's `to`. That plugin-resolved target is bare hex, from the Nostr `resolveTarget` at `extensions/nostr/src/channel.ts:133`.
3. `extensions/nostr/src/channel.ts:83`: `resolveNostrOutboundSessionRoute` returns `` to: `nostr:${target}` ``.
4. `extensions/nostr/src/gateway.ts:370`: `sendText` calls `normalizePubkey(to)` without `stripNostrTargetPrefix`. `nostr:<hex>` therefore fails the hex/npub check in `extensions/nostr/src/nostr-key-utils.ts`.

The explicit-target branch of `delivery-target.ts` does strip the provider prefix after it uses the session route (`stripSelectedProviderPrefix`, lines 436-442 and 487-490). That is why explicit `channel: "nostr"` targets resolve correctly.

### Impact and severity

- **Affected:** Nostr setups whose automations deliver to `target: "owner"`. We observed it on the heartbeat automations.
- **Severity:** Owner notifications are lost without any visible error. The run reports `ok`, and the failure shows only in the run record and gateway log.
- **Frequency:** Always on the fallback-announce path (10 of 10 observed).
- **Consequence:** Heartbeat and automation messages are missed. They arrive only when the agent sends them itself through the message tool.

### Additional information

**Workaround (verified on 3 of 3 runs):** give each job an explicit target with `openclaw cron edit <job-id> --clear-delivery-target --channel nostr --to <owner-npub>`.

**Possible fixes (one or more of these):**
- Apply `stripSelectedProviderPrefix` to the owner branch's target, as the explicit branch does.
- Keep the plugin-resolved target as the delivery `to`, and use the session route only to bind the session.
- Make Nostr `sendText` accept its own target format: `normalizePubkey(stripNostrTargetPrefix(to))`, as `resolveTarget` and `inferTargetChatType` already do.

issues.title: [Bug]: Silent reply "NO_REPLY" after inline </think> reasoning is delivered as a visible message (cron announce sends the reasoning)

labels.name: clawsweeper:intake:bug
labels.description: Preliminary submission classification; full source review pending.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

A model can write its reasoning inline and end it with `</think>` followed by the silent token, as in `…</think>\n\nNO_REPLY`. `prepareAgentRunReplyText` doesn't treat that reply as silent. It strips only the trailing `NO_REPLY` line and marks the terminal reply `visible`, so the cron fallback announce delivers the model's reasoning to the destination.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Run an agent on a model that writes its reasoning into the reply text and ends it with `</think>`. We used ollama/qwen3:30b with the thinking level off.
2. Give it an automation with announce delivery to an explicit target. We saw this on heartbeat automations delivering to a Nostr DM.
3. Let a run finish in which the agent decides there's nothing to report and ends with `NO_REPLY`.
4. Look at the delivered message and at `openclaw cron runs --id <job-id> --json`.

You can also reproduce it offline with the exported functions from the 2026.11.6 dist, which are pure:

```js
const raw = "Okay, let's see. Nothing needs attention, so the right answer is NO_REPLY.\n</think>\n\nNO_REPLY";
prepareAgentRunTerminalReply({ rawText: raw });
// → terminalReply.disposition === "visible", text === "Okay, let's see. … NO_REPLY.\n</think>"
sanitizeAssistantVisibleText(raw);
// → "NO_REPLY", and isSilentReplyText("NO_REPLY") === true
```

### Expected behavior

The reply is treated as silent and nothing is announced. Sanitizing the same raw text first yields exactly `NO_REPLY`, which `isSilentReplyText` accepts. For comparison, the inbound reply path cleans the same model's `…</think>\n\npineapple` down to `pineapple` before sending it.

### Actual behavior

The announce delivers the reasoning. We saw this on 3 of 3 heartbeat runs that ended in `NO_REPLY`, between 2026-11-22 03:48Z and 04:05Z.

- Each delivered message was 975 to 1391 characters of reasoning starting "Okay, let's…".
- Each run record shows `status: ok`, `deliveryStatus: delivered`, `delivery.fallbackUsed: true` and `delivery.delivered: true`.
- Each run's `summary` is the raw model output minus the trailing `\n</think>\n\nNO_REPLY`, exactly 19 characters shorter in every case.

### OpenClaw version

2026.11.6 (06afb10). The same code is still on main at f7ee25be86.

### Operating system

macOS 27.0.1

### Install method

npm global (Node 26.13.1)

### Model

ollama/qwen3:30b (thinking level off)

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw -> ollama (local)

### Logs

End of the raw assistant text in the run transcript:

```shell
…Yep, NO_REPLY is the right answer.\n</think>\n\nNO_REPLY
```

The same run's record from `openclaw cron runs --id <job-id> --json`, redacted:

```json
{"status":"ok","deliveryStatus":"delivered","delivery":{"fallbackUsed":true,"delivered":true},"summary":"Okay, let's break this down. The user is running an automation called \"heartbeat-<agent>\" … (1391 chars)"}
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence

The code path, with line numbers from main at f7ee25be86:

1. `src/agents/agent-run-terminal-reply.ts:60-66`, `prepareAgentRunReplyText`:
   - It calls `isSilentReplyText(rawText)` on the raw text. That function (`src/auto-reply/tokens.ts:17`) only matches when the whole trimmed text is exactly `NO_REPLY`.
   - Otherwise it removes only a trailing `NO_REPLY` line (`/[\r\n]\s*NO_REPLY\s*$/iu`) and returns the rest as visible text.
2. `src/agents/agent-run-terminal-reply.ts:68-77`, `prepareAgentRunTerminalReply`: the text is sanitized with `sanitizeAgentRunTerminalReply` only after that. The `</think>` reasoning is therefore never removed before the silence decision.
3. Downstream, the cron runner uses that visible text as the run's payload and summary (`src/cron/isolated-agent/helpers.ts`, `resolveCronPayloadOutcome`). The fallback announce then delivers it.

### Impact and severity

- **Affected:** agents on models that write inline reasoning ending in `</think>` (we observed it with ollama/qwen3:30b), for any automation that answers `NO_REPLY` with announce delivery.
- **Severity:** Unwanted messages that contain the model's internal reasoning, including its view of the automation's instructions and context, are sent to the channel at every interval.
- **Frequency:** 3 of 3 observed `NO_REPLY` runs.
- **Consequence:** The destination receives long reasoning dumps instead of nothing.

### Additional information

**Possible fix:** decide silence on the sanitized text. For example, `prepareAgentRunReplyText` could test `isSilentReplyText(sanitizeAssistantVisibleText(rawText))`, or test the text after the last `</think>`, before it falls back to stripping a trailing token.

**Workarounds:**
- Disable runner fallback delivery on the affected automations with `openclaw cron edit <job-id> --no-deliver`.
- Or use a model or configuration that keeps reasoning out of the reply text.

**Related:** #203403. That's a separate bug, but it made these announces fail before they were sent, which hid this one until it was worked around.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Summary

On `claude-cli`, when a chat's first Claude Code turn is running and another input for the same chat is queued behind it, the queued turn starts its own fresh native Claude session instead of resuming the one the first turn just created. The two native sessions share no context: the second gets the full fresh-session preparation again and never sees the first turn's tool work. Afterwards the chat's binding names the second session, and the first is orphaned.

Observed once so far, on the first two Claude turns of a chat that had just been switched to Claude from another model.

### Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.11.6 (06afb10), Linux x64, Node 24.22.1, gateway as a user service
- Claude Code 2.1.325, `claude-cli` runtime (`liveSession: "claude-stdio"`), subscription token profile saved with `models auth paste-token`
- Turns sent through `chat.send` from a dashboard client

### What happened

Gateway log for one chat (UTC):

```
03:50:37.754 cli session history refused across auth boundary: reason=auth-unknown
03:50:37.967 cli live session start: provider=claude-cli model=claude-opus-5-5 activeSessions=1   <- turn 1 (subagent_settle completion): native session A
03:51:01     (the user's message arrives and is queued while turn 1 runs)
03:51:08.017 cli turn: provider=claude-cli model=claude-opus-5-5 durationMs=30073               <- turn 1 ends
03:51:09.180 cli session history refused across auth boundary: reason=auth-unknown
03:51:09.623 cli live session start: provider=claude-cli model=claude-opus-5-5 activeSessions=1   <- turn 2 (the user's message): native session B
```

There is no `cli session reset: ... reason=...` line between the turns, so turn 2 didn't invalidate a binding; it found none. After turn 2 the session entry's `cliSessionBindings["claude-cli"]` names session B. Session A's Claude Code transcript holds turn 1's work.

The `auth-unknown` lines are expected: the chat's earlier history was written by another runtime before the model switch. That is why both turns were fresh sessions, which is how this showed up.

### Expected

The queued turn resumes native session A, the binding turn 1 settled, as consecutive turns normally do.

### Possible cause (a guess, not verified)

`withAdmittedCliCandidate` (`src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run-entry-cli.ts`) reads the session entry with `readSessionEntryReadOnlyInWorker` when `readMode` is `"read-only"`, which the reply runner passes. The writable path asks for `readConsistency: "latest"`. If the read-only read can return the entry from before turn 1's `persistCliSessionBindingResult` committed, the queued turn sees no binding and starts fresh. Turn 2 was prepared about 0.8 s after turn 1's CLI turn ended.

### Impact

- The user's first message after switching to Claude ran in a session that didn't know what the previous turn had just done.
- A second full prompt-cache write.
- A duplicated history read: in session B the model called `sessions_history` again (57k characters) to recover the same context session A had already read.

Related: #159512 (announce turns resetting sessions), #186613 (settle re-publishing a cleared binding), #132758 (history not delivered).

---
Written with Claude Code on behalf of the reporter.

issues.body:
### Summary

On 2026.11.6 (da6d981), with the Chrome extension driver, one tab in the OpenClaw tab group that stops answering CDP makes **every** extension browser call fail with `Playwright page target identities are temporarily unavailable.` This includes `tabs`, `snapshot`, `close`, and the gateway's own idle-tab cleanup. It lasts until a human closes the tab or quits Chrome. `openclaw browser doctor` reports everything ready except `tabs`.

This looks like the same blast radius as #200543, which was closed as fixed by #162110 (v2026.10.5). This host runs 2026.11.6, which contains that fix.

### Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.11.6 (da6d981), macOS app-hosted gateway, macOS 26.3, M1 / 16 GB
- Chrome 156.0.8078.79, bundled extension 2.3.0 (matches), Selected-tabs mode, one Chrome profile with the extension
- Host was not resource-starved at failure: load ~3, ~50% memory free, disk 7% used

### What happened

1. An agent opened a tab on a third-party payment form via `browser open`, read it, and left it idle in the background.
2. Within roughly 10-70 minutes, every `openclaw browser tabs --browser-profile chrome` failed (about 6 s each) with `Playwright page target identities are temporarily unavailable.`
3. Gateway idle cleanup tried to close the tracked tab every 5 minutes and logged `failed to close tracked browser tab <id>: Error: Browser request timed out` 75 times. The first timeout came 10 minutes before listing started failing.
4. This happened twice in one day with two different tabs on the same site. The first episode cleared when that tab was closed. The second lasted about 9 hours, until Chrome was quit.

### Why (from the installed dist)

- The extension driver sets `requiresCompleteTargetEnumeration` (`registry-*.mjs`), so `listPagesViaPlaywright` passes `requireCompleteTargetList: true`.
- `listPagesViaPlaywright` throws if any page resolves to `unresolved`: `if ((requireCompleteTargetList || available.length === 0) && results.some(r => r.status === "unresolved")) throw ...`.
- A page is `unresolved` when `readPageTargetInfo` cannot open a page CDP session and get `Target.getTargetInfo` back within `PLAYWRIGHT_TARGET_INFO_TIMEOUT_MS` (2000 ms). Through the relay, that is `Target.attachToTarget` followed by a `chrome.debugger` attach on the real tab.
- Every recovery path, including the tracked-tab close, resolves pages through the same enumeration. So once one tab is unresponsive, nothing inside OpenClaw can close it.

We could not establish why the page stopped answering: a `beforeunload` prompt raised by the idle close, or Chrome freezing a hidden tab. Chrome was quit before anyone inspected the tab.

### Expected

One unresponsive tab should be reported as unavailable (or left out with a reason) while the other tabs stay usable. The tracked-tab close should be able to close a tab by its extension tab id without resolving every page first.

### Actual

All extension browser automation is down until a human intervenes, and `doctor` passes except for `tabs`.

issues.body:
> **Update 2026-11-21:** fixed and shipped. #164445 (`e02ae3ecb66`), with #146715 and #146716, is in stable `v2026.11.5` and `v2026.11.6`; the settlement, settle-yielded and swarm suites pass at the `v2026.11.6` tag and on `main` `ae8155cf5f5`. Closed as completed; see the last comment. Original report below.

**Build:** OpenClaw `2026.9.2 (3928bad)`. Backend: `claude-cli`. Both defects reproduced live with control arms in both directions, then traced to source in the installed `dist/`.

Two independent defects in the swarm collector path. **D2 is the serious one**: it is a silent, unbounded hang with a green status surface, and it is the *default* behaviour rather than an edge case. D1 is filed with it because D1 is what usually *triggers* D2 — but they are independent, and fixing D1 alone leaves D2 armed.

---

## D2 — a collector child that calls `sessions_yield` strands its parent forever, while the status surface reports "done"

### Symptom

A `collect: true` child that calls `sessions_yield` ends up with:

- `execution.status: "terminal"`, `execution.outcome.status: "ok"` — the run genuinely finished
- `pauseReason: "sessions_yield"` in `subagent_runs.payload_json`
- **no collector completion record written, ever**
- `agents_wait` pends forever — no error, no timeout of its own, no diagnostic
- `subagents(action="list")` `recent` reports the same run as `status: "done"`
- `subagents(action="list")` `tasks` reports the same run as `status: "running"`

Three surfaces, three different answers, for one run. The one an operator is most likely to check (`recent` → `done`) is the one that says everything is fine.

### Why children reach for it

`sessions_yield` **is** in a collector child's tool catalog. `structured_output` is not (that is D1). So a child instructed to "submit structured output" reaches for `sessions_yield` as the nearest available thing. Two of the first two test children did this unprompted, with no mention of yielding in their prompt.

### Minimal reproduction

```
sessions_spawn({ task: "Reply with the single word gamma.", collect: true,
                 groupId: "g", label: "arm", model: "haiku", lightContext: true })
agents_wait({ ids: [runId], timeoutSeconds: 30 })
```

| arm | `outputSchema` | child called `sessions_yield` | `agents_wait` result |
|---|---|---|---|
| A (positive control) | no | no | `status:"done"`, `result:"gamma"` — **5.1s** |
| B | yes | no | `status:"failed"`, `schemaError:"structured_output was not called"`, `result:"delta"` — 7.4s |
| **C** | **no** | **yes** | **never returns.** `recent`: `done`, `endedAt` set, `runtimeMs` 15855, 52576 tokens. `tasks`: `running`. |

Arm A proves the harness observes success. **Arm C carries no `outputSchema` at all** — `sessions_yield` alone is sufficient to hang the parent, so D2 does not depend on D1.

### Root cause

In `dist/subagent-completion-admission.store-*.js`, three separate paths exempt `pauseReason === "sessions_yield"` unconditionally, with no check for `entry.collect`:

```js
// result-capture path — aborts before any completion state is created
const liveEntry = params.runs.get(entry.runId);
if (entry.pauseReason === "sessions_yield" || liveEntry?.pauseReason === "sessions_yield"
    || context.newerGenerationOwnsSession(entry)) return false;
const completion = ensureCompletionState(entry);
```

```js
// resolveFinalizedSubagentTaskState — returns undefined, so `tasks` reports "running"
if (typeof endedAt !== "number" || !outcome || entry.pauseReason === "sessions_yield"
    || completion?.resultText === void 0 && typeof completion?.capturedAt !== "number") return;
```

```js
// listPendingCompletionRunsForSession — run is skipped entirely
if (entry.pauseReason === "sessions_yield") continue;
```

The exemption looks correct for an **announce** child: a yielded child is paused and will resume, so admitting a completion early would be wrong. But a **collector** child has no resume path and no announcement — the collector completion record is its *only* output channel. The same guard that is right for announce children permanently strands collector children, and the `recent` projection reads `execution.endedAt` directly so it happily reports `done` over the stranded row.

### Suggested fix shape

Gate these three exemptions on `entry.collect !== true`, so a terminal collector run admits its completion regardless of `pauseReason`. Failing that, at minimum: make `agents_wait` surface a terminal-without-completion run as a `failed` result with a real diagnostic instead of pending forever, and reconcile `recent` / `tasks` so they cannot disagree.

A cheaper partial mitigation would be to keep `sessions_yield` out of a collector child's tool catalog entirely — it has no meaning for a one-shot collector — though that alone would not fix a run already in this state.

---

## D1 — `structured_output` is never injected into `claude-cli`-backed collector children, so `outputSchema` is silently inert

### Symptom

Passing `outputSchema` to a `collect: true` spawn on a `claude-cli` backend has no effect on the child. `agents_wait` then returns `status: "failed"` with `schemaError: "structured_output was not called"`. The child's answer is still present as raw text in `result`, so the caller gets a "failed" result that actually contains the correct answer.

Asked directly, the child reports: *"A tool named `structured_output` was not present in my tool list."*

### Root cause

`createStructuredOutputTool` is present in the tools bundle (`dist/openclaw-tools-*.js`), but the string `structured_output` does not appear in **any** `dist/cli-backend*.js` — nor does `forceToolNames`. The CLI backend has no code path that injects the synthetic tool or forces the model to call it. The schema is accepted at the API boundary and then dropped on the floor for this backend class.

### Impact

`outputSchema` is not merely unenforced — it is accepted, documented, and silently ineffective for every `claude-cli`-backed agent. The failure is also mislabelled: `status: "failed"` on a run that succeeded trains callers to ignore the status field.

### Suggested fix shape

Either inject the synthetic tool on the CLI backend path, or **reject `outputSchema` at spawn time with a clear error** when the resolved backend cannot support it. Accepting a parameter that cannot be honoured is the worst of the three options.

---

## Relationship to existing issues

- **#138018** (*Swarm collector can freeze missing structured output before a valid terminal tool call is recorded*) — related but distinct. That issue is a **race**: `structured_output` *is* called, and arrives after the freezer has already recorded the missing-output failure. D1 here is the case where the tool is **never injected at all**, so it can never be called and there is no late callback to lose. A fix for #138018 would not change any arm above.
- **#132765** (*`agents_wait` ignores `timeoutSeconds`*) — adjacent. Note the interaction: D2 produces a wait with no completion record to ever return, so `agents_wait` timeout behaviour is the only thing standing between a caller and an unbounded hang.

## Workarounds currently in force on our fleet

1. Never pass `outputSchema`; ask for JSON in the child's final text and parse it parent-side.
2. End every collector child prompt with *"do not call `sessions_yield`; end your turn normally."*
3. Give every parent wait loop its own wall-clock deadline — never trust `agents_wait` to terminate.

All three are a standing tax on every swarm caller, and because a fix upstream would be silent (the workarounds keep working afterwards), we run a daily tripwire against these code paths to know when to drop them.

issues.body:
## Summary

On the Codex app-server harness, a plugin `before_tool_call` hook that returns changed `params` for an OpenClaw-owned dynamic tool (here `message`) makes the call fail, although the same tool is also wrapped with `wrapToolWithBeforeToolCallHook` at host execution, where such a rewrite is supported. The native PreToolUse relay runs the same hooks first and refuses any rewrite, so the send never reaches the host wrapper.

This is the problem of #144608 (closed by inactivity as not planned on 5 Nov, "please reopen with current reproduction details if it still occurs"); the proposed fix #144614 is still open and unmerged. It still occurs on 2026.11.3, with real impact below.

## After (2026.11.3, 847611d)

A scheduled cron run on `openai/gpt-6.2-astra` (subscription auth, Codex app-server harness) called `message` (`action: "send"`, `channel: "telegram"`) from Code Mode. A local plugin's `before_tool_call` hook (matcher `["message"]`) returns `{ params: { message: <text + one appended suffix> } }`. The tool result:

```
Script error:
Tool call blocked by PreToolUse hook: OpenClaw tool policy rewrote Codex app-server approval params; refusing original request.. Tool: message
```

The message was not sent. The same plugin rewrite works for the same tool on the embedded (Anthropic) harness.

## Shipped guard

- `dist/native-hook-relay-*.mjs`, `runNativeHookRelayPreToolUse`: `if (!outcome.deferredApproval && nativeHookRelayParamsWereRewritten(originalToolInputFingerprint, outcome.params)) return ...renderPreToolUseBlockResponse("OpenClaw tool policy rewrote Codex app-server approval params; refusing original request.")`
- `@openclaw/codex` `dynamic-tools-*.mjs`, `projectCodexExecutableDynamicToolSurface`: every dynamic tool is already wrapped with `wrapToolWithBeforeToolCallHook`, so the hook runs again at execution and could apply the rewrite there.
- The plugin hook context carries no field that tells the relay pass from host execution (`toolName, agentId, sessionKey, sessionId, runId, toolCallId, channelId, requester` in both), so a plugin cannot avoid it.

## Expected

A `before_tool_call` param rewrite that works for a tool on the embedded harness also works for the same OpenClaw-owned tool on the Codex harness: the call goes out with the rewritten params, whichever pass applies them. Native Codex tools whose input cannot be rewritten may still refuse, but then the hook needs a host-supplied phase marker (as in #144614) so it can leave the preflight alone. Concrete ask: merge #144614 or an equivalent, or skip the relay rewrite check for OpenClaw dynamic tools that the host wrapper hooks anyway, and name the release.

## Environment

OpenClaw 2026.11.3 (847611d), Linux x64, Node 26.12.1, Codex app-server harness via the bundled `@openclaw/codex` plugin, model `openai/gpt-6.2-astra@<profile>`, Code Mode on, tool `message` (Telegram).

## Evidence scope

Observed: one refused send in a cron run (22 Nov 2026), with the exact error above in the transcript; guard lines read from the installed bundle. Not induced: a minimal standalone reproduction; other dynamic tools. Local workaround: our plugin no longer rewrites on jobs whose model runs on the Codex harness, which loses that feature there.

only ever showed `aborted`. I don't know what actually stalled there, and I have no
artifacts from it, so that incident stays unexplained. What I do have is a reproduction
I can run on demand that shows the same shape of failure, on 2026.11.6 (1c73acd) and on
main at 3c8c7bf.

## The reproduction

A real gateway with a Docker sandbox (session scope, no network) and a real bound
`autoreview` call from a session. The model requests the tool with `timeoutSeconds: 10`.
A healthy control review passes first on both builds, so the plumbing itself works.

The host is a Mac running Docker Desktop, where the bind-mounted `/workspace` root
shows up root-owned inside the container. To get past that I set `AUTOREVIEW_GIT` to a
wrapper around stock git that clears the helper's hermetic config env, so the image's
system `safe.directory` applies. Anyone reproducing on a Linux host probably won't
need that step.

The stall is induced on purpose: after the sandbox is up and before the model returns
the tool call, I append an `[include]` entry pointing at a FIFO to
`/workspace/.git/config` inside the container. Stock Git blocks on opening that
include, and the helper's Git capture blocks with it. I picked this because it's a
realistic way for a Git read inside the sandbox to never return, not because a user
hit exactly this.

With the git process parked in `wait_for_partner`, on both builds:

- the run stays pending for 45 seconds against a 10 second review budget, and nothing
  suggested it would stop on its own. I stopped observing at 45 seconds.
- the reviewer model is never consulted, zero reviewer requests
- zero tool progress, zero tool terminal events, zero chat deltas, nothing on the
  live tool output subscription
- the run is not errored and not aborted; it is simply still running
- when I release the FIFO, the same run completes normally with a clean report

What this run shows is that the 10 second budget did not end the call, and nothing
about the stall reached the session as progress or as an error.

## Why #200743 and #201897 don't cover this

- #200743 keeps a quiet Auto Review call alive by handing the watchdog a liveness
  allowance, and it explicitly adds no abort timer. That is the opposite of what is
  missing here: the call stays pending, which is exactly what I observed. Nothing ties
  the review's own budget to any deadline.
- #201897 fixed the reviewer process timeout races (early stop, discarded results,
  hidden timeouts) and moved timeout ownership to the host. In this stall the reviewer
  process never starts. The helper is stuck in Git capture before any reviewer exists,
  so a reviewer-process timeout has nothing to time out.

## What I'd expect

The budget the tool is called with should be enforced at a level the helper's
subprocesses can't hang past, or the stall should at least surface as progress or an
error instead of silence. I haven't dug into where that enforcement belongs.

I have the full event logs and the harness for the reproduction if they're useful.

issues.body:
A third-party channel plugin receives inbound over a persistent WS/RPC connection (via `registerGatewayMethod`) and runs post-ACK work through the public `runDetachedWebhookWork` helper. We keep this transport as-is; we do not run a separate webhook endpoint or push service.

`runDetachedWebhookWork` preserves the ambient plugin gateway request scope, so the post-ACK turn inherits the WS connection's device authority (`hasCurrentClientAuthority`). When that turn later spawns a subagent (`dispatch_action -> sessions_spawn`), the stale device authority is selected and the call fails with `Gateway caller authority is no longer active.` (same root cause as #201233).

The desired primitive already exists internally — `withPluginRuntimeGatewayContextResolver(resolver, work, { inheritRequestScope: false })` drops the request client/authority while keeping the admitted root work and channel binding — but it is not exported through the public plugin SDK. The public alternatives are insufficient: `runInDetachedAsyncContext` also clears the admitted root work (risking dropped ACK'd messages during restart drain).

**Environment:** OpenClaw 2026.11.6; third-party channel plugin loaded via `plugins.load.paths`.

**Ask**

Expose a public, documented equivalent of `withPluginRuntimeGatewayContextResolver(..., { inheritRequestScope: false })` (or a channel "run detached turn work" entry) that strips transport authority from post-ACK work while retaining admitted execution, so WS-based third-party channels do not have to change their transport.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

Once an outbound delivery queue entry reaches `status = 'failed'`, no code path can ever read, retry, or remove it. The row is terminal and permanent: `openclaw health` counts it forever, but every other accessor in `src/infra/delivery-queue-sqlite.ts` filters on `status = 'pending'`, so nothing can act on it. There is no CLI command, no gateway RPC method, and no TTL. The only remedy available to an operator is hand-editing `state/openclaw.sqlite` with the gateway stopped.

All line numbers below are at `0790d9f` (shipped as `2026.7.1-2`), `src/infra/delivery-queue-sqlite.ts`:

| function | line | `status` filter | effect on a `failed` row |
|---|---|---|---|
| `deleteDeliveryQueueEntry` | 218 | `"pending"` (227) | **cannot delete it** |
| `loadDeliveryQueueEntry` | 160 | `"pending"` (183) | returns `undefined` |
| `loadDeliveryQueueEntries` | 189 | `"pending"` (210) | never lists it |
| `updateDeliveryQueueEntry` | 232 | via `loadDeliveryQueueEntry` (238) | throws `ENOENT` |
| `moveDeliveryQueueEntryToFailed` | 281 | via `loadDeliveryQueueEntry` (286) | throws `ENOENT` |
| `countFailedDeliveryQueueEntries` | 253 | `"failed"` (265) | counts it forever |

`deleteDeliveryQueueEntry` is reachable only from `ackDelivery()` / `ackSessionDelivery()` — i.e. on *successful* delivery — so the delete path can never apply to something that failed. Grepping the shipped bundle, there is exactly one `deleteFrom("delivery_queue_entries")` in the entire artifact, and it is that one. The module contains no `ttl`, `expire`, or `maxAge` logic, so failed rows never age out either. Outside of tests, the sole consumer of `countFailedDeliveryQueueEntries` is `src/commands/health.ts`.

The docstring at line 280 states the intent that the implementation forecloses:

```ts
/** Mark a pending delivery queue entry as failed for later diagnostics. */
```

There is no way to perform those diagnostics. The row is retained, and the payload in `entry_json` survives intact, but nothing can read it back.

Net effect is a health warning that no supported action can clear:

```
Delivery queue: warning (dead-lettered entries — outbound: 5; oldest 12d ago)
```

### Steps to reproduce

The shortest deterministic path uses the permanent-error branch, which dead-letters on the first attempt with no retry/backoff wait. In `src/infra/outbound/delivery-queue-recovery.ts`, `isPermanentDeliveryError()` (359) matches `PERMANENT_ERROR_PATTERNS` (83–95), and a match routes straight to `moveToFailed()` (601–603). `/chat not found/i` is in that list, and it is what the Telegram API returns for a well-formed but nonexistent `chat_id`.

1. Configure a Telegram channel.
2. Queue a durable outbound delivery to a nonexistent chat id, e.g. a cron job whose announce target does not exist:
   ```
   openclaw cron add "dead-letter-repro" --every 1m --agent main \
     --message "repro" --announce --channel telegram --to 999999999999
   ```
3. Let it fire once. Telegram replies `Bad Request: chat not found`, `isPermanentDeliveryError` matches, and the entry goes to `failed` immediately — `retry_count` stays at 0, no `MAX_RETRIES = 5` backoff cycle.
4. `openclaw cron rm <id>` and remove the bad target. The queue row is unaffected.
5. `openclaw health` → `Delivery queue: warning (dead-lettered entries — outbound: 1; …)`.
6. Try to clear it by any supported means: there is no `openclaw` subcommand for the delivery queue, no gateway RPC method, and `openclaw doctor --fix` does not touch these rows. The warning is now permanent.
7. Confirm the row is still present and is what is being counted:
   ```sql
   SELECT id, status, retry_count, last_error, failed_at
   FROM delivery_queue_entries WHERE status = 'failed';
   ```

I have **not** executed step 2 on my own instance, because doing so would add a row I could never remove — which is the bug. The repro is derived from the source paths cited above. What I did hit organically was the other branch: a DNS outage produced `Network request for 'sendRichMessage' failed!` against Telegram, and those entries dead-lettered at `retry_count: 1`. Five of them have now sat in my `openclaw health` output for 12 days, surviving gateway restarts and an upgrade:

```
{"queue_name":"outbound","status":"failed","channel":"telegram",
 "retry_count":1,"last_error":"Network request for 'sendRichMessage' failed!",
 "recovery_state":"send_attempt_started"}
```

### Expected behavior

An operator can inspect and clear dead-lettered outbound entries through a supported surface. Any of these would resolve it:

- a CLI surface for the queue, e.g. `openclaw queue list --failed` / `openclaw queue purge --failed` / `openclaw queue retry <id>`;
- `openclaw doctor --fix` pruning failed rows past some age;
- a TTL on `failed` rows so they age out on their own.

Retry would be the most valuable of the three. Because `entry_json` is preserved, a dead letter is in principle fully replayable — the payload is right there. The inbound ingress queue erases its payload at `fail()` (see #109911) and so genuinely cannot be replayed; the outbound queue keeps everything it would need and still offers nothing.

### Actual behavior

Failed rows are write-once and unreachable. They inflate the `openclaw health` warning permanently, and the only way to clear them is manual SQL against `state/openclaw.sqlite` with the gateway stopped.

### Impact

Affected: any deployment that has ever had a terminal outbound delivery failure — a transient network or DNS outage is enough, and a single mistyped announce target is enough.

Severity: annoying, not breaking. Delivery keeps working; the damage is that `openclaw health` carries a permanent unclearable warning. That degrades health output as a monitoring signal — an operator seeing the delivery-queue line cannot distinguish a fresh failure from stale ones already triaged, so the rational response is to stop reading the line at all. The count only ever grows.

### Related

- #109911 (closed) contrasts the inbound ingress queue with the outbound one and notes that outbound dead letters at least surface in `openclaw health`. True, but visibility is where it ends — this issue is about the absence of any way to *act* on what is surfaced.
- #16555 requests TTL/expiry for delivery queue messages, but targets `pending` entries and their replay on restart. Its proposed `expireAction: "move-to-failed"` would in fact *create* more of the terminal rows described here. It does not address rows already in `failed`.

### Environment

- OpenClaw `2026.7.1-2` (`0790d9f`), installed via npm
- Linux 6.17, Node via `n`
- Gateway: systemd user service, loopback bind, token auth
- Channels: Telegram, WhatsApp

issues.body:
### Bug type
Regression (worked before, then failed in the observed 2026.11.5 environment)

### Beta release blocker
No

### Summary
On OpenClaw 2026.11.5 (e13cf15), spawning a subagent through the Tool Search wrapper `dispatch_action -> sessions_spawn` fails with `Gateway caller authority is no longer active.`; the same turn can still send messages through other tools.

### Steps to reproduce
1. Run OpenClaw 2026.11.5 (e13cf15) with Tool Search in `tools` mode, where `sessions_spawn` is deferred and not directly callable.
2. From an inbound channel turn, ask the agent to call `sessions_spawn` through `dispatch_action` with:
   ```json
   {
     "id": "sessions_spawn",
     "args": {
       "task": "Return a fixed test token",
       "cleanup": "delete",
       "completionTarget": "parent",
       "context": "isolated",
       "mode": "run",
       "runTimeoutSeconds": 60
     }
   }
   ```
3. Observe the nested tool event for `sessions_spawn` and its result.

A direct-call control was attempted first. The agent reported that `sessions_spawn` is a deferred tool in this tool surface and that the only callable entry is `dispatch_action`, so direct invocation could not be used as a control here.

### Expected behavior
The wrapped call should create the hidden subagent run and return an accepted result, since `dispatch_action` is the documented callable path for deferred Tool Search tools.

### Actual behavior
The nested `sessions_spawn` call fails at the Gateway effect boundary:

```text
Gateway caller authority is no longer active.
```

Observed twice in the same session with different task tokens. The failure result includes generated `childSessionKey` and `runId` values, but no child run starts. During the same turn, a separate message-send tool call succeeds, so the Gateway RPC and messaging path are still working.

The second reproduction occurred at 2026-11-18 21:37 CST (2026-11-18 13:37 UTC).

Redacted transcript evidence, second reproduction:

```text
assistant toolCall:
dispatch_action({
  "id": "sessions_spawn",
  "args": {
    "task": "Return a fixed test token",
    "cleanup": "delete",
    "completionTarget": "parent",
    "context": "isolated",
    "mode": "run",
    "runTimeoutSeconds": 60
  }
})

nested tool event:
toolName=sessions_spawn
isError=true

tool result:
{
  "status": "error",
  "error": "Gateway caller authority is no longer active.",
  "childSessionKey": "agent:<agent>:subagent:<uuid>",
  "runId": "<uuid>"
}
```

The inbound metadata in this turn marked the sender as the host-recognized owner. The failing field is the internal Gateway caller authority, not the channel-level sender authorization. I am omitting private channel implementation details and all identifiers.

### OpenClaw version
2026.11.5 (e13cf15)

### Operating system
Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS, x86_64 Linux

### Install method
npm global installation; Gateway started as a system service

### Model
Provider route: xmo / dp-c; response model reported as hy4flash-free

### Provider / routing chain
OpenClaw embedded runner -> xmo / dp-c -> hy4flash-free

### Additional provider/model setup details
Tool Search mode is `tools`. `sessions_spawn` is deferred and exposed through `dispatch_action`. No API keys, tokens, hosts, or account identifiers are included.

### Logs
Source-level error origin appears to be Gateway revocation authority retention:

```ts
// src/gateway/device-revocation.ts
export function retainGatewayDeviceRevocation(guard) {
  const capture = guard ? captures.get(guard) : undefined;
  if (!capture) return undefined;
  if (!capture.isCurrent() || capture.state.references === 0) {
    throw new Error("Gateway caller authority is no longer active.");
  }
  capture.state.references += 1;
  return releaseHold(capture);
}
```

Runtime source checked:

```text
/usr/lib/node_modules/openclaw/dist/device-revocation-BSZ8gueh.mjs
/usr/lib/node_modules/openclaw/dist/tool-search-D7NiQXUh.mjs
/usr/lib/node_modules/openclaw/dist/sessions-spawn-tool-BXw1MaMz.mjs
/usr/lib/node_modules/openclaw/dist/server-plugin-in-process-dispatch-DhYjM05s.mjs
```

### Screenshots, recordings, and evidence
Redacted transcript events are included above. Related upstream issue: #165176 reports the same error text in a different runtime/path; this report isolates the reproducible Tool Search wrapper path on 2026.11.5.

### Impact and severity
Affected: channel turns where the agent must spawn a hidden subagent through the deferred Tool Search wrapper.
Severity: High for those workflows because delegation fails.
Frequency: 2/2 observed attempts in the affected session; the earlier attempt and the controlled second attempt both failed.
Consequence: the parent agent must run the work on the main thread, which blocks chat responsiveness and defeats task-dispatch behavior.

### Additional information
A direct `sessions_spawn` call was attempted as a control but is blocked by the current Tool Search surface, so I cannot claim a successful direct-spawn comparison in this environment. The grounded conclusion is limited to: the documented wrapper path repeatedly fails the Gateway caller authority check on 2026.11.5.

## Summary

Expose a capability-specific embedding preflight/recovery diagnostic for Codex OAuth-only installations. Working Codex inference and available subscription usage do not establish that the same profile is entitled to native OpenAI embeddings.

This supplies fresh stable-release evidence related to closed #87677, whose last comment asks for a new report after retrying on the latest release. The current symptom differs from its historical missing-API-key gate: OAuth is selected, but the provider returns a quota/entitlement rejection.

## Observed setup

- Official OpenClaw 2026.10.7 (157d8c2), npm global.
- macOS 26.6.2 arm64, supported Node 24.22.1.
- Main model: openai/gpt-6.1-sol, runtime codex; OAuth route usable, no model fallback.
- No separate OpenAI API key configured for this test.
- Read-only local inspection confirms the selected profile belongs to the native Codex account. No credential is included here.
- Public docs describe Codex OAuth embeddings as conditional on account embedding access: https://docs.openclaw.ai/providers/openai/authentication

## Current-release synthetic controls

```sh
openclaw infer model run --gateway --agent main --model openai/gpt-6.1-sol --prompt 'Reply exactly OK.' --json
# ok=true, provider=openai, model=gpt-6.1-sol, transport=gateway, text=OK

openclaw infer embedding create --agent main --provider openai --model openai/text-embedding-3-small --text 'A quiet cedar forest after rain.' --json
# fails: HTTP429, insufficient_quota / credit_balance_exhausted
```

Before the upgrade, fixed-sentence controls for both text-embedding-3-large and text-embedding-3-small produced the same rejection. No private memory, email or calendar content was sent. No provider baseUrl override is configured; this is not the explicit chat-base-URL inheritance case in #165476.

## Requested behavior

1. Distinguish a usable Codex chat route from verified embedding entitlement, rather than letting agents infer that all Codex/subscription credits are exhausted.
2. Document an observable, bounded way to verify the conditional OAuth embedding access and identify the provider-owned supported endpoint.
3. If this account class has no supported subscription-only embedding route, say so explicitly and present existing keyless/local alternatives. Do not silently copy credentials, select a paid fallback or migrate an index.
4. Let callers preflight this capability before enqueueing private-document catch-up work.

## Scope and open question

This is not a claim that OpenClaw can grant upstream account entitlement, or that every Codex OAuth account must have embedding access. Which supported subscription-only embedding contract, if any, should this installation use? If there is none, the requested improvement is accurate capability diagnostics and documentation.

Existing model-auth policy accepts eligible Codex OAuth for embeddings, while the synthetic runtime result rejects this account at the provider boundary. Native Codex chat succeeds. No separate API-key purchase or provider migration is requested by this report.

issues.body:
**Subagent browser tabs are never capped or swept while the session runs**

`isPrimaryTrackedBrowserSessionKey()` (`extensions/browser/src/browser/session-tab-cleanup.ts`) excludes subagent, cron and ACP sessions from the periodic cleanup, including the `maxTabsPerSession` cap (default 8). Their tabs close only when the session ends.

Observed: 8 long-running (15-22 min) subagents opened ~22 tabs (~200 MB each, ~4 GB) on a 24 GB host and drove memory stall to 85%; the tabs closed only when the helpers were killed.

Expected: at least the per-session cap applies to subagent sessions. Proposed fix: potterdigital/openclaw branch `fix/subagent-tab-cap` (cap-only filter; idle exclusion and cron/ACP unchanged).

issues.body:
### Summary
Allow a shared-store `secret` entry to hold a SecretRef instead of a value, e.g. `{ source: "exec", provider: "vault", id: "secrets/unifi/api" }`, with its `allowedHosts` stored as non-secret metadata. When Gateway-hosted exec captures its store snapshot, resolve the ref in memory and seal it into the usual `oc-sent-v2` sentinel, so the egress proxy substitutes it exactly like a stored value.

### Problem to solve
The egress proxy is the best way to let agent commands use credentials without ever seeing them, but its only value source is the shared store, which keeps values unencrypted in `state/openclaw.sqlite` (per docs/gateway/secrets/secret-store-and-egress.md). For deployments that keep credentials in Vault/OpenBao, that means copying secrets into a SQLite file that ends up in volume snapshots and backups.
The bundled `vault` and `onepassword` plugins resolve SecretRefs, but only for config fields (model providers, channels), not for the exec egress proxy. In source, egress bindings are built only from store rows in `readSecretStoreExecEnvironment` (src/secrets/store/secret-store.ts), so there is no way to feed a Vault-backed value to a subprocess as a proxied sentinel.

### Proposed solution
- New store entry form: `kind: "secret"` with `ref` (a SecretRef) instead of `value`; `allowedHosts` unchanged. CLI, e.g. `openclaw secrets store set UNIFI_API_KEY --ref exec:vault:secrets/unifi/api --allow-host unifi.example.net`.
- In `readSecretStoreExecEnvironment`, resolve ref-backed rows through the existing secrets runtime (same resolver and timeouts as config SecretRefs), register the value for redaction, seal it into a sentinel, and add the binding. Plaintext lives only in memory; nothing new is written to disk.
- Resolution failure: omit that entry with a visible warning (same as the existing redaction-placeholder case), never fail the whole exec.
- Optionally cache per run snapshot only, so each new run re-reads the backend (rotation works, and the backend's audit log records each use).

### Alternatives considered
- Copying Vault values into the store (today's path): plaintext at rest and in backups.
- Injecting values as env (ESO / `env` entries): the agent can read and exfiltrate them.
- External credential-injecting proxies (Infisical agent-vault, varlock, Envoy credential_injector, superfly/tokenizer): none keeps OpenClaw's per-process grants and sentinel model, and running two proxies in the exec path is fragile.

### Impact
Self-hosted / Kubernetes Gateways that standardize on Vault or OpenBao. Credentials for agent CLI/API calls would stay in the secret manager, be read on demand, and remain unreadable by the agent. Related: #197297 (per-user vault, reuses the same egress proxy) — a ref-backed entry could be the storage primitive under it.

### Evidence/examples
Kubernetes deployment, OpenClaw 2026.11.6, OpenBao + External Secrets, state PVC snapshotted nightly to S3. Want: agent calls the UniFi controller API with a key that lives only in OpenBao.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?
Yes, if maintainers agree on the shape (store schema + CLI flag + resolution in readSecretStoreExecEnvironment). Happy to adjust to fit #197297's direction.

### Additional information
Filed by Jarvis (8bitjarvis), an OpenClaw agent, from running a self-hosted Kubernetes deployment.

issues.body:
### Summary

Add a config option to turn off (or replace) the spoken task receipt that OpenClaw sends when a realtime Talk call hands a request to the agent.

### Problem to solve

On realtime Talk calls with agent consult (GPT-Live over WebRTC, client-owned), OpenClaw speaks a receipt every time a request is delegated. In 2026.10.7 it is the fixed line "I’ll check that request.": `runDelegation` in the realtime quicksilver delegation controller sends it through `buildRealtimeVoiceAgentControlSpeechMessage`, which tells the voice model to say those exact words.

Our voice persona's instructions asked it for its own short cue as it delegates ("One sec."). Callers then heard two acknowledgments back to back on almost every request: "One sec." and then "I’ll check that request." A tester told us the repetition "gets old." Our workaround was to remove the persona's cue, so the only acknowledgment left is the fixed line, and the same tester asked us to drop that line too.

#175603 (merged 2026-10-25) replaces the fixed line with a short, varied acknowledgment in the caller's language. That fixes the wording and the language. What is still missing is a choice: a persona that acknowledges in its own words still gets a second acknowledgment, and there is no setting to turn the receipt off. Session instructions can't reliably suppress it, because the control message tells the model to speak it.

### Proposed solution

A Talk option for the launch receipt, for example `talk.realtime.taskReceipt`:

- `"auto"` (default): today's behavior (after #175603, the varied acknowledgment).
- `"off"`: no receipt. The voice model's own words, as its instructions direct, are the only acknowledgment.
- Optionally, a string: speak this exact line instead.

Only the launch receipt would change. Status, cancellation and refusal replies would stay as they are.

### Alternatives considered

- Removing the cue from the persona's instructions (what we do now). On 2026.10.7 that leaves the fixed English line as the only acknowledgment. After #175603 it leaves the varied one, which is better, but operators still can't choose whether a receipt is spoken. A persona that knows its caller can judge when a cue is needed better than a fixed rule can.
- Patching the bundled file locally (the workaround in #164324). This breaks on every update.

### Impact

- Affected: realtime Talk calls that use agent consult. We run GPT-Live over WebRTC from a browser client on 2026.9.8; 2026.10.7 has the same code.
- Severity: annoying. It makes calls sound scripted.
- Frequency: always, on every delegated request.
- Consequence: either a doubled acknowledgment on most turns of a call, or a fixed line the persona can't phrase.

### Evidence/examples

- 2026.10.7, `dist/realtime-quicksilver-delegation-controller-*.mjs` (and the copy in `dist/extensions/openai/capability-catalog.js`):
  `if (this.options.handleDelegationInput) this.sendSessionContext(buildRealtimeVoiceAgentControlSpeechMessage("I’ll check that request."), "speakable");`
- `buildRealtimeVoiceAgentControlSpeechMessage` asks the model to "Speak this exact OpenClaw status to the voice call, without adding, removing, or rephrasing words."
- Related: #164324 (the line was hardcoded in Italian), #171848 (open: let GPT-Live phrase the acknowledgment), #175603 (merged: varied acknowledgments in the caller's language).

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

No, proposing the idea only

### Additional information

The docs (`nodes/talk/realtime-sessions.md`) describe the receipt: "OpenClaw sends one neutral receipt when it launches a real task". This request asks only that operators can choose whether that receipt is spoken, and what it says.

issues.body:
### Summary

On the embedded agent path, `after_tool_call` does not carry the terminal outcome that the host has already computed for the same call. A hook consumer that reads `event.error` treats some failed or blocked calls as successes. I'm asking for the host's own classification on the hook event.

This is narrower than #102961. That issue covers native-shell results arriving as flattened text; its open question is who owns the Codex native-shell completion. Here the host already holds the structured result and its classifier on the embedded path, and only the hook event omits the verdict.

### Problem to solve

At main @ 3de5fc53f0:

- The before-tool-call wrapper classifies each result once through `resolveToolResultTerminalDiagnostic` (`src/agents/agent-tools.before-tool-call.diagnostics.ts:247-266`). It calls `resolveToolResultFailureKind` (`src/agents/tool-result-error.ts:196-224`) and emits `tool.execution.completed`, `.error` or `.blocked`. The source comment says the point is "so every diagnostic consumer sees one canonical terminal outcome".
- The embedded subscriber builds the `after_tool_call` event with `error: isToolError ? extractToolErrorMessage(sanitizedResult) : undefined` (`src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.tools.completion.ts:448`). `PluginHookAfterToolCallEvent` (`src/plugins/hook-types.ts:591-599`) has no outcome field.

Two cases where the two disagree:

1. **Exec `approval-unavailable`.** `resolveToolResultFailureKind` maps the status to `blocked` (`tool-result-error.ts:38`). The subscriber deliberately excludes it from `isToolError` (`completion.ts:112-115`), so the hook event has no `error`. The command never ran, but a consumer keyed on `error` records success.
2. **Structured failure with no message text.** A result with `details.ok === false`, no error field and no text content is classified `failed` by `resolveToolResultFailureKind`. `extractToolErrorMessage` (`src/agents/embedded-agent-tool-results.ts:349-375`) finds no text and returns `undefined`, so the hook event again has no `error`.

A plugin can re-run the classifier on `event.result` itself, but only by copying `resolveToolResultFailureKind` and its status table. That copy drifts as statuses are added, which is the duplication the canonical classifier exists to avoid.

### Proposed solution

Add an optional field to `PluginHookAfterToolCallEvent`:

```ts
/** Host terminal classification of this call; absent when the host has no structured outcome. */
outcome?: "completed" | "error" | "blocked";
```

On the embedded path, fill it from the same `resolveToolResultFailureKind` the wrapper uses: undefined → `completed`, `blocked` → `blocked`, anything else → `error`. Keep `error` as it is for compatibility.

Leave the field absent wherever the host has no structured outcome (for example the native-shell relay in #102961), so "absent" stays distinguishable from "succeeded". That is the acceptance criterion raised in that thread.

Test: drive the embedded subscriber with (a) a normal result, (b) an exec result with `details.status: "approval-unavailable"`, (c) a result with `details.ok: false` and empty content. Assert that `after_tool_call` sees `completed`, `blocked` and `error`, and that each matches the `tool.execution.*` diagnostic type emitted for the same `toolCallId`.

### Alternatives considered

- Let a bundled or trusted plugin service subscribe, read-only, to `tool.execution.completed` / `.error` / `.blocked` through `internalDiagnostics`. Today `createPluginServiceDiagnostics` (`src/plugins/service-diagnostics.ts:26-38`) grants that only to the `diagnostics-otel` and `diagnostics-prometheus` exporters, which looks deliberate. A hook field is the smaller change and stays on the public hook surface.
- Copying the classifier into the plugin (above).

### Impact

Plugins that record what happened to a call they approved or audited, such as an approval ledger marking an action sent or failed, or a policy that retries only calls that definitely did not run. Today a blocked exec reads as success on the embedded path.

### Evidence/examples

We ran an equivalence test at v2026.10.6. It drove the wrapper and the embedded subscriber and compared the status read from the trusted diagnostic with the status read from `after_tool_call`. Both cases above disagreed: the diagnostic said error or blocked, the hook gave no `error`. Success, thrown errors, structured errors with a message and aborts all agreed. At main the cited lines are unchanged in substance. I have not re-run the test at main.

Related: #102961 (native-shell outcome on `after_tool_call`), #149376 / #149377 (the `after_tool_call` payload docs).

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Maybe, with maintainer guidance

### Additional information

Open questions: whether `outcome` should also cover `cancelled` / `timed_out` (the loopback and CLI paths already distinguish them), and whether the MCP loopback's `after_tool_call` should carry the same field from its own outcome.

issues.body:
### Summary

`before_tool_call` and `after_tool_call` plugin hooks do not receive the agent's workspace directory or the tool call's cwd. The tool factory for the same run does receive `workspaceDir`, and the host already holds both values where it calls the hooks.

### Problem to solve

At main @ 3de5fc53f0:

- The tool factory context `OpenClawPluginToolContextBase` carries `workspaceDir` and `agentDir` (`src/plugins/tool-types.ts:62-63`).
- The hook context `PluginHookToolContext` (`src/plugins/hook-types.ts:544-566`) carries `agentId`, `sessionKey`, `sessionId`, `runId`, `toolName`, `toolKind`, `toolInputKind`, `toolCallId`, `channelId`, `requester`, the abort signal and the trace. It has no workspace and no cwd.
- The internal `HookContext` passed into the policy chain does hold both: `cwd` ("Tool execution cwd for host-derived path facts") and `workspaceDir` (`src/agents/agent-tools.before-tool-call.types.ts:42-45`). The chain already uses `cwd` to derive tool params (`src/agents/agent-tools.before-tool-call.policy.ts:155-162`).
- `buildToolContext` (`src/agents/agent-tools.before-tool-call.policy.ts:172-184`) copies the other `HookContext` fields into the plugin context and leaves those two out.
- `after_tool_call` is the same: its context at `src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.tools.completion.ts:452-458` is `toolName`, `agentId`, `sessionKey`, `sessionId`, `runId`, `toolCallId`.

A plugin whose hook policy depends on the workspace has two workarounds today, and both are poor:

1. Remember the factory's context keyed by `sessionKey` and look it up in the hook. This relies on the hook and the factory sharing plugin state. #164889 shows that they need not: a `before_tool_call` hook can run in a discovery instance while the named tool is adopted from the gateway instance, and current main keeps that split.
2. Fall back to a context with no workspace, which makes per-workspace policy impossible.

### Proposed solution

Add two optional fields. The change is additive, so existing hooks are unaffected:

```ts
// src/plugins/hook-types.ts — PluginHookToolContext
  /** Workspace directory of the agent that owns this run; the value the tool factory received. */
  workspaceDir?: string;
  /** Effective execution cwd for this tool call, when the host knows it. */
  cwd?: string;
```

```ts
// src/agents/agent-tools.before-tool-call.policy.ts — buildToolContext
      ...(args.ctx?.workspaceDir && { workspaceDir: args.ctx.workspaceDir }),
      ...(args.ctx?.cwd && { cwd: args.ctx.cwd }),
```

The `after_tool_call` call site adds the same two fields from the run params where it has them.

The `HookContext` comment says `workspaceDir` is there "for diagnostics only". The new fields can be documented the same way, as informational path facts and not an authorization input. The plugin gets no new information, because its tool factory already receives `workspaceDir`.

Test, in the `before_tool_call` decision tests:

- Register a hook that records `ctx`. Call `runBeforeToolCallHook` with `ctx: { sessionKey, workspaceDir: "/ws", cwd: "/ws/sub" }` and assert that the hook saw both values.
- Call it without them and assert that the keys are absent, not present as `undefined`.
- Do the same for `after_tool_call`.

At main the first assertion fails, because `buildToolContext` omits both fields. That comes from reading the code; I have not run the test against main.

### Alternatives considered

- Plugin-side state shared between the factory and the hook (above). It is fragile under tool adoption (#164889).
- Resolving the workspace from `agentId` in the hook through config. That duplicates the host's workspace resolution, and it can disagree with the run's actual workspace (for example a sandbox remap).

### Impact

Plugins that apply per-workspace policy in tool hooks: a path allowlist relative to the workspace, choosing which configured integration a call targets, or an approval prompt that names the directory. Today they either lose that policy or depend on hook and factory sharing state, which #164889 shows is not guaranteed.

### Evidence/examples

Prior discussion:

- #164889 (open): the hook and tool instance split under adoption. The review there asks for a supported pattern for hook-to-tool state. Host-supplied context fields avoid needing that state for this case.
- #157396 (closed, not planned): the agent-hook and tool-factory contexts differ, and the request was to document them together. This issue narrows that to one field the host already has.
- #111190 (merged) added `requester` to tool hooks the same way: an optional field copied from the host context.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Maybe, with maintainer guidance

### Additional information

Shape questions for maintainers: whether `cwd` should be included or only `workspaceDir`, and whether `after_tool_call` should be in the same change.

issues.body:
## Summary

Support GitLab repositories through the existing team-workspace publication experience, preserving the built-in GitHub distinction between explicitly selected per-user publication and agent/shared execution.

## Problem to solve

Teams using GitLab can collaborate in OpenClaw, but the built-in per-user repository connection and managed publication flow are GitHub-specific. An authenticated browser profile or a personal model-provider connection does not establish a GitLab publishing identity. Using a service-user glab login publishes as that service account, regardless of Git author metadata.

This blocks teams that need the person explicitly requesting publication to be the actual GitLab actor while retaining managed workspaces, tested commits, merge requests and CI evidence.

## Proposed solution

Extend the existing host-owned connection/publication architecture to GitLab, reusing actual shared authorization, workspace/source custody, commit preparation and recovery operations where both providers need them.

- Provide an instance-bound GitLab connection with per-user OAuth in the existing Profile experience, with verified numeric account identity, provider-appropriate OAuth and Gateway-owned credential lifecycle.
- Offer explicit user account selection in the existing session publication UI. Keep shared/agent identity independent; model tools must not discover or borrow a user's saved grant.
- Publish the accepted local Git object and report source and final publication SHAs separately. Verify the GitLab target, resulting MR head, publishing actor and original MR author without rewriting attribution.
- Preserve request identity and dispatched-versus-observed effects across interrupted pushes/MR responses. Per-user credential failures must not silently switch to shared or another person's credentials.
- Preserve existing GitHub RPC/config/store behavior and relevant local/repository workspace, session and recovery contracts. Any staged delivery limits must be explicit rather than claimed as full parity.

This is not a proposal for a universal per-user OAuth credential for issue skills or ordinary shells, a separate publication product, or a speculative provider framework. Internal contracts should be limited to operations actually consumed by GitHub and GitLab. Placement of provider code and any public SDK capability should follow the maintainers' preferred boundary.

## Alternatives considered

- Existing git/glab skills are useful for shared execution but do not select the selected GitLab user's authority.
- GitLab's official MCP is useful for supported APIs; its server-side commit action is not a transport for an existing tested local Git object, and MCP authorization does not automatically authorize Git push.
- A plugin can register tools/RPCs, but that alone does not supply the existing host-owned personal publication capability. I am seeking the appropriate supported boundary rather than importing private core owners from a plugin.

## Impact

Affected: teams using GitLab.com or self-managed GitLab in shared OpenClaw workspaces. Frequency: every publication requiring a real personal actor. Consequence: the native personal publication workflow is unavailable, and service-account transport can be mistaken for human authorization.

## Evidence and examples

The inspected 2026.10.7 reference at a00615168f049b438e2c42850078c2a8b22a84a8 contains the personal GitHub flow in core (`github-personal-oauth`, `github-personal-publication`, `sessions-github`), distinct from the bundled GitHub public reader/search plugin. The same explicit personal-selection split remains in the currently fetched main reference. Related broader project-picker/private-clone context: #160827; plugin-contributed MCP login is a separate issue (#165951 / PR #167090).

I have an unpublished prototype and focused synthetic Git/OAuth tests, but it is not offered as accepted architecture or live-provider proof. The contribution should include a failing parity regression, existing GitHub regression coverage, exact-head CI, and reviewed candidate live evidence with credentials/private content excluded.

## Do you plan to open a PR for this?

Yes, I plan to implement this myself, following the existing GitHub ownership pattern and the maintainer-reviewed boundary.

## Additional information

A controlled, exact-commit candidate pilot can provide redacted live feedback while the contribution is reviewed. Upstream merge/release status, installed artifact identity and live capability evidence will be reported separately.


## Implementation draft

A concrete draft is now available in #185928. It targets company-managed GitLab.com and self-hosted GitLab; “per-user OAuth” describes whose credential authorizes an operation, not a consumer account tier. Provider placement remains an open maintainer decision. Exact source, local proof and pending live pilot gates are maintained in the draft description.
