prs.title: feat: add per-account proxy credentials with Shellgate
prs.body:
Related: #202751

## What Problem This Solves

Local reverse proxies can give people separate Basic-auth logins, but Bearer-capable automation needs individually revocable credentials too. Sharing the Gateway token/password instead authenticates clients as the shared owner rather than distinct proxy identities.

## User Impact

User impact: enable optional Shellgate to issue, list, rotate, and revoke per-account proxy Bearer tokens while retaining existing Caddy Basic accounts and Gateway profiles. `openclaw shellgate caddy` prints a maintained drop-in; existing Caddy configuration needs two imports inside an ordered route, not a separately maintained authentication service. Bearer-only ingress is supported too.

Keep HTTPS/private ingress and configure Gateway named-role ceilings: stripping client scopes alone is not least privilege. Nothing edits a live proxy or Gateway configuration. Tokens are not Gateway/device tokens, local accounts do not establish verified email/GitHub identity, and proxy revocation does not close already-upgraded WebSockets or revoke paired devices. Normal security/dependency review remains required before merge.

## Why This Change Was Made

Shellgate owns only random-token verifiers and stable subject bindings, using existing asynchronous plugin SQLite storage and administrator-scoped RPCs. Caddy owns Basic authentication/TLS/proxying; Gateway owns profiles, roles, pairing, and session permissions. No new core auth mode, custom database schema, external dependency, credential cache, or background service.

The generated drop-in hides verification, strips client identity/scope claims and consumed credentials, preserves HTTP bodies, and verifies WebSocket requests without upgrading the verification subrequest. Invalid Bearer never falls back to Basic. CLI output is declared machine-readable so diagnostics cannot corrupt redirected Caddy configuration or credential JSON. The complete production implementation is 292 TypeScript lines, including the 39-line Caddy template; this follow-up adds 48 production lines rather than another proxy implementation.

## Evidence

**Real Caddy 2.11.9 → built isolated Gateway passed on the source published as `496a124d3cb1d3edbd5ffe21824426a84aadd7b8`:** actual administrator CLI/RPC issuance; signed-device pairing; Basic and Bearer bind to one human profile; a service gets a distinct limited profile; forged identity/scope headers do not grant admin; rotation/revocation and cold-restart persistence work. The run consumed the exact snippet printed by the real CLI, not a parallel test recipe.

Four focused tests pass (real SQLite/HTTP plus lazy CLI metadata). The committed optional real-Caddy test passes HTTP/body forwarding, custom identity-header handling, WebSocket upgrades, stripping, no fallback, revocation, and a stalled-request abort with process cleanup. Multi-space Bearer parsing and missing machine-output metadata each failed before their fixes and pass afterward. Full build, targeted package typecheck/lint/format, MDX and diff checks pass.

[Hosted ClawSweeper review](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/203178#issuecomment-7066507286) of `496a124d3cb1d3edbd5ffe21824426a84aadd7b8`: **4/6 readiness, 4/6 proof confidence, 4/6 patch quality; no actionable findings.** It accepted the public live output as sufficient. The latest follow-up `d994e8408304021d96c5fd93558b62ce75eaf80e` changes only the disposable test WebSocket server to an explicit 64 KiB payload bound, addressing the scanner comment; its real-Caddy test and focused lint/format pass. Production code and the live Gateway proof remain exactly those reviewed at `496a124d`—the rating is not relabeled as a fresh review of the test-only follow-up.

Independent source review also identified machine-readable CLI metadata and bounded test cleanup; both were fixed before `496a124d`. Standard Auto Review is unavailable because its installed helper is missing; this is not an Auto Review pass.

<details>
<summary>Actual sanitized Caddy/Gateway output and reproduction</summary>

Run on Node 24.20.0 with Caddy 2.11.9, disposable state and generated synthetic credentials. No production configuration or credentials were used. Published source snapshot: Git tree `9671c04922b61c1116f24519882c12f2d5c63df8`, integrated base `282121402940c47c87a68bf08bb6e66097818884`. Generated snippet SHA-256: `c9acfebb02e7c984e5a43cc3be128e15d9c1224e0de45f88fb5ce501873dc96c`.

```text
PASS offline CLI redirected stdout equals generated snippet; startup warning on stderr
PASS isolated built Gateway ready
PASS real administrator CLI and RPC issue credentials {"cliTokenIssued":true,"rpcTokenIssued":true}
PASS initial Basic sign-in admitted
PASS administrator Basic sign-in admitted
PASS Basic and Bearer preserve one human profile with signed-device pairing {"sameProfile":true,"basicScopes":["operator.questions","operator.sessions.write","operator.admin"],"bearerScopes":["operator.questions","operator.sessions.write","operator.admin"]}
PASS distinct service profile and admin-only credential RPC despite forged claims {"distinctProfile":true,"scopes":["operator.questions","operator.sessions.write"],"adminRpcOk":false,"error":"missing scope: operator.admin"}
PASS HTTP named-role ceiling prevents scope-header escalation {"basicHttp":200,"serviceHttp":500,"error":"missing scope: operator.admin"}
PASS private verifier hidden and invalid Bearer refused
PASS revocation refuses new authentication without claiming existing-socket termination
PASS rotation invalidates old token while Basic remains independent {"oldBearer":401,"newBearer":200,"basic":200}
PASS cold Gateway restart retains rotated credentials and revocations {"rotatedBearer":200,"revokedBearer":401}
CLEANUP owned processes stopped
```

The HTTP admin RPC adapter returned HTTP 500 with the explicit missing-scope error for the limited subject; this is an observed authorization rejection, not a claim of HTTP 403. The same operation succeeded for the administrator. Existing sockets intentionally remained usable after proxy-token revocation, as documented.

Reproducible committed proxy test (locally available Caddy binary):

```sh
pnpm test:extension shellgate --maxWorkers=1
SHELLGATE_CADDY_BINARY=/path/to/caddy node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.live.config.ts extensions/shellgate/src/caddy.live.test.ts
pnpm build
node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p extensions/shellgate/tsconfig.json --noEmit
node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig extensions/tsconfig.json extensions/shellgate
```

The full isolated Gateway run additionally used the documented setup, real `shellgate issue`, `users.self`, `users.setRole`, signed protocol handshakes, administrator RPCs, token rotation/revocation, and a cold Gateway restart. It did not exercise inference or a real user's browser. All owned listeners/processes were stopped.

</details>

**CI/review:** current-head CI is authoritative; no all-green claim. The three earlier failing jobs passed on `586809ba` in [run 44927782859](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44927782859); that is prior-head evidence. The plugin adds only the existing SDK workspace link, but its manifest/lockfile still require repository-admin or active SecOps approval. Generated baseline growth is exactly 24 standard plugin-wrapper paths, with an empty custom configuration schema; no check was disabled.

Not claimed: production deployment, Android changes, external EDGE/TLS validation, real-user browser login, or inference.

### Clean artwork comparison

| Before | After |
| --- | --- |
| ![Shellgate before: missing package artwork](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/02ff1644-a369-4683-bd4d-0b952ffd85e8) | ![Shellgate after: packaged identity artwork](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f7a4908a-5437-4b2e-b062-61ca34834567) |

### Annotated artwork comparison

prs.title: fix: open legacy session links from the terminal
prs.body:
Closes #202569.

## What Problem This Solves

An older Control UI link can open in the browser and return
`No session found` in the terminal when its literal key looks like a short ID.

## User Impact

`openclaw tui` and `openclaw attach` can reuse those links to open an
existing session. If the short ID matches more than one session, the CLI
still asks the user to disambiguate.

## Why This Change Was Made

The URL parser already provides the exact key. Keep it through CLI
resolution and ask the same Gateway for that key after a short lookup
reports no match.

## Evidence

At `8d0cd99f4b09`, the production CLI resolver returned
`No session found: deadbeef` for `/chat/ops/release-deadbeef`.
The same local Gateway response fixture resolves the exact key after the change.
The suite also checks that ambiguous short IDs still stop resolution. The
three focused suites passed all 56 tests on Windows with Node 24.22.3
(61.2 s runner time). Core typechecking and the touched-file lint and format
checks passed.

```sh
pnpm test src/cli/session-ref.test.ts src/cli/session-target.test.ts src/cli/attach-cli.action.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```

### Running Gateway proof

Built the QA runtime with `pnpm build qaRuntime` and started
`node openclaw.mjs gateway run` with a fresh state directory on Windows
(Node 24.22.3). The build used base `8d0cd99f4b09` plus the three review
patches in this local batch. The two changed CLI source files matched this
PR's head `8355e969898e` byte for byte.

Created `agent:main:release-deadbeef` through the running Gateway's
`sessions.create` RPC. In that same Gateway, called `sessions.resolve`
with `{"shortId":"deadbeef","slugHint":"release","allowMissing":true}`.
Then ran the built CLI against the legacy URL using an explicit Gateway
token and a 30 s grant lifetime. The loopback address and tokens are
redacted below. The final line is a projection of the printed config.

```text
sessions.resolve (short ID) -> {"ok":false}
node openclaw.mjs attach http://<loopback>/chat/main/release-deadbeef --token <redacted> --ttl 30000 --print-config
exit=0  sessionKey=agent:main:release-deadbeef  scopedGrantIssued=true
```

The CLI opened the existing literal session key after the Gateway's short-ID
miss. I revoked the scoped grant after checking the returned config.

prs.title: fix: explain why computer use is unavailable on text-only models
prs.body:
Closes #202433.

## What Problem This Solves

A text-only model cannot use the computer tool. The session capability list
can still say the tool is available, so the user has no reason to switch models.

## User Impact

The capability list identifies image input as the missing requirement for the
selected model. Existing tool-policy exclusions keep their own reasons.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use the selected model's input metadata when building the capability list.
That lets the existing tool builder enforce the same vision requirement in
the preview and at runtime. Add the reason to the tool access report.

## Evidence

At `8d0cd99f4b09`, the real inventory builder listed `computer` for a
text-only model. With the fix, the text-only model reports that it cannot
accept image input. A model with image input still lists `computer`.
The test uses local model fixtures without a provider request or a paired desktop.
The three focused suites passed all 19 tests on Windows with Node 24.22.3.
The new file took 58.1 s including test setup and transformation.
Core typechecking and the touched-file lint and format checks passed.

```sh
pnpm test src/agents/tools-effective-inventory.computer.test.ts src/agents/tools-effective-inventory.test.ts src/agents/tools/session-status-capabilities.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```

### Running Gateway proof

Built the QA runtime with `pnpm build qaRuntime` and started
`node openclaw.mjs gateway run` with a fresh state directory on Windows
(Node 24.22.3). The build used base `8d0cd99f4b09` plus the three review
patches in this local batch. The inventory source file matched this PR's
head `bad375fae610` byte for byte.

Configured two local model definitions with `input: ["text"]` and
`input: ["text", "image"]` and set the tool profile to `full`.
Created a separate session per model through `sessions.create` with the
model explicitly selected. Queried each with
`openclaw gateway call tools.effective --params '{"agentId":"main","sessionKey":"<session key>"}' --json`.
The provider URL was local and the inventory requests made no inference calls.

Redacted projection of the two RPC responses (`listed` checks
`groups[].tools[]` and the other fields come from `toolAccess`):

```text
review-local/text-only  listed=false  status=unavailable  reason="The selected model does not support image input"
review-local/vision     listed=true   status=available    reasons=[]
```

Red-on-base: with only this PR's regression test applied to
`8d0cd99f4b09`, the following command exited 1 with
`expected [ 'agents_list', 'apply_patch', …(39) ] to not include 'computer'`.
The same test passed with the production fix.

```sh
pnpm test src/agents/tools-effective-inventory.computer.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```

prs.title: fix(whatsapp): show the sender number in group quotes
prs.body:
Closes #202554.

## What Problem This Solves

When a message quotes a WhatsApp group participant, OpenClaw can show an internal
`@lid` address even when the linked account already knows the sender's number.
That makes it harder to tell who wrote the quoted message.

## User Impact

The quote shows the mapped number when the linked account has a mapping. Quotes
still show the WhatsApp address if there is no mapping.

## Why This Change Was Made

Pass the receiving account's auth directory from the inbox to the existing
identity resolver. Use the resolved identity for both the quote label and the
structured sender data.

## Evidence

The local inbox test sent a group message that quotes `555@lid`. The receiving
account had a synthetic reverse mapping for `+1555`. At `8d0cd99f4b09`,
the displayed label was `555@lid`. With the fix, the same event produced
`+1555` and kept the original LID in the quoted identity. The three focused
suites passed all 35 tests on Windows with Node 24.22.3 (122.4 s runner time).
The touched files passed local lint and formatting checks.

```sh
pnpm test extensions/whatsapp/src/monitor-inbox.reply-context.test.ts extensions/whatsapp/src/inbound/extract.test.ts extensions/whatsapp/src/inbound/message-enrichment.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
```

The test runs the WhatsApp inbox with a simulated socket event and a real
mapping file in an isolated local account directory.

prs.title: fix(models): model picker switches chat to models the user cannot sign in to from chat
prs.body: Supersedes #180828, which Barnacle closed for inactivity on 2026-11-18 and which GitHub cannot reopen. This is the same branch, updated to current `main` and with the open ClawSweeper finding fixed. Live proof is below. ## What Problem This Solves Fixes: selecting a listed but unauthenticated model in the chat model picker (for example `meta/muse-spark-1.3` before Meta sign-in) reports success, pins the chat to a model that can only fail authentication, and then answers every message with a generic HTTP 401 that gives no direct way to authorize — forcing the user to switch back to another model and hunt for the sign-in flow. ## User Impact Tapping a model whose provider has no working sign-in now keeps the current model and immediately shows how to connect that provider: a tappable sign-in button for OAuth/device-code providers, secure API-key entry instructions for API-key-only providers (for example OpenCode Go), and a deep link to Control UI → Settings → Model Providers (carrying `?provider=&agent=`) when the gateway advertises a public origin. Auth failures at run time name the provider and carry the same buttons instead of generic boilerplate. Not blocked: ready, unconfirmed, and cooling-down models; reset-to-default and default selections; and selections on a gateway whose `cloudWorkers.requiredProfile` is a worker-inference device profile (provider credentials live on the node there, per #170132), unless the selection pins an explicit Gateway account. No secrets are requested or stored in chat, and no credential-bearing links are placed in chat. ## Why This Change Was Made The picker already computed per-model readiness for display, but selection ignored it, and failure copy dropped the provider before rendering. - The policy lives in the shared selection owner (`applySessionModelSelectionInternal`). Adapters opt in by passing the exact menu facts they rendered (`authReadinessMenu`); a rejection is a dedicated `reason: "auth"` result with a required `authBlock`. Telegram only renders the result. Typed `/model` and `sessions.patch` keep their current behavior and only gain the better failure guidance. - Menu readiness describes Gateway credentials, so it cannot judge required worker-local inference. The #170132 exception is now one exported predicate in the runtime-normalization owner (`isProviderAuthOwnedByRequiredWorker`), used both by runtime preparation and by the picker gate. Gateway inference, optional placement, and explicit account pins stay gated. - Each provider's concrete login route is resolved so recovery can tell API-key entry from OAuth sign-in. The provider is carried through failover facts, including typed auth errors buried in the cause graph. Provider ids are slug-validated before they are embedded in commands or guidance. **Needs a maintainer decision (ClawSweeper "Decision needed"):** should Telegram reject unauthenticated picker selections through the new optional `authReadinessMenu` SDK parameter and `reason: "auth"` result variant, while other selection surfaces (Discord/Mattermost pickers, typed `/model`, `sessions.patch`) keep their current behavior? The PR is built so other adapters can opt in with the same contract later. ## Evidence Head `3605425fd50`. Current `main` (`8479dacd2e1`) was merged in `7941ecf947f`; there were conflicts in the failover copy files and `agent-runner-error-handler.ts`: - Upstream's `user-copy.ts` is at 699 of its 700-line limit, so this PR's provider-aware copy moved into `src/agents/failover/provider-auth-user-copy.ts`, with its own test. `user-copy.ts` and its test are byte-identical to upstream. - New strings say "the OpenClaw app" and "Open OpenClaw", following upstream #199226. **[P2] Ignore incompatible old account pins in the worker-auth exemption (`06c5420739b`).** `shouldPreserveSessionAuthProfileForSelection` in `auth-profile-preservation.ts` is now shared by the gate and by `applyModelOverrideWithAuthProfileCompatibility`. The worker exemption therefore judges only the account pin that survives the selection. Regression: with an old `anthropic:work` pin, before the fix the result was `rejected` where `applied` was expected; after the fix it is `applied`. A same-provider pin is still gated. **Plugin SDK declaration budget (`3605425fd50`).** The combined build failed `check-plugin-sdk-exports` by 590 bytes. This PR's long JSDoc on SDK-visible types became line comments. No types or behavior changed. Regression for the worker-local finding (`src/model-picker/apply-session-model-selection.test.ts`, "shared auth gate defers Gateway readiness only to required worker inference"; cases `worker`, `gateway`, `optional`, `account`): - Without the fix: `worker` fails (`Expected: "applied"`, `Received: "rejected"`); the other three pass. - With the fix: 4/4 pass. Focused suites (`node scripts/test-projects.mts --maxWorkers=1`), all passing. After the merge: 11 files, 237 tests. The combined proof branch ran all three PRs' focused suites: 21 files, 598 tests, 0 failed. Files: - `src/model-picker/apply-session-model-selection.test.ts` - `src/auto-reply/reply/commands-models-menu.test.ts` - `src/agents/failover/user-copy.test.ts`, `src/agents/failover/failover-classification.corpus.test.ts` - `src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-failure-reply.test.ts`, `src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-execution-provider-failures.test.ts` - `src/plugin-sdk/provider-auth-login-flow-runtime.test.ts` - `src/agents/model-runtime-choice.native.test.ts` (the #170132 worker/gateway/optional/account suite, still green after moving its predicate) - `extensions/telegram/src/model-callback.loopback.integration.test.ts` (blocked selection keeps the current model and renders the Sign in button) - `ui/src/pages/model-providers/route.test.ts` Typecheck: `tsgo` core, extensions, UI, and the `messaging`, `other`, and extensions test projects are clean. `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` are clean on touched files. Removed per review: the `buildModelsMenu` "exposes per-model readiness and login providers" case, which only checked copied input identity. Before the fix, observed on a real Telegram + gateway install: selecting `meta/muse-spark-1.3` printed "✅ Model changed", then every message returned "⚠️ Authentication failed (provider returned HTTP 401)…", and `/login meta` answered with setup text and no link. ## Live proof Real Telegram private chat with a live Gateway on 2026-11-20. The Gateway ran upstream `main` `8479dacd2e1` merged with #180828, #180830 and #180831 (combined build `28efb83`; the three PRs were merged together because the author runs them together). Telegram IDs and device codes are redacted. Screenshots are hosted at [ivankuznetsov/openclaw@224a663](https://github.com/ivankuznetsov/openclaw/tree/224a6636a4ada057f2c61f0e7445f364e765e967). **(1) Blocked picker selection with recovery.** In `/models`, tapping a model labeled `Sign-in needed` replies `⚠️ Model not changed: … needs a working sign-in first … Your current model is unchanged.` with a **Sign in** button. A `/status` afterwards shows the model unchanged. Two providers were checked: Meta (Muse, native) and xAI. The Sign in button started the Meta device sign-in in chat, captured in #180831. | Meta: models | Meta: selection blocked | `/status` after | xAI: selection blocked | |---|---|---|---| | | | | | **(1b) Full recovery path to a working reply (xAI).** Tapping Grok 4.6, labeled `Sign-in needed`, replies `Model not changed … Sign in`. **Sign in** starts xAI's device-code sign-in in the chat. After approval the chat says `xAI (Grok) login complete`, the xai models show as available, and a turn returns a real reply: `OK, I am Grok (xai/grok-4.3)`. Selecting `xai/grok-4.7` also returns a real reply: `OK, I am xai/grok-4.7`. | Blocked, with Sign in | Device code in chat | Login complete | Models available | Real reply | |---|---|---|---|---| | | | | | | Observations outside this PR's changes: - After a sign-in started from the picker, the completion text `Try your request again now` (upstream `formatProviderLoginCompletion`) reads as if a request had failed. "Select the model again" would match the gate's own wording. This is a small follow-up. - When `xai/grok-4.7` was not yet in `modelPolicy.allow`, `/model xai/grok-4.7` silently selected `xai/grok-4.3` through fuzzy matching. The documented `Model override … is not allowed` error never appeared. That is upstream behavior and not changed here. Ready models are not blocked: after sign-in, selecting the Muse model and switching to DeepSeek both apply normally (captures in #180830). **Upgrade with real data.** The same Gateway was upgraded in place from a 2026.10.10 build (base 2026-11-04) to this build. The state migration ran (`state/openclaw.sqlite` v39 and agent databases v40 to 2026.11.5) and the background integrity checks passed. All 158 stored sessions are present afterwards. None changed `model`, `modelProvider`, `providerOverride`, `modelOverride`, `agentRuntime`, `thinkingLevel` or `authProfileOverride`. This is a real operator state, not the latest stable tag; a v2026.11.6 → head run is not included. **Not covered live:** - (2) The Control UI handoff for an API-key-only provider. Every API-key provider in this operator's config is signed in. - (3) A run-time 401 with provider buttons. That would have required breaking a working key on a live Gateway. - The required-worker case. There is no worker node. These stay covered by the tests listed above, including the Telegram loopback integration test. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

prs.title: fix: avoid rereading unchanged sandbox files on reuse
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The first reuse of a sandbox workspace cloned from a prepared template reads every unchanged source file again. On the 62,006-file synthetic workspace this adds roughly five seconds to preparation, even though the template producer already established the file contents.

## User Impact

Sessions can reuse the template-derived workspace without that redundant content read. Both live metadata walks, external-edit detection, recent-write safety, and recovery remain. Initial observation of the live canonical workspace is unchanged. No configuration, schema, migration, or operator action is added.

The measured tradeoffs below have separate performance-owner acceptance for this PR, recorded verbatim below.

## Why This Change Was Made

The template manifest producer already visits the immutable files. It now carries their existing fingerprint format through the existing 64 MiB byte-bounded manifest LRU and the existing baseline publication. Btrfs preserves inode and ctime during the native clone; the publication worker rebinds the clone device and the prepared-directory tree root. Other clone backends retain their current behavior. There is no new cache, persistence format, scan shortcut, or retention policy.

Production delta: +84 lines across the existing producer, transport, codec, and publication owners. The growth carries prepared facts across those boundaries; it removes the repeated full-content read rather than creating a second scan owner.

## Evidence

Acceptance rule: two baseline A/A controls and five serial counterbalanced pairs on the same native Btrfs rig, using fresh outputs and the same frozen harness. Require identical accepted bytes/types/symlinks/deletions, two live metadata probes, 62,006→0 first-reuse content hashes, and at least 5% lower first-reuse latency. Report cold preparation, every later phase, CPU, allocation and tails. No adverse metric is implicitly accepted.

All twelve runs completed with identical final contents. Baseline first reuse reads 1,142,784,919 bytes; candidate reads zero. A/A first-reuse controls: 4,880.94 / 4,408.98 ms. Five-pair medians:

| Phase | Wall ms baseline → candidate | Main CPU ms | Process CPU ms | Main allocation MiB |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| first | 19,988.58 → 19,939.82 | 1,022.08 → 1,044.90 | 22,095.33 → 22,759.91 | 402.46 → 414.45 |
| unchanged-1 | 4,887.90 → 1,144.19 | 60.81 → 48.32 | 7,015.70 → 1,244.54 | 11.50 → 11.18 |
| unchanged-2 | 845.14 → 988.43 | 42.52 → 49.12 | 925.20 → 1,005.98 | 7.43 → 7.87 |
| guest-export | 3,099.93 → 3,094.12 | 167.29 → 166.25 | 3,562.77 → 3,502.03 | 35.97 → 32.02 |
| host-import | 2,617.42 → 2,769.27 | 211.05 → 225.29 | 2,661.31 → 2,800.58 | 25.59 → 21.07 |
| post-import-reuse | 987.04 → 1,104.78 | 47.56 → 50.10 | 1,181.45 → 1,264.35 | 8.19 → 9.38 |
| post-import-steady | 914.20 → 1,020.66 | 51.06 → 67.35 | 1,089.20 → 1,204.95 | 5.93 → 6.23 |
| sum | 33,139.36 → 30,508.24 | 1,675.93 → 1,689.22 | 38,707.70 → 34,217.13 | 488.56 → 496.70 |

First-reuse median improves 76.6%, process CPU 82.3%, and matched-worker allocation 1,984.0→868.5 MiB. The seven-phase sum improves 7.9% in wall time and 11.6% in process CPU; matched-worker allocation falls 7,542,306,960→6,399,456,144 bytes. Worker deltas exclude newly started/unavailable workers; cold worker allocation is incomplete, not zero. Process CPU excludes native child processes. Main allocation is measured separately.

**Adverse metrics:** total main CPU +0.8%, main allocation +1.7%; cold preparation process CPU +3.0% and main allocation +3.0%. Second unchanged reuse wall +17.0%, host import +5.8%, post-import reuse +11.9%, post-import steady +11.6%. Post-import steady main CPU rises 51.1→67.4 ms (+31.9%). The separately sampled profile pass does not reproduce those later-reuse slowdowns; it does not replace the timing rows or establish acceptance.

First-reuse min–max: 4,608.85–6,375.73 ms → 850.28–1,209.50 ms. With five samples, maximum is nearest-rank p95. Whole-sequence maximum: 36,652.97→31,856.25 ms.

<details><summary>Every phase maximum (nearest-rank p95, five samples)</summary>

| Phase | Wall ms | Main CPU ms | Process CPU ms | Main allocation MiB |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| first | 21,256.56 → 21,112.08 | 1,283.27 → 1,171.57 | 23,110.85 → 24,417.93 | 411.49 → 417.20 |
| unchanged-1 | 6,375.73 → 1,209.50 | 74.20 → 50.90 | 8,871.66 → 1,328.29 | 13.46 → 14.18 |
| unchanged-2 | 909.73 → 1,039.91 | 47.19 → 50.86 | 974.62 → 1,154.42 | 8.78 → 10.76 |
| guest-export | 3,342.44 → 3,592.18 | 234.41 → 182.32 | 4,197.01 → 4,140.92 | 36.28 → 35.57 |
| host-import | 3,100.72 → 3,480.92 | 218.07 → 243.84 | 3,168.63 → 3,340.55 | 33.70 → 26.05 |
| post-import-reuse | 1,107.36 → 1,345.53 | 65.32 → 53.97 | 1,212.74 → 1,428.42 | 12.82 → 11.17 |
| post-import-steady | 1,132.26 → 1,103.60 | 84.77 → 80.88 | 1,121.15 → 1,383.86 | 6.33 → 6.42 |
| sum | 36,652.97 → 31,856.25 | 1,901.16 → 1,806.93 | 41,897.86 → 36,058.44 | 502.00 → 509.13 |

</details>

The separate CPU/heap profiles attribute baseline first-reuse work to file open/read/close and abort bookkeeping. Profiled Git-worker CPU falls 4,995.5→828.3 ms. Both metadata walks remain. Main profiles are dominated by waits, existing spawn/GC, and profiler controls. Timing and profile samples are not pooled.

Focused producer/codec tests and the 118 consumer cases pass (two existing consumer skips); core, core-test and script typechecks, lint, format, database guards pass. Isolated Codex P0–P2 review is clean. Both frozen compiled runtime builds pass. The compiled Gateway completed three real `openai/gpt-4.1-mini` calls per revision with successful terminal events through ordinary WebSocket `sessions.create` / `chat.send`, preserving exact HEAD, clean index, source and installed dependencies. Its history-wide sentinel check also matched the input prompt, so that assertion does not establish exact assistant reply text; the timing and filesystem assertions are independent. The first reuse is the second send in this reproduction: startup **5,342→1,361 ms**, `reuse.reconcile` **4,841→944 ms**, model completion **7,451→4,663 ms**. The initial send still pays the separate canonical observation: startup 10,041→9,946 ms, initial checkpoint 4,015→4,132 ms. Third-send startup 1,129→1,196 ms and reuse 742→794 ms are disclosed unaffected variation, not claimed gains. This PR does not claim to fix the initial canonical scan.

`pnpm check:changed` passed all selected gates except two dead exports in untouched hook owners. A clean detached checkout of the exact parent c6a27e6a3484ad923ff77ced84d76a0ece87cac8, with its own frozen install, reproduces the identical findings under `node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/check-deadcode-exports.mts`:

prs.title: fix: show storage waits in chat startup diagnostics
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A first chat send can wait on input persistence, session-writer admission, or other preparation before the existing `attempt.*` phases begin. The operator sees the startup delay without a phase naming the earlier wait.

## User Impact

The existing slow-chat-send details and diagnostic phase exports now name those waits. This is observability work: it does not reduce storage latency or change turn ordering, authority, or durability. No new product configuration, schema, cache, persistence policy, or log stream is introduced.

Owner direction: the Team perf-loop lead (an agent acting under Peter's standing unattended instruction), not Peter. This is lane 2699's separate storage-observability owner PR, after #202960 and #203112. MCP materialization timeout work remains with its separate owner.

## Implementation

Input, runner, session-bootstrap, placement, and dispatch owners mark their awaited preparation with the existing timeline observer. Scopes end before inference, including the placement callback and execution-start handoff. The unchanged deferred-maintenance/projection wait moves into session bootstrap to keep the runner within its module limit.

Useful fields include `detail.reply.storage.input.read`, `detail.reply.storage.input.persist`, `detail.run.storage.session_admission`, `detail.run.storage.transcript_projection`, `detail.run.storage.writer_admission`, and `detail.run.storage.writer_claim`. Existing exporters receive `chat.send.detail.*` events. Nested phases can overlap; do not sum every detail field.

Production growth is +106 lines for phase coverage and imports; tests +19 and benchmark/docs +447, total +572. No new scan, storage operation, or competing owner is added.

## Correctness and Storage Attribution

The existing real session-actor admission regression fails on exact parent `c9cf00b31d596665cd79393bac414fcbad1f0fea`: blocked input has no active storage phase. It passes here while retaining exact committed-input and adoption assertions. Focused consumers pass 208 tests in 17 files; targeted UI suites pass five tests, including real-Gateway worker-placement admission. Codex P0–P2 review is clean.

A compiled Gateway with a real model and a synthetic 250 ms explicit-COMMIT hold produced:

```text
detail.reply.prepare.input_admission=542ms
detail.reply.storage.input.read=1ms
detail.reply.storage.input.persist=540ms
detail.run.storage.writer_admission=1ms
detail.run.storage.writer_claim=273ms
```

The persistence interval contains a 255 ms read-snapshot commit followed by one 251 ms actor write. The actor already combines admitted input and running lifecycle in that write. These are not two redundant writes to batch, and this evidence does not justify deferring durability. Exact assistant-only replies and once-only committed inputs pass. This staged-input qualification is separate from the idle-admission overhead cohorts.

## Reproduction and Predeclared Rule

Committed workload:

```sh
node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/startup-storage-measure.mts \
  --workspace /absolute/synthetic-repository --output /absolute/new-output \
  --entry dist/entry.js --samples 1 --commit-delay-ms 250 \
  --sandbox-image prepared-local-podman-image
```

Each fresh compiled Gateway/session receives two undelayed warmups and one measured send. Run two A/A controls and five serial counterbalanced parent/candidate pairs at 250 ms COMMIT delay, then separately at zero delay. CPU profiles use a separate pair; allocation uses a separate two A/A controls plus five pairs. The rig has 62,000 files/~1.1 GB on Btrfs and separate 35 GiB synthetic storage. Active Gateway databases are fresh: this is not an active 35 GiB database-scan benchmark. The real provider is `openai/gpt-4.1-mini`.

Every measurement now extends through native `agent.wait` completion and `sessions.describe.hasActiveRun === false`, including the last sample. Chat final and subsequent settlement are recorded separately. The preload delays real explicit COMMITs, including read snapshots; records are not write/fsync counts and do not reproduce Btrfs internals. Main/process CPU excludes native subprocess CPU. Allocation is sampled on the main isolate, including collected objects. Profiled timings do not supply latency acceptance. Cold-session rows remain separate; shared filesystem caches are not reset.

The published rule requires exact replies/inputs, active phases during blocked operations, unchanged foreground storage ownership/counts, and disclosure of every worse metric. A worse metric requires explicit performance-owner acceptance. Report medians and observed maxima for n=5, not an estimated tail distribution. The performance owner rejected this change as-is; the exact decision is recorded below.

## Corrected Full-Turn Results (v3)

All measured sends pass exact assistant/input checks. Ordinary timing runs have 16 explicit COMMITs each. Delayed candidates also have 16; parent pairs 3 and 5 have 17 because a background cold-transcript selection read snapshot overlaps the window. Stack attribution distinguishes that read from admitted-input writes.

Median (maximum), milliseconds:

| Metric | Parent | Candidate |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 250 ms hold: startup | 3,850 (5,768) | 3,674 (4,112) |
| 250 ms hold: chat final | 6,454.99 (7,979.01) | 6,091.39 (6,658.81) |
| 250 ms hold: complete turn | 6,991.58 (8,509.28) | 6,632.61 (7,225.38) |
| 250 ms hold: settlement | 527.05 (565.00) | 554.01 (573.66) |
| 250 ms hold: main CPU | 791.97 (1,091.87) | 718.30 (761.03) |
| 250 ms hold: process CPU | 2,948.58 (3,975.35) | 2,731.70 (2,966.87) |
| Zero hold: startup | 1,340 (1,415) | 1,284 (1,618) |
| Zero hold: chat final | 2,193.29 (2,409.64) | 2,647.67 (2,875.72) |
| Zero hold: complete turn | 2,196.67 (2,438.39) | 2,673.19 (2,879.62) |
| Zero hold: settlement | 18.57 (27.58) | 7.37 (24.04) |
| Zero hold: main CPU | 290.91 (301.59) | 289.50 (380.19) |
| Zero hold: process CPU | 1,543.09 (1,610.04) | 1,564.78 (1,883.47) |

Delayed complete-wall A/A: 8,239.34/7,023.95 ms; ordinary A/A: 2,434.72/2,252.72 ms. This instrumentation claims no speedup. Adverse cells include delayed settlement median +5.11%, ordinary complete wall **+21.69%**, process CPU +1.41%, and ordinary startup/CPU maxima. They remain unaccepted.

Existing provider records show one user-model logical call per measured ordinary turn: median 799→1,060 ms. All output seven tokens and read 7,296 cached tokens; prompt lengths vary with synthetic session/workspace context, so the requests are not byte-identical. Per-sample complete wall minus provider duration has median 1,461.67→1,396.19 ms. This arithmetic residual helps attribution but does not replace the adverse user-facing metric; medians do not add.

Cold first-send complete-wall median/max in the delayed cohort: 25.725/29.275→23.513/24.647 s. In the ordinary cohort: **20.666/28.704→21.211/41.626 s**; startup 18.745/26.627→19.413/39.652 s. Ordinary cold main-CPU median 2,165.67→2,265.99 ms and process CPU 22,280.63→22,737.93 ms. The 41.626 s candidate row spends 15.041 s materializing the checkout versus paired parent 3.726 s, with no SQLite-busy warning. It is retained as an adverse tail; timing attribution to an unchanged path does not establish absence of causality.

Separate full-turn allocation (two A/A controls plus five counterbalanced pairs): sampled main bytes median **59,389,544→63,288,320 (+6.56%, +3.72 MiB)**, maxima 62,449,176→66,372,776. A/A 61,927,744/61,939,704 bytes. GC total per capture median **5.133→17.183 ms**, maxima 7.705→28.055; GC count median 2→8. Event-loop maximum median 33.079→38.470 ms, largest 39.748→40.731. These adverse cells are unaccepted. All measured allocation samples have 16 COMMITs and pass exact reply/input assertions. The pre-measurement warmup failure below is retained separately.

## Preserved Adverse Evidence and Profiling Limits

The earlier v2 workload ended at chat final, omitting native settlement from resource accounting. Its latency results remain valid: ordinary startup **1,457→2,580 ms (+77.08%)**, chat-final wall **2,857.94→4,290.62 ms (+50.13%)**, main CPU +18.79%, process CPU +3.68%, sampled main allocation +4.59%. Three candidate canonical probes took 2,242/1,379/2,951 ms versus parent 755/689/568. This remains an unresolved adverse observation, not accepted spread or silently superseded evidence.

A separate corrected lightweight-diagnostics cohort (two A/A plus five pairs) did not reproduce that startup anomaly: median 1,622→1,415 ms. Main CPU rose 7.60% and process CPU 3.70%. Worker queue max 0.114 ms and host admission max 90.823 ms locate slow probes in worker execution rather than seconds in a queue. Largest event-loop delay was 44.073→58.294 ms; GC medians 6.433→22.132 ms. These adverse observations remain disclosed. A baseline cold send in this cohort took 59.420 s; it is separate from warm timing.

Corrected separate CPU captures show maximum consecutive non-idle sampled spans 58.714→34.826 ms, event-loop maxima 27.574→25.919 ms, and GC maxima 2.827→3.369 ms. Candidate has no sampled non-idle span over 50 ms in this capture. Sample spans include GC/native waits/descheduling and are not precise blocking durations; this one capture does not erase the separate 58.294 ms timer delay. Profiler startup is excluded.

The first exploratory campaign mixed idle and queued admission because chat final preceded previous ownership release; those samples are excluded from overhead conclusions. One later baseline cold warmup briefly overlapped a lint process and is excluded from cold evidence; the measured warm send began after lint stopped. Setup branch collisions and an unsupported shared-layout declaration build are retained as setup failures, not product results. Supported compiled builds pass. An earlier whole-history sentinel assertion was replaced with assistant-only exact reply and input-count checks.

One corrected allocation run failed before measurement: candidate pair 3's first provider call took 111.953 s, and its second warmup then returned `SandboxProvisioningError: Aborted` after a 5.100 s container-start interval. Existing container probes have 5 s deadlines; the precise failed command was not recorded. A direct mountinfo probe of the same still-running guest subsequently passed in 202.284 ms. The failed warmup/logs are retained, the fixture was retired, and one fresh-fixture continuation completed successfully. All 38 declared v3 measurements are complete; no successful sample was replaced. This is not claimed as proven inherited behavior or a successful sample.

## Review and Gates

At `8ab639048441ef74aa6f6fb6b84c3245f7b3e31c`, `pnpm check:changed`, full scripts lint, the 14-case suppression inventory test, and exact-head CI [44924929842](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44924929842) pass. Earlier lint/inventory failures were this PR's failures, not inherited exceptions. The typed preload forwards its native receiver explicitly; its narrow documented exception remains inventoried. Native smoke retains exact value 7 after a 259.064 ms COMMIT hold.

[Final-head ClawSweeper review 7065467732](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/203135#issuecomment-7065467732) confirms both prior items are repaired and reports no new actionable code findings at `8ab639048441ef74aa6f6fb6b84c3245f7b3e31c`. Its performance-owner decision has now been supplied: **NOT ACCEPTED as is**, recorded below. This PR will close without merging; its diagnostic results remain evidence for the lane.


## Performance-owner decision (verbatim)

Performance-owner decisions by the Team perf-loop lead (an agent acting under Peter's standing unattended instruction), NOT Peter.

**#203135: NOT ACCEPTED as is.** Storage phase marks are instrumentation, and instrumentation must be near-zero cost. +6.56% main allocation and a worse cold tail (max 41.6 s), plus the unresolved v2 startup anomaly (1.457→2.580 s), aren't acceptable for phase marks. The complete-turn +21.69% you attribute to longer provider calls (external noise) is noted and not held against it. Either cut the marks' allocation to within A/A noise (lazy/structured once per phase, no per-call objects/strings) and re-measure, or close it and keep only the marks lane 2699 needs as a bounded diagnostic. Don't merge it before that.

After landing #202960 and #203112, write the final report and stop. Lane 2746 owns template generation selection now.

Disposition: close without merging. The synthetic storage-attribution results remain bounded diagnostic evidence; no production instrumentation from this PR will land. No further instrumentation campaign is being started in lane 2699.

prs.title: fix: let updates stop a Gateway that OpenClaw reran under a compatible Node
prs.body:
Refs #202954
Related: #202642, #202633

## What Problem This Solves

When the Node.js that a Linux systemd Gateway service starts with fails the Gateway's runtime check, OpenClaw reruns the Gateway under a compatible Node it finds, such as its private runtime in `~/.openclaw/tools/cli-node`. The service's main process is then that launcher, and the Gateway that actually serves is its child. Every update of such a service fails with `managed-service-stop-failed` ("Gateway process changed during maintenance drain"), although the Gateway is healthy. Automatic updates retry this every one to two hours. One reporter has about 330 failed runs, each taking ~10 minutes and leaving a ~1.9 GiB snapshot. 2026.10.8 and 2026.10.9 Gateways on Node 24 below 24.22.1 are in exactly this layout, and so is any release whose service Node is below its supported floor.

## User Impact

Updates succeed again for Gateways that OpenClaw reran under a compatible Node. The refusal comes from the installed updater's stop, before the package swap. The fix therefore applies to updates driven by a release that contains it. Installs already stuck on an older release need the one-time step posted on #202954: refresh the service definition from a CLI on a supported Node, or use the manual npm hop.

## Why This Change Was Made

Maintenance drain required the PID the Gateway reports to equal the service's main PID, which is never true in this layout. The restart path already treats a port listener whose parent is the service's main process as the service's own Gateway (`listenerOwnedByRuntimePid`). Drain now accepts the same relation, with a stricter rule: every listener on the Gateway port must be the reporting process, and its parent must be the service's main PID. Stopping the unit stops both processes. An unrelated listener, or a child of another parent, is still refused.

## Evidence

**Regression test.** `update-command-service-drain.test.ts` covers the normal and explicit drain for the child case, plus the two refusals. On base, the two child cases fail (2 failed / 62 passed). With the fix, 87 tests pass across the drain, native drain and resident-restart suites.

**Live proof.** Run on Crabbox Linux against a systemd user unit, with a private patched Node 24.22.1 in `~/.openclaw/tools/cli-node`. The resident layout was captured before each update: MainPID is the launcher, and the port listener is its child on the private Node.

| Lane | Unit Node | From → To (driver) | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| reporter path | 24.21.0 | 2026.10.9 → 2026.11.6 | fails: `Gateway process changed during maintenance drain`; Gateway left on 10.9 |
| main base | 24.21.0 | 2026.10.9 → main | fails (10.9 driver) |
| main base | 24.15.0 | main → main (CLI) | fails: same refusal |
| main base | 24.15.0 | main → main (Gateway `update.run`) | fails: same refusal |
| **fix** | 24.15.0 | fix → fix (CLI) | **passes**: drained, stopped and restarted; `/readyz` 200 on target, twice |
| workaround | 24.21.0 | 10.9, `openclaw gateway install --force` from a patched-Node CLI, then → 11.6 | passes |
| manual npm hop | 24.21.0 | 10.9 → 11.6 per update-methods.md | passes, all steps rc=0 |

A separate pre-existing problem showed up during this proof: main-driven Gateway `update.run` updates fail after the stop, with or without this layout and without this patch. It will be tracked separately and is unrelated to this change.

**Checks.** Format and lint are clean. `$autoreview` is scoped-clean, and an independent Codex read-only review reported no findings.

prs.title: fix(pr): reduce repeated hashing during baseline validation
prs.body:
Related: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/187440

## What Problem This Solves

Repeated baseline refreshes rehash identical retained review evidence in thousands of separate Git processes. Long correction histories make native preparation and publication unnecessarily slow.

## User Impact

Maintainer tooling only. Baseline validation can reuse a previously checked payload within the same invocation. This does not claim to fix the separately observed, unreproduced stdin stall.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing validation flow and reuse only successful native Git hashes after exact byte comparison. The cache owns its copied bytes and retains at most 1,024 payloads / 8 MiB. Every file is still reread, every signature and tree is checked, and object writes always invoke Git. New or changed payloads retain Git's collision detection.

Deleting validation, reusing authority verdicts, or deferring reads would weaken admission. Carrying a pathname-derived result would miss changed evidence. An invocation-local byte lookup removes repeated subprocesses without introducing a new batching protocol or persisted state.

## Evidence

Independent complete-owner review and local autoreview found no actionable issue. Autoreview covered P0–P2 on the five-file proposal; unchanged-context coverage was limited. Independent review then confirmed the exact formatted head. Canonical formatting and Node syntax checks pass.

[Focused Testbox proof](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44931543579): all 43 baseline-refresh, baseline-successor and captured-hash tests passed, plus the PR wrapper runtime-import inventory test (22 unrelated cases skipped by the explicit filter). This includes exact bytes, file changes between reads, forced lookup-digest collisions, both retention limits, failed native hashing, failed object writes and signed successor reconstruction.

[Paired benchmark passed](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/44932798105) on the exact candidate and base, using Node 24.22.1 on an observed 4-CPU / 16.56 GB Testbox. Three warmups preceded five alternating pairs. Validation stdout/stderr, statuses, unique native hash results and captured reads matched. Both validation arms make no object writes; the separate baseline suite covers actual write success/failure. All runs had zero temporary hash files and read the same 551,530 captured bytes.

| Metric | Base | Candidate |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Native hash calls | 31 | 15 |
| Bytes passed to native hashing | 546,744 | 272,334 |
| Wall median / p95 (ms) | 251.63 / 265.35 | 231.22 / 281.80 |
| Process-tree CPU median / p95 (ms) | 279.47 / 294.25 | 256.11 / 319.77 |
| Peak RSS median / p95 (KiB) | 75,000 / 77,844 | 74,388 / 76,352 |
| Sampled heap median / p95 (bytes) | 16,852,624 / 18,002,104 | 15,513,432 / 16,657,208 |
| Sampled external memory median / p95 (bytes) | 3,306,327 / 3,906,341 | 3,567,856 / 4,167,870 |

Here p95 is nearest-rank over five measured samples. Wall ranges were 246.72–265.35 ms versus 226.07–281.80 ms; CPU ranges were 273.31–294.25 ms versus 249.12–319.77 ms. The last candidate sample raised both timing maxima; the first four were below every base sample. Its cause is not established. Recorded host load stayed 0.73 / 0.23 / 0.08 and physical disk I/O was identical. This supports about 8% lower median wall/CPU and 52% fewer hash subprocesses, not improved tail latency.

The validator retains 15 distinct payloads totaling 272,334 bytes in this workload. The approximately 262 KB increase in sampled external memory is consistent with those owned buffer copies; allocator/GC snapshots do not give exact attribution. The unchanged 8 MiB / 1,024-entry bounds are covered by regression tests. No broad process-memory or stdin-stall fix is claimed.

Before this successful run, three setup attempts stopped before measurement (output parent, absent old baseline, inherited ESM fixture scope). Each lease completed cleanup. The successful run used the fixture's standalone temporary-directory contract, verified exact baseline bytes and removed its temporary fixture after exporting results.

**Performance acceptance rule, recorded before measurement:** use the committed `test/scripts/pr-baseline-hash-measure.test.ts` retained-history fixture, base `4a86f968f92f263d0f60a53db65ed04084c8e6ab`, candidate below, 32 synthetic files and a 256 KiB proof log. Warm up three times, then run five alternating base/candidate pairs on the same host. Require identical validation output/status, unique native hash results, object-write sequence and captured read-byte count; require fewer hash subprocesses. Report wall/CPU median, p95 and spread, host load and memory. Bound retained payload storage at 8 MiB; investigate any regressed metric before landing.

Verified source candidate: `73132fd276d9ca2f2b88a66ed390a9bbbbdb2c43`, tree `d5c1963ca87027171b87af914035b5e48e136ab9`.

Production delta: +26/-1 lines. Tests: +95/-10. Documentation: +5. Added state is bounded and owned by the existing baseline validator.

prs.title: fix: interrupted sessions still resume after a running Gateway's package is replaced in place
prs.body:
Related: #202700

## What Problem This Solves

When the installed package is replaced while a Gateway keeps running (for example `openclaw update --no-restart` with a running Gateway, or a manual `npm i -g openclaw@…`), that Gateway's next shutdown runs with its old files gone. Since 2026.11.5 the shutdown loads restart-marker persistence and subagent settlement only at that moment, so on a release-to-release swap it fails with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND` and records no resume markers: sessions that were working when the Gateway went down are not resumed after it starts again.

## User Impact

User impact: after an in-place package replacement, the old Gateway still records which interrupted sessions to resume, and settles its running subagents. Gateways already running 2026.11.5 or 2026.11.6 keep the old behavior for their next in-place replacement, because their running code cannot change; the updating docs say so. This does not make every in-place shutdown clean: four other shutdown paths still load code late (listed under Evidence) and are tracked separately.

## Why This Change Was Made

`prepareGatewayShutdownRuntime` already resolves and retains the shutdown graph at startup for exactly this reason (#160674). The 2026.10.28 restart-resume refactor (#185730) replaced a retained shutdown dependency with two close-time `import()` calls; 2026.11.1–11.4 and 10.33 still retained it. This moves both back under that owner: startup retains the `session-restart-resume` and `subagent-registry` module namespaces, and close calls through them without importing. Calling through the namespaces (instead of destructuring) keeps the existing tests that spy on those exports after startup working.

Production +11/−5 (net +6); tests +47; docs +4.

## Evidence

- Regression test `server-kernel.test.ts` › "records restart markers after an in-place update removes their installed chunks": a real kernel, both modules made unimportable (`ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`), then close. Red on base `abd57600624` (`Restart marker persistence failed … chunk was removed | ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`, `Subagent settlement failed`, close step failed); green on this head. `server-shutdown.runtime.test.ts` requires both modules during preparation: red on base, green here.
- Spy-dependent siblings (`server-close.queued-inputs`, `server-close.sandbox-registry`, `server.operator-observer-lifetime`) plus the two files: 5 files / 21 tests pass. Core and core-test typecheck, type-aware oxlint (core shard) and oxfmt clean.
- Live, Crabbox Linux (AWS), packaged builds installed from a local registry, foreground `gateway run`, then every hashed `dist` chunk deleted (stand-in for a release-to-release swap) and SIGTERM:

  | Build | `session-restart-resume` import failures at shutdown |
  |---|---|
  | published 2026.11.6 | 3 (`Restart marker persistence failed`) |
  | base `abd57600624` | 5 (`Restart marker persistence failed`) |
  | this head | 0 |

  Shutdown on base and on this head still fails on other late loads, which this PR does not change: the state worker's `restart-lifecycle.worker` (SIGTERM handling), memory-core's `runtime-provider`, `temp-artifact-cleanup` (plugin source capture), and the process `supervisor` chunk. On main both then wait about 325 s for the hard-exit watchdog, whereas published 2026.11.6 exits in 1 s.
- An `update --no-restart` lane between two relabelled copies of the same build (no chunk names change) completed on base and head alike; the foreground Gateway then exits by design (`replaced runtime must exit (unmanaged …)`), so that lane cannot show the difference.
- Reviews: autoreview scoped-clean; independent read-only Codex review: no findings.

prs.title: fix: explain when a web chat session reaches its subagent limit
prs.body:
Closes #202553

## What Problem This Solves

When a web chat session reaches its active subagent limit, a rejected launch can appear as an unknown outcome or a generic failure. Finding out why requires opening the tool result.

## User Impact

The failed launch row shows how many subagents are active and asks you to wait for one to finish before retrying. The config key stays in the expanded details.

## Why This Change Was Made

Web chat reads the count and limit from the recorded launch result. The refusal text wraps on narrow screens.

## Evidence

An isolated Gateway with a scripted model in Chromium accepted five launches and rejected the sixth while all five workers were still active. The screenshots show the refusal during the turn. The same explanation was visible after reload, and expanding the launch kept the config key visible.

**Before** (`44ec89e7187`)

![Worker 6 appears as an unknown launch outcome while five subagents are running](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/c65ee4b1a20bf23e0b7a8c8934a22e4e1329d83b/images/2026/11/e97031dd-c7f6-42b0-bc81-36ca89c0a917.png)

**After**

![Worker 6 is refused at 5 of 5 active subagents and the launch row tells the reader when to retry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/bdab48a2c3313983fef5e2cb806ac338547bc454/images/2026/11/4322159f-b5e0-4228-82a8-2cdfeb2f6cba.png)

Both regression cases fail on main with "Couldn't launch subagent Worker 6" and pass on `72bd0d6`.

All 35 focused chat tests passed, including grouped launches and live and saved refusals. A Chromium smoke test confirmed wrapping at 430 px and the config key in expanded details. The paired Control UI asset check passed with 1,745,213 raw CSS bytes on both sides. UI typecheck, targeted lint, and formatting passed. Broader coverage runs in CI.

prs.title: fix: memory_search offers a sessions corpus to agents that cannot search sessions
prs.body:
Closes #202543

## What Problem This Solves

An agent that has no session search configured is still offered `corpus: "sessions"` by `memory_search`, in both the tool's parameter schema and its description. Choosing it can only return "Chat history search is not enabled.", so a question like "what did I tell you before?" wastes a call on a search the agent cannot run.

## User Impact

User impact: an agent without session search is no longer offered a corpus it cannot use. Agents that search sessions (`sessions` in `searchSources`) and the Active Memory helper's sessions recall see exactly what they saw before.

## Why This Change Was Made

The tool's source list in the description already follows the agent's resolved `searchSources`; the offered `corpus` values and the `corpus=sessions` sentence now follow them too. `sessions` is offered when `searchSources` includes it or when the run carries the trusted sessions recall (`conversationRecall.corpus === "sessions"`). The runtime guard in `tools.ts`, its unavailable result, `prepareArguments` and the recall's forced corpus are unchanged. Through the Gateway, a model that still sends `corpus: "sessions"` to an agent that is no longer offered it now gets the agent loop's argument-validation error instead of the unavailable result; a caller that invokes `execute` directly still gets the unavailable result (see the Gateway evidence below). Production diff: +30/-8 lines in three files; no behavior change for agents that can search sessions.

## Evidence

### Gateway evidence (source builds, real Gateway process, recorded model requests)

Built from source in `node:24` (Node 24.22.3, pnpm 12.15.0): base `main@b8b173b6` and this PR's head `3da9e18d` (base + the 4 files of this PR, nothing else). Each configuration ran in a fresh `openclaw gateway --port 18789` process with bundled `memory-core`; every turn entered through the Gateway's own `POST /v1/chat/completions` (`model: "openclaw/service"`). The model is a local OpenAI Responses-compatible mock that records each request body verbatim. No real provider key was available, so no real model was called; the tools below are what the Gateway sent to the model. Config: `memory.search.provider: "none"`, `tools.toolSearch: false` so `memory_search` is in `tools[]` directly. With Tool Search at its default, `tool_describe({"id":"memory_search"})` returned the same `description` and `parameters` on both builds.

| Configuration | base: `corpus` enum / `corpus=sessions` sentence | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| (A) memory search on, no `sources`, no `experimental.sessionMemory` | `memory, wiki, all, sessions` / yes | `memory, wiki, all` / no |
| (B) `sources: ["memory","sessions"]` + `experimental.sessionMemory: true` | `memory, wiki, all, sessions` / yes | unchanged (byte-identical tool object) |
| (C) Active Memory recall helper sub-run, `conversationRecall.corpus: "sessions"` (Remember across conversations on, recall-phrase turn) | `memory, wiki, all, sessions` / yes | unchanged (byte-identical tool object) |
| (C) the same turn's main agent (recall-only indexing) | `memory, wiki, all, sessions` / yes | `memory, wiki, all` / no |

(A) `memory_search` from the captured model request: `type`, `name`, `query`, `maxResults` and `minScore` are identical; the only differences are:

```diff
       "corpus": {
         "type": "string",
-        "enum": ["memory", "wiki", "all", "sessions"]
+        "enum": ["memory", "wiki", "all"]
       }
```
```diff
-... `corpus=memory` restricts hits to indexed memory files (excludes session transcript chunks from ranking). `corpus=sessions` searches indexed session transcripts under the same visibility rules as session history tools and returns unavailable when semantic session indexing is disabled. Corpus outcomes cover each requested corpus; ...
+... `corpus=memory` restricts hits to indexed memory files (excludes session transcript chunks from ranking). Corpus outcomes cover each requested corpus; ...
```

Forced call in (A): the mock model returned `memory_search({"query":"trip decision","corpus":"sessions"})`. Tool result the Gateway fed back:

- base: `{"results":[],"disabled":true,"unavailable":true,"error":"Chat history search is not enabled.","warning":"Chat history search is unavailable for this agent.","action":"If an exact session-history capability is available for this run, use it. Otherwise, ask the operator to enable semantic session search by enabling memory.search.experimental.sessionMemory and adding \"sessions\" to memory.search.sources.",...}`
- this PR: the agent loop's argument validation (`validateToolArguments`) rejects the value before `execute` runs:
  ```
  Validation failed for tool "memory_search":
    - corpus: must be equal to one of the allowed values
  ```

This corrects the earlier statement that the same forced call returns the identical unavailable result. That was measured by calling `execute` directly in the test harness, which skips argument validation. The runtime guard in `tools.ts` is unchanged and still answers callers whose schema offers `sessions` ((B) and the helper in (C)).

### Real-model evidence on this PR's build (gpt-6.1-terra)

This PR's head `3da9e18d` (base `main@b8b173b6` plus the 4 memory-core files of this PR) was built from source in `node:24` (Node 24.22.3, pnpm 12.15.0) on a 2 vCPU / 8 GB VM with temporary swap. The build took 609 s, with a peak of 5.0 GiB RAM (the container's cap) plus 0.9 GiB swap. Each configuration ran in a fresh `openclaw gateway --port 18789` process with bundled `memory-core`. Every turn entered through the Gateway's `POST /v1/chat/completions` (`model: "openclaw/service"`), one new session per turn. The model was a **real** OpenAI model, `gpt-6.1-terra` (`api: "openai-responses"`), reached through a recording pass-through proxy that stores each request body and response verbatim. There were 23 model calls in total. Config: `memory.search.provider: "none"`, `tools.toolSearch: false`.

Offered `memory_search` schema, from the captured requests (stable across every request of each run):

| Configuration | `corpus` enum offered to the real model | `corpus=sessions` sentence in the description |
|---|---|---|
| (A) memory search on, no `sources`, no `experimental.sessionMemory` | `["memory", "wiki", "all"]` | no |
| (B) `sources: ["memory","sessions"]` + `experimental.sessionMemory: true` | `["memory", "wiki", "all", "sessions"]` | yes |
| (C) Active Memory recall helper sub-run (`conversationRecall.corpus: "sessions"`, Remember across conversations on) | `["memory", "wiki", "all", "sessions"]` | yes |
| (C) the same turn's main agent (recall-only indexing) | `["memory", "wiki", "all"]` | no |

Apart from one added `"strict": false` (this provider declares strict-mode support), each object is identical (`type`, `name`, `description`, `parameters`) to the one captured for the same configuration in the mock-model gateway run above. That run showed base `b8b173b6` offering `sessions` in all four rows.

(A) `corpus` property and description, verbatim from the request sent to `gpt-6.1-terra`:

```json
"corpus": { "type": "string", "enum": ["memory", "wiki", "all"] }
```
> Semantically search MEMORY.md, USER.md, Markdown files recursively under memory/ when an answer depends on prior work, decisions, dates, people, preferences, or todos not already present in the current turn. Do not repeat memory retrieval when supplied context fully answers the question. Omit `corpus` to search those configured sources. Session results are transcript search references, not readable memory-file paths. Optional `corpus=wiki` or `corpus=all` also searches registered compiled-wiki supplements; use `corpus=all` only when compiled wiki supplements are needed. `corpus=memory` restricts hits to indexed memory files (excludes session transcript chunks from ranking). Corpus outcomes cover each requested corpus; only a top-level corpus warning means results are partial and must be surfaced to the user. An optional corpus outcome of not-registered in a multi-corpus result is informational. If response has disabled=true or stale=true, tell the user and include the warning/action guidance.

(B) and the (C) helper keep the sentence `` `corpus=sessions` searches indexed session transcripts under the same visibility rules as session history tools and returns unavailable when semantic session indexing is disabled. `` and the `sessions` enum value.

What the real model did in (A), the agent without session search:

- "What did I tell you earlier about my trip?" (a new session, after an earlier turn where the model saved the trip to `MEMORY.md`): no tool call. It answered from the injected `MEMORY.md`: "You're planning a trip to Lisbon in March, and you decided to take the train from Madrid rather than fly."
- With a fresh state and a question about a fact stored nowhere, "Do you remember which hotel I told you I booked in Lisbon, in our earlier chat?": the model called `memory_search({"query":"Lisbon hotel booked earlier chat accommodation"})` with no `corpus` and got `{"results":[],"provider":"none",...}`. It then called the agent's exact session tool, `sessions_search` ("Lisbon", "hotel"), and replied "I can't find the hotel name in the conversation history or memory available to me, so I don't want to guess."
- Asked next, "Please search our past chat history for what I said about the hotel.", it again called `memory_search` without `corpus`, then `sessions_search` (×3) and `sessions_history`.
- Across the 11 model requests of (A) the model never sent `corpus: "sessions"`. No call failed argument validation, and no reply passed operator configuration advice on to the user.

In (C) the helper, offered `sessions`, called `memory_search` without `corpus` (empty results, `NONE`, `status=no_relevant_memory`). In (B) the model answered from the injected `MEMORY.md` without calling `memory_search`.

Limits: only this PR's head was built for the real-model run (base behaviour is from the mock run); one sample per configuration; FTS-only memory with nothing indexed, so the evidence covers what is offered and what the model calls, not recall quality.

### In-process harness (earlier run)

Behavior checked: the tool an agent without session search is offered, before and after this change, and one call with `corpus: "sessions"`. Source run on `main` `2f5bb506ef61ab6e327df88133bfc68d95e0c90a` through the plugin's real `register()` and its registered `memory_search` factory (Node v24.22.3):

| agent | `corpus` enum before | `corpus` enum after | `corpus=sessions` in description after |
|---|---|---|---|
| no `memory.search.sources` | `memory, wiki, all, sessions` | `memory, wiki, all` | no |
| `sources: ["memory","sessions"]` | `memory, wiki, all, sessions` | `memory, wiki, all, sessions` | yes |
| Active Memory helper (`conversationRecall.corpus: "sessions"`) | `memory, wiki, all, sessions` | `memory, wiki, all, sessions` | yes |

In this harness, which calls `execute` directly, `execute({ query, corpus: "sessions" })` on the agent without session search returns the identical unavailable result before and after (`disabled: true`, `unavailable: true`, `error: "Chat history search is not enabled."`); through the Gateway the same call is now rejected earlier by argument validation (see the Gateway evidence). import assert from "node:assert/strict";

```ts
} as unknown as OpenClawConfig;

function tools(cfg: OpenClawConfig) {
  const registerTool = vi.fn<OpenClawPluginApi["registerTool"]>();
  const api = createTestPluginApi({
    id: "memory-core",
    config: cfg,
    runtime: createPluginRuntimeMock({
      llm: { acquireLocalService: async () => undefined },
    } as never),
    registerTool,
  });
  plugin.register(api);
  return registerTool.mock.calls;
}

type Tool = {
  parameters: { properties: { corpus: unknown } };
  description: string;
  execute: (...a: unknown[]) => Promise<{ details: unknown }>;
};

function make(cfg: OpenClawConfig, extra: Record<string, unknown> = {}) {
  const factory = tools(cfg).find(([, o]) => o?.names?.includes("memory_search"))?.[0];
  assert(typeof factory === "function");
  const tool = factory({
    agentId: "main",
    sessionKey: "agent:main:main",
    config: cfg,
    runtimeConfig: cfg,
    ...extra,
  } as never);
  assert(tool && !Array.isArray(tool));
  return tool as unknown as Tool;
}

it("proof", async () => {
  const main = make(config);
  console.log("=== A. agent 'main' without session search (registered memory_search factory): offered parameters");
  console.log(JSON.stringify(main.parameters, null, 2));
  console.log("=== A. description sentences mentioning sessions");
  console.log(
    main.description
      .split(/(?<=\.) /)
      .filter((s) => /session/i.test(s))
      .join("\n"),
  );
  console.log("=== B. execute memory_search { query, corpus: 'sessions' }");
  const r = await main.execute("c1", {
    query: "what did I tell you about my cat",
    corpus: "sessions",
  });
  console.log(JSON.stringify(r.details, null, 2));
  console.log("=== C. agent 'main' WITH sessions configured: offered corpus enum");
  const withSessions = make({
    ...config,
    memory: { citations: "off", search: { sources: ["memory", "sessions"] } },
  } as unknown as OpenClawConfig);
  console.log(JSON.stringify(withSessions.parameters.properties.corpus));
  console.log("=== D. Active Memory helper (conversationRecall.corpus=sessions): offered corpus enum");
  const helper = make(config, {
    conversationRecall: {
      anchorSessionKey: "agent:main:main",
      scope: "same-agent-private",
      corpus: "sessions",
    },
  });
  console.log(JSON.stringify(helper.parameters.properties.corpus));
});
```

</details>

Tests, run locally in a sparse checkout (`pnpm exec vitest run <files> --maxWorkers=1`):

- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.test.ts` adds sessions offered / not offered for five configurations (not configured, recall-only indexing, `sources` including sessions, the helper's sessions recall, the helper's configured-only recall) and one test that the helper's forced sessions recall still searches `sessions` with no model-supplied corpus. Against base the three "not offered" cases fail; with the change all pass.
- With the change: 7 files, 102 tests passed (`index.test.ts`, `tools.test.ts`, `tools.citations.test.ts`, `tools.recall-tracking.test.ts`, `tools.local-fallback.test.ts`, `memory-corpus.test.ts`, `tools.real-manager.test.ts`).
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.extensions.json --noEmit` exits 0; `oxfmt --check` on the four touched files passes.

Left to CI (not runnable in the sparse checkout): `pnpm build`, `pnpm check`, `oxlint` (its JS plugin `tools/solid-lint` did not load here), the full `pnpm test`, the test-types project, and tests of other extensions. No provider or gateway process was run; the proof is the tool as the plugin registers it, not a live model turn.

<details>
<summary>Files</summary>

- `extensions/memory-core/src/memory-tool-contract.ts`: the source contract carries `sessions`; the schema and the description's corpus sentence are chosen from it.
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.shared.ts`, `extensions/memory-core/index.ts`: both tool factories take `parameters` from the resolved context, as they already do for `description`.
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.test.ts`: the tests above.

</details>

prs.title: fix: reconnect shared provider credentials outside the agent roster
prs.body:
Closes #195867

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: operators cannot reconnect shared provider credentials through native sign-in after the legacy `main` owner leaves the runnable agent roster.

## User Impact

An authorized operator can sign in once to the canonical shared credential owner. Inheriting agents continue to read through the common store while keeping their individual models, model policies, and private credential overrides. Shared sign-in rejects `--set-default`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Resolve this explicit login target only when inheritance names `main`, that agent is absent, and the existing canonical ownership rules admit the target. Use the current credential writer, profile-order owner, and runtime refresh path. Discovery uses the configured ambient agent; `main` remains a credential owner without becoming a runnable agent.

The normal unknown-agent guard stays intact. Shared login cannot cross the admitted state owner, and administrator admission, current authority, revocation, and ownership-change checks remain active. There are no new flags, configuration keys, protocol fields, schemas, dependencies, or token-copy operations.

The auth context is extracted into a sibling module to keep the existing file within its growth cap. The separate test allocation covers only the measured regression growth.

## Evidence

Historical proof snapshot: head `f4265dbc55fd5c1283312d78ad0fc238e746cb30`, based on `7ebc4f3e67137c34b0850dfa8cab2b8d68e6576d`. The test and runtime evidence below belongs to that source revision.

- Baseline: the actual shared-login RPC wizard rejects the absent canonical owner with `Unknown agent id "main"`.
- Fixed: 11/11 owner regressions and 113/113 related native-owner tests pass.
- Core types, targeted typed lint, runtime build, formatting, file-growth caps, and the native test-line budget pass. The allocation matches 272 net added test lines.
- An independent source review found no remaining actionable findings. Final fixture identifiers were anonymized bijectively; the 11 owner tests and formatting/budget checks were rerun afterward. Unchanged production hashes bind the preceding types, lint, sibling tests, and build; these were not described as rerun.
- The successful runtime build emits nonfatal UI size diagnostics: largest JS gzip 564575 versus 564484 bytes, chat boot 1267.2 versus 1266.4 KiB, and new boot 784.7 versus 784.4 KiB. Attribution to this change is unproven; no budget guard or override was changed.

The native owner fixture uses synthetic OAuth, real task-owned SQLite stores, and Gateway RPC. It checks shared persistence and profile order, refreshed inherited views, preserved private overrides and model policies, and rejection of unknown/mismatched owners, a changed owner, revoked authority, and a different state root. A successful shared login does not prove that every private override should be removed.

No real credentials, private configurations, personal sessions, or runtime logs are included in this PR. The public-head proof uses synthetic provider I/O. A separate integration was used to smoke-test native provider sign-in and ordinary inference; that is not presented as an exact-public-head live-provider test.

### Latest-main refresh — 21 November 2026

Rebased the single feature commit onto canonical `main` at `282121402940c47c87a68bf08bb6e66097818884`. One import conflict was resolved by retaining both the current main imports and the PR's shared-owner resolver. `git range-diff` confirms the intended change with the upstream auth API rename; the 11-file scoped diff and `git diff --check` pass. Current-head Codex Autoreview (P0–P2) completed `scoped-clean` with no actionable findings.

The focused owner/runtime tests above were not rerun at the rebased head. GitHub requires a maintainer to approve this PR revision before CI starts; the current CI gate is therefore blocked and is not green.
