prs.title: feat: run lean core workers in one shared host to cut small-machine memory
prs.body:
Fixes #202377
Related: #202373
Builds on #202422 (merged as 28aa5c88fd45)

## What Problem This Solves

On small machines the Gateway runs many background workers. Each worker loads its own copy of largely the same code, so worker memory grows past what a 1–2 GiB host can hold. The core SQLite, transcript, state-read and catalog workers are the biggest duplicates.

## User Impact

User impact: with the `lean` resource profile (auto-selected below 8 GiB of effective memory, or set explicitly), these four core workers run as endpoints inside **one** shared host worker. They load their common code once, which uses less memory. `standard` keeps today's worker layout; every new path is unreachable there.

Lean accepts one new failure mode: if a hosted task fails, is cancelled or times out, the whole shared host is replaced. Every hosted endpoint's in-flight work then fails with an explicit `Shared worker host failed: …` error, and the next request starts a fresh host. Callers never hang.

## Why This Change Was Made

The prototype in #202373 showed the memory saving but broke several guarantees. This version keeps them:

- **Code is shared, state is not.** Each hosted module starts once per endpoint with its own port, admission relay and queue. The per-worker SQLite admission upstream is now scoped to the endpoint instead of being isolate-global. The host samples its own memory; endpoints never do.
- **One live endpoint per kind** (per carrier class for the SQLite store). Extra slots of a kind keep their own dedicated workers: the state-read settlement floor of 2, bursts and the second agent carrier. Pool caps, floors, catalog custody (#161740) and retirement timings are unchanged.
- **Single writer per database.** Broker actor routing is unchanged. A hosted SQLite carrier stops logically only after every actor's native close is proven; any other stop replaces the host.
- **Real termination boundaries.** An idle stop (idle timeout, rotation, close, shutdown) is a logical stop. The endpoint first releases what isolate exit would have released (state-read retained readers, transcript history databases), with a 10 s deadline. Cancellation, failure, self-retirement or an unknown reason terminates the host. CPU-heavy and synchronous kinds (prompt state, skills discovery) are not hosted and keep their own killable workers.
- **Host failure is explicit and recoverable.** The host is created through the existing native-worker supervisor, so synchronous callers see its exit through `service()`. Host death fails every endpoint (error, exit and `terminalFailure`). A replacement starts only after the old host has exited: one host isolate at a time. The last endpoint's retirement joins the physical host.
- **Not hosted:** Knowledge (#202378), external databases, Postgres-engine installs, native-resource owners, non-canonical (update-generation or sealed) worker URLs, and runtimes whose explicit SQLite close is not qualified to release native resources (such as Bun on Windows), whose cleanup depends on worker exit.

The census reports the host as one worker. Its row adds `hosts N endpoints`, so budget admission (#202376) can charge one isolate. #202376 exports `registerHostedSlotPredicate(url, key?)`. Whichever of the two PRs merges second adds and registers a stateless predicate: lean, a canonical hosted entrypoint, not Postgres, and an `agent` or `shared-state` SQLite key. It is not the live `claimsSharedHostSlot` check, so a running hosted floor slot is still not charged as an isolate.

Accepted edge case: some agent-database reader caches are shared across the whole isolate. They are released by explicit close requests or when the host exits, not when a single endpoint stops.

## Review Repair (ClawSweeper 2/6 on `4795dee4`)

- **[P1] Unqualified native close keeps dedicated workers.** Confirmed in source: when `explicitSqliteCloseReleasesNativeResources` is false, `closeReadResources` and transcript discovery call `pool.rotate()` so worker exit releases native handles, sidecar locks and cleanup custody. A hosted endpoint treated `rotation` as a logical stop while a sibling kept the isolate alive. Of the two suggested fixes, I chose the smaller and safer one: `claimsSharedHostSlot` reuses the existing capability owner (`getSqliteRuntimeCapabilities`) and refuses every hosted kind when close is unqualified. The SQLite broker also requires its own captured close policy, so an early conservative broker never hosts a carrier. Forcing physical host termination would instead fail every sibling on each routine rotation. The capability is decided once and only moves from pending (false) to decided, so a slot hosted under qualified close is never retired under an unqualified policy.
- **[P2] Export guard.** `startHostedWorker` is registered in `workerProtocolModules` for exactly the four hosted modules, using the guard's existing subset check. Collision checking is otherwise unchanged.
- **Benchmark applicability.** On Node, `bun-sqlite-library.ts` decides `explicitSqliteCloseReleasesNativeResources: true` ("Node runtime") before any other branch, including early broker captures. The measured Linux Node v26.12.1 campaign path hosts the same endpoints as before, so the evidence below still applies. Only Bun runtimes with unqualified close (for example Bun Windows) change; they now use the standard dedicated layout.
- **Rebase.** Rebased once onto `main` `5a4f6a82681f` because `src/infra/worker-task-host.ts` conflicted with main commit `8bbb3539` ("keep Code Mode usable after read-only workers retire"). Resolution: hosted endpoints still return early, because the physical host registers its one thread for admission. Dedicated workers, including read-only ones, now track admission unconditionally, as on main. A hosted endpoint's logical stop closes its retained connections, which decrements their admission references. Range-diff: only that hunk differs. The three earlier fix commits are identical.

New tests (`src/infra/shared-worker-host.unqualified-close.test.ts`; both fail on `4795dee4` and pass after the fix):
- `never hosts a core worker when native SQLite close is unqualified`: all four kinds; it failed with `expected true to be false`.
- `rotates an unqualified reader by physical worker exit while a shared host stays up`: a real state-read pool with a live hosted sibling. The reader is a dedicated worker (census `hostedEndpoints: 1`; it failed with 2), and `closeReadResources` rotation removes its physical worker while the sibling stays up.

CI attribution for `4795dee4` (run 44849044890):

| Check | Cause | Evidence | Resolution |
|---|---|---|---|
| check-source-contracts | PR | `lint:tmp:export-name-collisions`: `startHostedWorker` repeated in 3 modules | Fixed (P2) |
| checks-fast-baseline-ratchets | PR | `assertion-safety`: `src/infra/shared-worker-host.worker.ts: 1 > 0` (SAFETY comment not adjacent to the cast) | Fixed; ratchet OK locally |
| checks-node-changed-compact-large-8 | PR | Bun `session-history-read.imports.test.ts`: mock lacks `closeHistoryDatabaseScopes` | Mock completed; passes on Bun |
| checks-node-changed-compact-large-9 | Inherited | Bun `mcp-config-mutation.test.ts` keep/replace custody: `identity` 8/4, expected 0 | Same file fails identically under `OPENCLAW_VITEST_RUNTIME=bun` at exact base `28aa5c88` (identity 8 and 4); the PR does not touch it |
| checks-ui-e2e (2/5) | Inherited | `route-asset-requests` plugins: `expected 57 to be less than or equal to 56` | Reproduced on main `2d13f968` (57>56); the PR touches no `ui/`. #202795 on the new base restores this budget |
| PostgreSQL conformance (pg16-smoke) | Not PR-caused (timing) | `server-database-engine-cron.postgres.test.ts` "drains accepted cron finalization…" timed out at 90 s | Local pg16 (same image) passed 4/4 on head and exact base; that test took 46.3 s and 45.4 s. Postgres installs never claim the shared host |

## Evidence

Current head: `40fc34f0df162c1d5bfdf0cb51b1bff7e46ac285`, rebased onto `main` `5a4f6a82681f`. The four feature commits match measured head `c58ffafd503d918fd1fc58f5ffade1cb9dc2b599` except for the `worker-task-host.ts` admission-tracking merge described above. Three review-repair commits follow. Fresh validation on this head: 42 focused files (shared-host, unqualified-close, worker-task host/pool/server, SQLite broker/relay, state-read, transcript worker/lanes/readers, catalog-read, history imports, resource-profile, status-resources, export guard), 476 tests in 6 Vitest shards; `pnpm tsgo:core`; type-aware oxlint and oxfmt on touched files; the export-collision guard; the assertion-safety ratchet; `pnpm config:docs:check`; and `git diff --check` all pass.

**Measured campaign (complete, on `c58ffafd503d`):** Crabbox Linux `local-container` leases on one Mac Studio, Node v26.12.1, 8-CPU quota, no swap, each arm pinning `gateway.resources.profile`, inspector detached. 24 matrix cases (single-bot and personal-assistant workloads × 1.5/3 GiB × lean/standard × 3 interleaved rounds), plus 3 qualifications and 4 fault cases. 29 of 31 exited 0. Every lease was stopped and every receipt matches its Crabbox terminal receipt. The measured commit is patch-equivalent to this head's four feature commits apart from the admission-tracking merge hunk; the review repair changes no hosting on Node (see above). The benchmark did not run on this head.

Completion:

| Workload | 1.5 GiB lean | 1.5 GiB standard | 3 GiB lean | 3 GiB standard |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| single | 3/3 | 3/3 | 3/3 | 3/3 |
| personal | 3/3, no OOM | **1/3**: r1 and r2 `agent.wait timeout` with cgroup OOM kills (`oom_kill` 2 and 1); r3 completed | 3/3 | 3/3 |

At 1.5 GiB both arms reach the cgroup limit. Lean records reclaim pressure (`memory.events max` 5,082–22,740 on personal) but no OOM. The one completed standard personal-1.5 GiB round recorded 302,867 `max` events.

Gateway process RSS (excludes child processes; not heap), busy-phase median, median (range) across rounds, MiB:

| Workload | Memory | Lean | Standard | Paired lean − standard per round |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| single | 1.5 GiB | 1,124 (1,111–1,150) | 1,209 (1,207–1,212) | −88, −98, −57 |
| single | 3 GiB | 1,292 (1,250–1,313) | 1,337 (1,335–1,364) | −85, −71, −24 |
| personal | 1.5 GiB | 1,219 (1,197–1,241) | 1,244 (r3 only) | r3 only: −25 (busy peak +5) |
| personal | 3 GiB | 1,450 (1,448–1,493) | 1,578 (1,529–1,680) | −232, −85, −79 |

Lean busy-phase Gateway RSS is lower in all 10 paired rounds, busy peak in 9 of 10, and post-work median in all 10. Max registered physical workers is lower or equal in every pair (lean 18–26, standard 18–29), with 4–5 hosted endpoints on lean. Child-process RSS is reported separately and shows no consistent difference (−90 to +91 MiB). The informational event-loop stall p95 is comparable (lean 47–68 ms, standard 58–61 ms medians), except for the pressured standard personal-1.5 GiB round (210 ms p95, ~1 s worst). Full per-phase figures (fresh, busy, peak, post-work), cgroup, worker and stall data: `campaign-summary.md` / `.json` in the evidence bundle.

Shared-host fault (`f2-crash-3072-lean`): a fatal throw at a dispatched hosted request (`requestObserved=true`) produced explicit endpoint errors:

```
session-transcript         Shared worker host failed: Synthetic lean benchmark worker fault
sqlite-store:agent         Shared worker host failed: Synthetic lean benchmark worker fault
plugin-model-catalog-read  Shared worker host failed: Synthetic lean benchmark worker fault
```

Up to 4 endpoints were hosted during this case; errors were recorded for the 3 with in-flight or subsequent work, and the harness asserts that every recorded error carries this prefix, not that there is one error per endpoint. The Gateway survived and a replacement host started. The interrupted turn completed, the next turn was `ok`, history was preserved, 7/7 SQLite integrity checks passed and 33 turns were verified. The standard control (`f2-crash-3072-standard`, SQLite-store fault, no shared host) recorded no endpoint errors. Its interrupted turn failed (`'error' !== 'ok'`), and the Gateway survived and the next turn was `ok`.

Caveats: the built image carried three untracked legacy files that are not in the measured tree (`src/infra/lean-worker-host.ts`, `lean-worker-host.worker.ts`, `lean-worker-scope.ts`). They are not shown to have no runtime effect. Receipt manifest hashes are read at completion, so they do not identify the harness that ran. prs.title: fix: keep Gemini NO_REPLY replies silent when the signature arrives on its own part
prs.body:
Root cause: src/shared/assistant-answer-text.ts:24 picks only text blocks that carry a signature as the answer, which is meant for OpenAI Responses item ids. Since #170534 (first shipped in 2026.11.5) it also picks empty signed blocks. Gemini 3 sends its thought signature on a separate empty part after the answer, so the selected answer is `""`, the turn is marked empty rather than silent, and the `NO_REPLY` text is delivered.

Fixes #203131

Thanks @Avi711 for the clear report and trace.

## What Problem This Solves

With Gemini 3 on a `google-generative-ai` provider, a reply of exactly `NO_REPLY` reaches the chat as the text "NO_REPLY" instead of ending the turn silently. It happens in direct chats and in automations that announce their result. 2026.8.2 stayed silent.

## User Impact

Gemini 3 replies of exactly `NO_REPLY` end the turn silently again, in direct chats and in announced automations. Normal Gemini answers are delivered as before.

## Why This Change Was Made

Signed-block selection now applies only to OpenAI Responses messages, where a text signature is an output item id. A Gemini thought signature is not an item id, so Gemini answers use all of their text blocks.

The Google stream reader still keeps the signature-only part as its own block. That keeps the next request byte-identical: the signature is replayed as its own empty part, as Gemini sent it. Attaching the signature to the previous text block would change those replayed bytes. Responses answer selection is unchanged.

## Evidence

Real Gateway (`ocx src`, isolated profile state) with the QA channel recording deliveries and a local `google-generative-ai` fixture that streams `{"text":"NO_REPLY"}` and then `{"text":"","thoughtSignature":"..."}`. Base is the merge base 423ae0907203.

| Check | Base | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| Direct chat, exact `NO_REPLY` | "NO_REPLY" delivered | nothing delivered |
| Announced automation, exact `NO_REPLY` | "NO_REPLY" delivered (`deliveryStatus: delivered`) | nothing delivered (`not-delivered`) |
| Normal answer with trailing signature part, 2 turns | delivered once per turn | delivered once per turn |
| Next request replays the signature | `[{"text":"Here is…"},{"text":"","thoughtSignature":"Q2lN…Sw=="}]` | identical bytes |

The new regression test fails on base (`disposition: 'empty'`, expected `'silent'`) and passes here; its OpenAI Responses row (signed empty item still wins) passes on both.

Observed proof lines: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/203174#issuecomment-7065560757

Merge danger: two-way door. No stored state, config or published contract changes; a revert fully restores the old behavior. Blast radius: answer text selection for non-Responses messages that carry text signatures (Google Gemini), which now use all of their text blocks.

prs.title: fix(skills): retry Meme Maker renders after a failed template cache write
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a template download only partially writes to disk, Meme Maker leaves the incomplete image in its cache. The next render can exit successfully while embedding a broken template in the SVG.

## User Impact

After a cache write fails, retrying the render downloads a fresh template. If an earlier version already cached a broken image, remove that cached JPEG once to trigger a fresh download.

## Why This Change Was Made

The bundled CLI writes the template beside its cache destination and renames it into place after the write completes. A failed write removes the temporary file. Readers can open the cache entry as soon as it appears.

## Evidence

Verified on Linux with Node 24.18.0 and the real Imgflip Drake template. In a fresh cache, Bash's `ulimit -f 1` forced the write to fail with `EFBIG`. The system limit was removed for the retry.

| Revision | Failed write | Retry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main `238160cf99b` | Exited 1 and left a 1,024-byte cached JPEG | Exited 0 and embedded that truncated JPEG in the SVG |
| Release `v2026.11.6` | Exited 1 and left a 1,024-byte cached JPEG | Exited 0 and produced a JPEG that FFmpeg could not decode |
| This change `cf4746a42a6` | Exited 1 with no output or cache file | Exited 0 and embedded a 92,771-byte JPEG that FFmpeg decoded successfully |

A subsequent render reused the cache and produced byte-identical SVG output. The real Chromium renderer also produced a 1200 × 1200 PNG from the recovered cache, and FFmpeg decoded it successfully. The Linux regression failed on main and passed on this change. The focused test file had three passes and one opt-in PNG test skipped. Focused TypeScript and lint checks, Node syntax, formatting, and diff checks passed. Local Codex autoreview reported no actionable P0–P2 findings. macOS and Windows were outside this run.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction command</summary>

```sh
scratch=$(mktemp -d)
(
  trap '' XFSZ
  ulimit -f 1
  XDG_CACHE_HOME="$scratch/cache" node skills/meme-maker/scripts/meme.mjs \
    render drake --text "Choice A" --out "$scratch/first.svg"
)
XDG_CACHE_HOME="$scratch/cache" node skills/meme-maker/scripts/meme.mjs \
  render drake --text "Choice A" --out "$scratch/retry.svg"
ffmpeg -v error -xerror -i "$scratch/cache/openclaw/meme-maker/drake-181913649.jpg" -f null -
```

The test host invoked Node with `--use-env-proxy` to reach Imgflip. The focused suite ran via `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/meme-maker.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`. Production +14/−5, regression test +35.

</details>

prs.title: fix: align nested rows in the desktop Subagents panel
prs.body:
Related: #192810

## What Problem This Solves

In Chat → Panels → Subagents, the connector to a nested run starts off-center under its parent avatar. When the family ends, the divider also shifts to the indented child column, making the Done list look uneven.

## User Impact

Nested runs are easier to scan: connectors follow the avatar centers, dividers share the top-level title column, and durations stay right-aligned. Opening, stopping, and grouping runs are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use the row’s avatar and indentation geometry for the connector and divider. Continue branch lines only while another sibling follows, including across a deeper row. Remove the fixed overlap into the previous row, which did not follow its actual height.

## Evidence

- The focused Chromium regression measured an 8 px stem offset on the pre-fix base (`8479dacd2e105`) and passed with the fix. A second browser test verified nested navigation, scoped Stop, and live sibling changes. Both ran against the built Control UI with simulated Gateway data, not a live provider.

prs.title: fix(github): release unused reader response bodies
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Opening GitHub reader documents retained their parsed API response in the document cache even after rendering finished. Only pull-request and commit overviews can reuse that response to load another section; completed documents and other sections never read it again.

## User Impact

GitHub reader documents use less retained memory while returning the same content and making the same requests. Overview reuse, ETag revalidation, cache capacity, and access checks are preserved. No configuration or migration is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the raw page only in reusable non-issue overview entries. The existing plugin cache remains the owner; there is no new cache or lifecycle. Production LOC delta is zero.

## Evidence

The raw-response release regression fails on the parent for issues, pull requests, and commits. It also verifies that rendered-document cache hits make no additional requests. Existing section tests protect overview reuse.

Synthetic owner fixture: 2,080 issue documents with 14,769-byte API bodies, 32 live cache entries, five alternating A/B pairs and one A/A pair. Acceptance was identical output/request counts, collection of unused raw responses, lower post-GC heap, and preserved CPU/allocation. The fixture omits ETags to isolate the document cache; the separate bounded ETag cache may still retain the same response until its own eviction.

| Metric | Parent median | Candidate median |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Live raw response objects | 32 | 0 |
| Post-GC heap | 30,177,856 B | 29,691,512 B |
| Retained heap above warm baseline | 4,333,416 B | 3,863,952 B |
| Owner workload wall time | 104.23 ms | 99.35 ms |
| Process CPU | 156.70 ms | 139.14 ms |
| Allocated bytes | 197,365,168 | 197,190,272 |
| HTTP fixture requests | 4,160 | 4,160 |

Every output checksum matched. Post-GC heap decreased in all five pairs (0.27–0.78 MB); A/A heap differed by 1,616 B. Allocation is effectively unchanged; no allocation-speedup claim. This removes a bounded redundant retention, not a demonstrated source of unbounded heap growth.

Rerun: `node --expose-gc --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/perf/github-detail-retention.ts [baseline-detail.ts]`. Freeze the baseline owner with `git show BASE:extensions/github/src/detail.ts > baseline-detail.ts`.

Final focused plugin tests passed 113/113 (9.60 s wrapper wall); real Gateway GitHub tool integration passed 22/22 (42.57 s). Codex autoreview is scoped-clean through P2 on the complete local candidate against parent `165f1297b8c0e139257f85597dafd9127b983499`. Production/test/script typechecks, focused lint, formatting, import-cycle and other selected guards passed. Production and full-tree unused-file scans passed with zero entries.

`pnpm check:changed` found one benchmark lint error, corrected and rechecked, plus five unrelated dead exports in Feishu/Teams. The unchanged exact parent `165f1297b8c0e139257f85597dafd9127b983499` reproduces the identical five production and three full-tree findings. Introducing changes: #203108 (`483f025ea389d`) left `bot.ts:FeishuBotAddedEvent` and `message-content.ts:formatFeishuMediaContent` exported after their external consumers moved; #203084 (`ec270048434f3`) moved `htmlTagAttributeValues`, `isLikelyImageAttachment`, and `safeHostForUrl` into `attachments/html.ts`, leaving exports with only same-module production consumers. These are main regressions requiring follow-up, not waived checks. No owned path appears in either failure set.

prs.title: fix(models): signed-in native runtime loses to a runtime preference pinned before sign-in
prs.body: ## What Problem This Solves Fixes: after completing a native/CLI subscription sign-in (for example Muse), chats keep resolving the model to the default API runtime and fail with missing-auth errors, because a runtime preference stored while unauthenticated suppresses the signed-in runtime forever — and runtime-choice preparation never validated the stored preference at all. ## User Impact On re-selection, the stored runtime preference is now validated against current availability: - A stored preference that is still available always wins (unchanged behavior). - A stored preference that no longer evaluates available (missing credential, expired sign-in, cooldown) makes selection fail with provider sign-in guidance for that runtime — it is **never silently replaced** by another runtime. This follows the no-silent-switching principle from #150224: re-selection validates the pin, it does not replace it. The user recovers by signing in (chat sign-in buttons / Control UI handoff) or by explicitly choosing a different runtime. - Sessions without a stored preference keep existing discovery behavior: a claiming CLI/native runtime may be selected when available. Stored rows holding the "no preference" values `auto` or `default` (any casing) are read the same way and are never treated as a pin. - A required `inference="worker"` profile keeps ownership of runtime selection (pinned or unpinned), so re-selection never validates worker-local credentials on the gateway. Plain turns without re-selection are untouched; implicit runtime choices saved as pins at write time are a separate follow-up. ## Why This Change Was Made Two stacked causes: session runtime overrides skipped CLI/native runtime discovery entirely, and dual-route models that list the API catalog row first skipped runtime-choice preparation even when a native variant exists. The change always discovers claiming runtimes, treats a native variant as requiring runtime choice, and passes a stored real runtime id (not `auto`/`default`) to runtime-choice preparation as a dedicated `pinnedRuntimeId`. Availability-filtered choices (`runtimeChoices` only contains runtimes that evaluated available) decide the outcome: pin available → pin wins; pin unavailable → selection returns the existing unavailable message with sign-in guidance instead of falling through to `choices[0]`. ## Evidence Head `a2403ff6771`. Current `main` (`8479dacd2e1`) merged cleanly in `0b8a6a393ee`. `a2403ff6771` fixes a regression in this PR that was found during live proof (see **Live proof**). **Data-model compatibility (new on this head).** No schema, config, or migration changes. Existing session rows are read as stored, not rewritten. A new stored-row test, "reads a stored runtime override … from an existing session row", feeds session rows shaped like those earlier releases persisted (`sessionId`, `updatedAt`, `providerOverride`, `modelOverride`, optional `agentRuntimeOverride`) through re-selection. Values covered: absent, `"auto"`, `"default"`, unnormalized `" Auto "`, legacy alias `"pi"`, and `"OpenClaw"`. This test found a real regression in the previous head: rows storing `auto`/`default` became a hard pin on a runtime id that is never a choice, so re-selection was rejected. Fixed in `8a46c50e100`; those rows now stay unpinned. - Previous PR head `1e2a8b9438a`: `auto`, `default`, and `" Auto "` fail (`rejected`); the others pass. - This head: 6/6 pass. **Red on base.** These are this PR's regressions run against `main`'s `model-runtime-choice.ts` and `model-runtime-normalization.ts` with this branch's tests. All fail with assertion errors; on `main`, every case returns `ready` with the runtime `unchanged`, because API-first dual-route re-selection never reaches runtime-choice validation: - "does not silently switch from a stored openclaw preference pinned while signed out…": expected `rejected`, got `ready`. - "keeps a stored openclaw preference when its route is still signed in": expected `{ kind: "set", runtime: "openclaw" }`, got `{ kind: "unchanged" }`. - All 6 stored-row cases fail. - Base totals: 8 failed, 21 passed. This head: 29/29. The two required-worker re-selection tests pass on both base and head. They guard the earlier P1 against regression and are not red-on-base proofs. Focused suites on this head (`node scripts/test-projects.mts --maxWorkers=1`), 6 files, 208 tests, all passing: - `src/agents/model-runtime-choice.native.test.ts` - `src/agents/model-runtime-choice.test.ts` - `src/auto-reply/reply/directive-handling.model.test.ts` - `src/gateway/server-methods/agents-model-selection.test.ts` - `src/gateway/server-methods/sessions-mutations.sticky-model.test.ts` - `src/model-picker/apply-session-model-selection.test.ts` `tsgo:core` and `tsgo:core:test` are clean. `oxlint` and `oxfmt --check` are clean on touched files. Before the fix, on a real install: `meta/muse-spark-1.3` turns kept failing after a completed Muse subscription sign-in, because every turn resolved to the `openclaw` API route ("No API key found for provider meta"). ## Live proof Real Telegram private chat with a live Gateway on 2026-11-20. The Gateway ran upstream `main` `8479dacd2e1` merged with #180828, #180830 and #180831 (combined build `28efb83`; the three PRs were merged together because the author runs them together). Telegram IDs and device codes are redacted. Screenshots are hosted at [ivankuznetsov/openclaw@224a663](https://github.com/ivankuznetsov/openclaw/tree/224a6636a4ada057f2c61f0e7445f364e765e967). **Regression found live, fixed in `a2403ff6771`.** After a Muse model was selected (`Runtime set to muse`), a plain `/model deepseek/deepseek-flash` was rejected with `Runtime "muse" is not available for deepseek/deepseek-flash`. `resolveCompatibleAgentRuntimeForProvider` treats any registered harness as compatible with any provider, so the stored `muse` pin reached runtime choice, and this PR made it strict. A stored runtime is now pinned only when it can serve the selected model: `openclaw`, the discovered CLI runtime, or a native catalog row for this exact model. Any other stored runtime stays a preference, which matches the documented rule that an incompatible pin is cleared. New test "does not let a stored native runtime that cannot serve the selected model block a model-only switch": red before the fix (`rejected`), green after. | Before the fix | After the fix: Muse selected | After the fix: plain switch back | |---|---|---| | | | | **Explicit native runtime.** Selecting `meta/muse-spark-1.3` replies `Runtime set to muse`, and a turn runs through the Muse runtime to Meta. Meta answered `429 … Subscription quota exhausted` (the quota resets 2026-11-23), so a completed reply is still pending. The 429, rather than a 401, shows that routing and the signed-in account work. Captures are in #180831. **Upgrade with real data.** The same Gateway was upgraded in place from a 2026.10.10 build (base 2026-11-04) to this build. prs.title: fix: preserve private child results during restart
prs.body:
Related: #203132

## What Problem This Solves

A completed child result queued behind a private requester continuation can be permanently discarded when a Gateway restart aborts that continuation. The private delivery branch treats the restart as an intentional cancellation and marks the undelivered result failed.

## User Impact

Completed results that have not reached their requester remain pending across restart and are delivered by startup recovery. Results already committed to the requester stay in its saved context without duplicate delivery. No migration, configuration change, or operator action is required.

## Why This Change Was Made

The private completion owner now excludes the existing `stopReason=restart` from intentional non-delivery, leaving its existing retryable outcome in charge. Ordinary cancellation retains its suppression behavior. This is one changed production line, net zero production LOC, with no new persistent states or recovery policy.

Already-consumed private results do not need re-admission: consumption is recorded after transcript commitment. Eligible root requesters resume through existing restart recovery; spawned requesters are not independently resumed, but their next turn sees the saved completion. This does not claim that an aborted private turn already produced a user-visible reply, or that a replacement session inherits another session's context.

## Evidence

A real isolated Gateway regression finishes two children, holds a private continuation consuming the first result, queues the second result, sends SIGTERM, and starts a fresh Gateway on the same isolated state and port. Before the fix, the second result becomes `failed`; after the fix, it remains pending with zero committed inputs, then delivers once. Another restart leaves exactly one committed input and one completion model response.

The consumed-result controls also pass: a top-level private continuation resumes, and an actual spawned requester has no independent restart marker but receives exactly one saved completion in its next model request and produces one reply. All three process cases pass with the current built runtime. The synthetic loopback model observes actual provider requests; no live deployment or production data is used.

151 focused owner/settlement tests passed, plus the two final direct-delivery cancellation controls and the three process restart cases. Final Codex autoreview is scoped-clean through P2. Targeted lint, root E2E typecheck, formatting, and the line-cap check pass.

`pnpm check:changed` passed its type/lint/format/guard phases but reports inherited dead-export regressions, reproduced on the exact parent `b8b06c4824f381e6a53ace20d3f8b1f9b5de509a`:

- #203108 (`483f025ea389d198a4083dbe0d79b50ad2db2754`) leaves `FeishuBotAddedEvent` and `formatFeishuMediaContent` exports unused after moving their consumers.
- #203084 (`ec270048434f3194393a00dbf9a8951cf5711a7f`) leaves `htmlTagAttributeValues`, `isLikelyImageAttachment`, and `safeHostForUrl` exports unused after moving their callers into the same module.

These are main regressions, outside this delivery repair. An initial line-cap failure from placing the test in the larger suite was fixed by moving it to the direct-delivery suite; the final line-cap check passes.

<details>
<summary>Focused commands and process runtimes</summary>

```sh
OPENCLAW_E2E_USE_PREBUILT_DIST=1 node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/gateway-subagent-completion-restart.e2e.test.ts src/agents/subagents/announce/subagent-announce-direct-delivery.test.ts --maxWorkers=1 -t 'restart \((private-queued-announcing|spawned-private-announcing|private-announcing)\)|private completion interrupted'
pnpm check:changed
node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig tsconfig.core.json src/agents/subagents/announce/subagent-announce-completion-delivery.ts src/agents/subagents/announce/subagent-announce-direct-delivery.test.ts test/gateway-subagent-completion-restart.e2e.test.ts
node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.test.root.e2e.json --incremental
node scripts/check-line-cap-ratchet.mjs --base origin/main
```

Private root: 20.459 s; queued private: 29.462 s; spawned private: 18.212 s. These are test runtimes, not latency benchmarks.

</details>

prs.title: feat(browser): add opt-in headless user-agent compatibility
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Some public booking pages fail in managed headless Chrome while loading in visible Chrome. Operators can already supply a fixed user-agent through browser.extraArgs, but must maintain its version/platform string and have no documented, profile-scoped diagnostic for the native HeadlessChrome marker.

## User Impact

Operators can opt into browser.headlessUserAgent="chrome" globally or for one managed profile. The default remains "native"; existing profiles do not change behavior unless opted in. Enable/reset through openclaw config set, then stop/start the browser. Status reports the normalization applied by the running launch, not merely the desired configuration.

The option affects locally launched headless Chromium only. Explicit --user-agent launch arguments take precedence. It is not full browser-identity emulation: Chromium may omit or reduce User-Agent Client Hints, and sites can still fail. Opting in adds one bounded, no-startup-window native-UA probe before the final launch; default launches incur no probe.

## Why This Change Was Made

Reuse the existing managed launch/bootstrap and cleanup owner to read the selected executable's actual native user-agent. Replace only the HeadlessChrome/ product marker and pass the result to the final Chromium process before page navigation. This avoids hard-coded version/platform templates and page-event races that miss popup or frame first requests.

Config inheritance, launch-setting refresh, status, schema help, documentation and the packaged browser-automation skill use the same option. Agent guidance calls for a bounded comparison within the user's troubleshooting request, not automatic enablement on every error. Externally owned browsers and headed launches remain unchanged.

## Evidence

### Live symptom investigation — motivation, not a deterministic site guarantee

Public pages only; no passenger details or bookings submitted. Same Mac and managed profile. A same-version Chrome 158.0.8127.37 comparison observed:

| Public booking page | Native headless UA | Per-page CDP override replacing HeadlessChrome/158 with Chrome/158 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| British Airways: https://www.britishairways.com/travel/managebooking/public/en_gb | Navigation stalled; the bounded control was stopped. A timeout does not establish deliberate blocking. | Redirected to “Find my booking”; final HTTP 200 with booking-reference and surname fields. |
| Iberia: https://www.iberia.com/gb/manage-my-booking/ | Main document HTTP 200, embedded content reported “Access Denied.” | Main/login page loaded without that denial; booking lookup remained unverified. |

Earlier visible-mode comparisons loaded both public lookup forms. Chrome updated from 157 to 158 between investigations, so the UA experiment was repeated against a native-headless control on 158. Cookies/session state and request order were not randomized: these observations support a compatibility option, not a claim that the marker is the sole cause.

The original live experiment used a page-level CDP override; this PR uses a process-level launch override. The local real-browser fixture tests the actual implementation separately.

### Candidate validation

The committed real-browser test passed with Chrome 158.0.8127.37 through production launchOpenClawChrome: native mode, compatibility mode, compatibility restart, and explicit custom override. Every first HTTP user-agent and JavaScript navigator.userAgent matched the expected value across a top-level navigation, cross-origin iframe, popup and second tab. Low-entropy Client Hints were unchanged in this build; high-entropy hints were not tested. Test execution: 12.423s; suite including cold compilation: 128.97s. Only temporary state and local HTTP fixtures were used.

Launcher regression proof: substituting the original launcher produced 4 failures / 8 passes; restoring the implementation passed 12/12. Config suite: 95 passed, 1 skipped. Schema/engine suite: 15 passed. Hot-reload suite: 8 passed. Final launcher/status/CLI/passkey batch: 58 passed, 1 skipped (102.30s including cold compilation; 111.67s wrapper). Live website outcomes are not asserted by CI.

Build: production CI-artifacts build completed successfully (5m31.5s execution, excluding lock wait). Extension production typecheck passed. Targeted type-aware lint, formatting, generated config docs, diff whitespace and line-cap/max-lines ratchets passed. Extension test typecheck also passed. Independent Codex autoreview returned scoped-clean at P0–P2 (no actionable findings). Subsequent changes were limited to test typing/cleanup lint corrections; production code was unchanged.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction and validation commands</summary>

Enable for an existing managed profile:

~~~sh
openclaw config set browser.profiles.openclaw.headlessUserAgent chrome
openclaw browser --browser-profile openclaw stop
openclaw browser --browser-profile openclaw start --headless
openclaw browser --browser-profile openclaw status
~~~

Reset the setting to native and restart to revert. No gateway permission or identity changes are required.

Focused suites were run with the repository wrapper:

~~~sh
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/browser/src/browser/config.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/config.browser-engines.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/browser/src/browser/server-context.hot-reload-defaults.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/browser/src/browser/chrome.headless-launch.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/routes/basic.existing-session.test.ts extensions/browser/src/cli/browser-cli-manage.test.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/pw-session.webauthn.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/build-all.mts ciArtifacts
node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.extensions.json
~~~

For the committed live fixture, set LIVE=1, PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE_PATH to the local Chrome binary, OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR to an empty temporary directory, and OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH to a nonexistent file inside that directory. Then:

~~~sh
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs --config test/vitest/vitest.live.config.ts extensions/browser/src/browser/chrome.headless-user-agent.live.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
~~~

Isolation matters: the default live harness stages operator auth, which is unnecessary for this browser-only test. The fixture creates and cleans up its own browser profile and loopback receiver. No airline requests are made by the test.

</details>

Scope/limitations: real-browser execution was on macOS/Chrome 158, not Windows/Linux. No end-to-end booking or login guarantee, no high-entropy Client Hints equivalence claim. Build emitted advisory UI size-budget warnings; it exited successfully. Hosted CI covers broader platforms and suites.

Simplification: no new browser/session manager, persistent UA cache, per-tab event hook, or hard-coded platform/version template. The additional launch branch reuses the existing bootstrap cleanup owner; config/status/docs make the opt-in discoverable and reversible. Against the base: production TypeScript +76/-8 lines; test TypeScript +310/-28 lines (including the opt-in live fixture).

prs.title: fix(signal): unblock approvals while the requesting turn is waiting
prs.body:
Closes #194029

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes: Signal approval responses wait behind the turn they need to release. Once dispatched, UUID approvers can be rejected after command normalization, and a typed approval confirmation can cancel the waiting turn with a transcript conflict.

## User Impact

An authorized owner can approve a waiting command from Signal using `/approve` or a supported reaction. Ordinary messages and session-mutating commands retain their conversation ordering. Existing access, exact-target approval checks, and durable audit records remain enforced.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Route the existing narrow set of Signal controls and canonical approval-reaction candidates through a conversation-scoped control lane. Previously stored controls can move only from their exact original conversation lane to that conversation's control lane.
- Supply text-command facts for core active-run admission.
- Preserve UUIDs through Signal command/allowlist normalization instead of stripping their letters into phone-number-like values.
- Keep fast `/approve` exchanges visible in history but outside model context, using the existing context-free recorder contract. Their confirmations must not invalidate the transcript snapshot of the turn waiting for approval; the decision still reaches the model through the tool result.

The lifecycle type lives in the existing leaf types module, removing the review's import cycle. The existing routing helper moves unchanged into the context sibling to respect the oversized handler's growth guard. No schema, dependency, public SDK surface, or configuration option is added.

Related reviews: #175345 does not change Signal ingress; #191787 concerns native-approval capability metadata; merged #153829 supplies the Telegram control-lane precedent. The final recorder fix follows the existing context-free status mechanism from #192585.

## Conflict refresh — 2026-11-22

Merged upstream `5e371a0b7799801eb738b993ae3b9687f78dd636` into the existing branch. Updated head: `9a127a4edc681600339ba441ccdd6459aa567e48`.

The sole conflict was in the slash-command guide. The resolution documents both the context-free fast `/approve` exchange and upstream's deferred recording of other command exchanges during an active turn. The TypeScript patch introduced by this PR is identical to the previous revision.

- **152 focused tests passed across 10 files** on the merged tree. Coverage includes Signal approval scheduling, replay, UUID handling, mentions, view-once attachment handling, and command history during an active turn, including late `/stop` delivery.
- Scoped review found no issue in the manual resolution or the overlapping automatic merges. Targeted lint, formatting, diff checks, the test-line budget, pre-commit, and the import-cycle check passed.
- The earlier live Signal/model, upgrade, and authorization tests below remain evidence for their recorded revision. GitHub CI on the refreshed head is tracked separately in the PR checks.

## Conflict refresh — 2026-11-17

Merged upstream `edbc5bcea9b605a826cc722d298c784c6a8fef78` into the existing branch, preserving its four original commits. Updated head: `8ce7760f3ebe8ea065b5f00099fbc6c0448fafab`.

The only textual conflict was in Signal's inbound context helper: this branch relocates the existing routing helper, while upstream #200058 renders native mentions in quoted messages. The resolution retains both. Automatically merged changes preserve upstream response-prefix handling and restart tests alongside the approval fixes. The introduced PR diff remains 15 files, +269/-70.

- **176 focused cases pass in 10 files** on the resolved tree: 81 Signal cases (including upstream quoted-mention and group-mention tests), and 95 shared command/transcript cases. Signal wrapper wall time: 120.55 seconds; shared wrapper wall time: 98.78 seconds, including compilation.
- Production core and Signal package type checks, focused regression-test types, targeted lint, formatting, diff checks, pre-commit guard, and import-cycle check pass (0 runtime value cycles). The current test-line budget passes: +138 test lines, 400 allowance, 138 existing allocation credit; no baseline or allocation changes.
- Fresh independent read-only review of the public conflict-resolution bundle found no actionable merge regression. The initial agy review timed out without a result; the completed fallback review covered the manual resolution and overlapping automatic merges.
- The first sandboxed test attempt was stopped after process-identity/loopback restrictions caused fixture failures. The completed run used the required local process and loopback permissions. One type-check attempt overlapped lint's artifact ownership; it was rerun successfully after lint completed.
- Live Signal/model, stable-upgrade, and final-effect authorization receipts below remain evidence for the explicitly pinned earlier head `d24bc8ab8ccbd869accc368c9b6a595016e65055`; those external/live checks were not repeated for this conflict refresh. New-head GitHub CI is separate from the earlier passing runs. [CI run 43902495410](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/43902495410) currently reports `action_required` with zero jobs; no new-head CI pass is claimed. GitHub reports the updated PR mergeable; maintainer review and the workflow action remain pending.

## Evidence from the earlier tested head

- Base used for local proof: `8b023da72a1a595450b3071782ec1d4940bd459f`. Previously live-tested candidate: `d24bc8ab8ccbd869accc368c9b6a595016e65055`.
- Red before repair: DM/group queue controls do not dispatch; command context is `normal` rather than `text-slash`; three UUID formats fail approval authorization after command formatting; the fast-approval recording boundary omits `contextFreeCommand`. Corresponding regressions pass after repair.
- **206 relevant cases pass across 11 test files**: 113 Signal cases and 93 shared command/transcript cases. The final consolidated fixture was also verified by rerunning its 74-case lifecycle suite. Signal validation took 63.80 seconds; shared validation took 103.85 seconds, including compilation. Existing authorization, wrong-target, ordinary FIFO, replay, and routing controls remain covered.
- Official production-core and extension type checks, focused changed-test type checks, type-aware lint, formatting, diff and pre-commit checks pass. Temporary test configurations extend the repository configuration; no compiler settings were committed.
- Final clean Linux CLI-startup build passed in **2m 10.7s**. This is the startup profile, not a full release/package/declaration build. Local architecture check reports **0 cycles**.
- Independent reviews of the cycle repair, UUID repair, and final recorder diff returned scoped-clean. The test fixture stays in its existing suite and shrinks by consolidating repeated values.

### Live Signal and model proof

Verified the exact clean candidate with a real agent, configured OpenAI model, and the registered Signal account through Signal Desktop. Approval mode remained gated; only allow-once decisions were used.

```text
candidate: d24bc8ab8ccbd869accc368c9b6a595016e65055
whoami request: pending
/status during the wait: replied; displayed d24bc8a
/approve <redacted> allow-once: allowed via channel policy
whoami final reply: stdout openclaw
separate printf signal-final-ok request: pending
thumbs-up on its native prompt: allowed via channel policy
final reply: signal-final-ok
ingress after both cases: completed=20, pending=0, claimed=0, failed=0
```

These checks exposed and reproduced both the UUID normalization refusal and the typed-confirmation transcript conflict before their repairs. The final run completed without those failures. Only sanitized decision metadata and receipts are included here; no private transcript, account identifier, credential, or screenshot is published.

### Actual stable upgrade

The installed stable core and official Signal plugin, both 2026.11.1, accepted real Signal events into a separate state directory. The stable journal contained an ordinary completion, a claimed typed approval, and a pending reaction in the original direct-conversation lane. After stopping stable, applying the supported offline Doctor migration to the test copy, and starting the candidate, all three records were completed, with the pending reaction reconciled to the control lane; no pending or failed ingress remained.

Account, account UUID, owner allowlist, agent/session filters, default model, and exec/elevated/filesystem policies were checked against the verified native backup and retained. The fixture uses a separate workspace and disables scheduled jobs. Native reaction tests explicitly use forwarding mode `session` with the existing private-session filter; `targets` alone does not start Signal's native approval handler. This demonstrates real packaged-state transport replay, not continuation of an already terminated process's exec call.

### Final-effect authorization proof

The follow-up security review requested rejection at the actual decision owner, beyond the identity helper. On the same exact built head, a separate credential-free Gateway loaded the real Signal plugin and approval capability. Its real exec tool requested a harmless file-marker command; no approval or execution callback was mocked.

For each public resolver used by Signal—legacy `exec.approval.resolve` for typed commands and canonical `approval.resolve` for reactions—both checks passed:

| Resolver | Refused actor | Approval after refusal | Decision waiter released | Command ran before current approval | Same command ran after current approval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `exec.approval.resolve` | Unlisted UUID | pending; no decision | no | no | yes |
| `exec.approval.resolve` | Queued, then revoked UUID | pending; no decision | no | no | yes |
| `approval.resolve` | Unlisted UUID | pending; no decision | no | no | yes |
| `approval.resolve` | Queued, then revoked UUID | pending; no decision | no | no | yes |

The unlisted UUID differs from the listed UUID only in letters, retaining the same numeric projection. In each revocation case, the old actor's control was first persisted with the real SQLite channel-ingress queue, and its pending row was checked. The Gateway's runtime configuration publisher then replaced the Signal approver policy while the original exec request remained alive. Only after publication was the unchanged queued control claimed and submitted to the real resolver. It was refused with `APPROVAL_NOT_FOUND`; `approval.get` still showed pending without a decision, the real decision waiter remained blocked, and the command's marker did not exist. A current listed actor then approved that exact request; the waiter returned allow-once and the real command created its marker. This positive control was repeated for all four cases.

This is an owner-boundary integration proof with synthetic identities and a test-controlled dispatch barrier, not another live Signal-network/model run. It deliberately submits to the final resolver rather than relying on earlier channel rejection. Runtime policy publication isolates the custody guard from file-reload scheduling; no authorization checks or process guards were bypassed. Separately, an attempted public `config.patch` policy reload was observed deferring Signal reload until active Gateway requests finish, so that timed-out attempt is **not** counted as revocation proof. The earlier exact-head live Signal/model proof remains the transport/user-flow evidence. The final isolated Gateway closed cleanly. No production source change was needed for this additional proof.

### Check boundaries

The local test-line guard against the historical base remains **25 lines over due to inherited debt**: base 6,533,876/6,533,851; candidate 6,534,014/6,533,989. The patch adds 138 counted regression lines and exactly 138 allocation credit. The shared baseline and unrelated tests were not changed.

The SQLite and HTTP fixtures were run on a qualified host with process-owner and loopback access. The exact candidate's [CI gate](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42223925652/job/127915523030) and [architecture guard](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/42223925652/job/127913150828) pass.

The candidate was used for bounded tests, and the normal stable service was restored. No permanent deployment or merge has been performed. Maintainer/security review remains required.

prs.body:
Bumps the bundler group with 1 update in the /apps/ios directory: [addressable](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable). Bumps the bundler group with 1 update in the /apps/android directory: [addressable](https://github.com/sporkmonger/addressable). Updates `addressable` from 2.9.0 to 2.9.1
Changelog

Sourced from addressable's changelog.

Addressable 2.9.1

  • fixes denial of service in Addressable::URI.normalize_path, which took quadratic time on paths with many dot segments; URI#normalize, #join, #== and #=== were affected (GHSA-qq38-m9mg-xjj5)
  • fixes Addressable::URI.normalize_path keeping segments that a .. should have removed after a .. above the root, e.g. /../../public/x/../../secret normalized to /public/x/secret instead of /secret (GHSA-8gmh-2hhj-2hv9)
  • fixes Addressable::URI.normalize_path treating a raw line feed as a segment boundary, e.g. joining ..\n/secret onto /public/ gave /\n/secret
  • deprecates Addressable::URI::RULE_2A, RULE_2B_2C, RULE_2D and RULE_PREFIXED_PARENT, which are no longer used; they will be removed in 2.10.0
  • fixes denial of service in Addressable::Template#match and #extract, which still backtracked exponentially in 2.9.0 for exploded /, ., ;, ? and & expressions (e.g. {/path*}) on regex engines without match memoization, such as JRuby, TruffleRuby and MRI before 3.2; match results are unchanged (GHSA-j82w-28jv-3pmj)
  • fixes denial of service in Addressable::Template#match and #extract, which backtracked polynomially or exponentially on the same regex engines for expressions with several variables (e.g. {/owner,repo,ref}, or {+a,b,c} with many variables), for ; expressions, and for adjacent expressions (e.g. {+a}{+b}{+c} or {+a}{b}); match results are unchanged (GHSA-9f42-57jx-vpp3)
  • fixes denial of service in Addressable::Template#match and #extract, which backtracked polynomially for expressions with several exploded variables (e.g. {+a*,b*}), including on MRI 3.2; match results are unchanged (GHSA-4w5q-wg7v-w6gp)
  • fixes Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode in the pure-Ruby backend decoding Punycode labels that aren't valid A-labels: labels that decode to only ASCII characters (e.g. xn--google- decoded to google) and labels that don't convert back to themselves; such a label is now returned unchanged, as with libidn, so Addressable::URI#display_uri no longer shows a host that differs from #normalized_host (GHSA-9crm-g4mf-wc5j)
  • fixes Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode decoding Punycode labels with characters that change how a host displays without being visible themselves, such as bidi overrides and isolates (e.g. U+202E and U+2066), zero width characters and control characters; such a label is now returned unchanged, so Addressable::URI#display_uri no longer shows them. The pure-Ruby backend also no longer decodes labels with other characters that nameprep prohibits, as with libidn (GHSA-539f-xcgw-2gjg)
  • fixes Addressable::URI#route_from and #route_to raising InvalidURIError when the route's first segment contains a colon (e.g. /a:b from /a); the route is now ./a:b (#625)
  • fixes Addressable::IDNA.to_unicode raising in the pure-Ruby backend for Punycode labels that are too long, overflow the decoder, or decode past U+10FFFF; the label is now returned unchanged, as with libidn, so Addressable::URI#display_uri no longer raises for such hosts (#620)
  • fixes Addressable::URI#display_uri raising InvalidURIError for URIs

prs.title: fix: distinguish Code Mode bridge errors from failed runs
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Code Mode logs a rejected bridge request as “Code Mode execution failed,” even when the script catches the rejection and completes. Operators investigating failures can mistake a recovered request for a failed execution.

## User Impact

Operators see “Code Mode bridge request failed” for individual bridge requests. The execution result, log levels, and structured diagnostic fields are unchanged. Exact-text log filters can use the new message or match `failurePhase: bridge`.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing diagnostic logger already knows which phase produced the error, so it can name the failed request without changing the execution or adding another log entry. The patch adds no state or config (production +6/−1; tests +3).

## Evidence

- The log regression failed on main for all four bridge cases and passed with the fix. The logging and Code Mode failure-origin suites passed: 93 tests, including caught and uncaught bridge rejections on Node and QuickJS.
- Changed-file lint and format, core and core-test typechecks, and `git diff --check` passed.
- Independent read-only source review of the exact two-file diff against `eb7ca3d33375` found no actionable findings at P2 or higher. The local autoreview helper could not run with the managed workspace’s required temporary directory; the independent review is not a helper attestation. External exact-text alerts were not checked.

prs.title: fix(net): close live streams when the provider dispatcher pool shuts down
prs.body:
Closes #202405

## What Problem This Solves

On a paired-node or provider HTTP transport, shutting down the provider dispatcher pool can return successfully while an unfinished streaming response is still connected. The pooled socket then keeps the Node process alive, so a bounded shutdown that reports completion leaves the process hanging instead of exiting.

The report reproduces this with the published package helpers: two client workers (`abort-first` positive control and `fallback`) against a loopback SSE server that never finishes its response. In `fallback`, the pool shutdown helper returns but the worker never exits and is killed after the timeout.

## User Impact

A provider pool shutdown now tears down the sockets of live streaming responses, so the process can exit after shutdown instead of hanging on an abandoned stream. Connection reuse and the graceful-close path are unchanged.

## Why This Change Was Made

`closeDispatcher` (`src/infra/net/ssrf.ts:710`) races `dispatcher.close()` against a 100 ms timeout and calls `dispatcher.destroy()` on timeout. For an undici `Agent`, that fallback cannot reach a live child:

- `Agent[kClose]` starts each child close and then **synchronously clears `kClients`** (`node_modules/undici/lib/dispatcher/agent.js:150-157`).
- When the timeout fires, `Agent[kDestroy]` iterates that **already-empty** `kClients` map, so no child holding an unfinished response is destroyed.

`createHttp1Agent` (`src/infra/net/undici-runtime.ts`) now wraps the agent's `factory` to record every origin dispatcher it creates, and the returned proxy's `destroy()` tears down those tracked children in addition to the agent itself. This mirrors the existing owned-set lifecycle wrapper in `createHttp1EnvHttpProxyAgent` in the same file. An agent keeps one child per origin behind `kClients`, so the owned set stays bounded by the pool's origin count, and entries are pruned once destroyed.

`ssrf.ts` and the graceful `close()` path are untouched; only the destroy fallback now also reaches the children it previously lost. Fix classification: `behavior-completing` (the destroy fallback was meant to abort live transports but could not reach them).

### P2 review repair: normalize the origin dispatcher factory

`buildHttp1AgentOptions` returned `NonNullable<UndiciAgentOptions>`, whose `factory` member stays optional in pinned Undici 8.12.4. The destroy-tracking wrapper then invoked a possibly-undefined factory, failing strict TypeScript and crashing on first dispatch when a caller passed `{ factory: undefined }` (Undici would have applied its own default factory there).

The factory is now normalized in the options owner (`undici-dispatcher-options.ts`): an explicit custom factory wins, `undefined` falls back to the HTTP/1-only origin dispatcher, and the guaranteed-callable shape is exposed as `Http1AgentOptions` so the wrapper can rely on it without asserting away the optional member. `createHttp1Agent` uses `Http1AgentOptions["factory"]` as its wrapper signature.

## Evidence

### Published npm package: the report's own setup and reproducer

The report's exact `setup.sh` and `repro.mjs` (from #202405, unmodified) run against the **published npm tarball** `openclaw@2026.11.6`. The tarball and its four dependencies (`undici@8.12.3`, `@openclaw/fs-safe@0.26.13`, `chalk@6.0.1`, `tslog@5.4.4`) were pre-fetched and installed from local tarballs, because this test host sits behind a TLS-intercepting proxy that the registry client rejects; the installed tree is identical to what `setup.sh` produces. Runs use the report's own `env -i PATH=... HOME=... TMPDIR=... node repro.mjs <count>` invocation.

| Streams | Package | mode | `helperReturned` | `streamsAtReturn` | `timedOut` | `exitCode` / `signal` |
|---:|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | npm `2026.11.6` | abort-first | true (5 ms) | 0 | false | 0 / null |
| 1 | npm `2026.11.6` | fallback | true (102 ms) | **1** | **true** | **null / SIGKILL** |
| 3 | npm `2026.11.6` | abort-first | true (6 ms) | 0 | false | 0 / null |
| 3 | npm `2026.11.6` | fallback | true (100 ms) | **3** | **true** | **null / SIGKILL** |
| 15 | npm `2026.11.6` | abort-first | true (7 ms) | 0 | false | 0 / null |
| 15 | npm `2026.11.6` | fallback | true (101 ms) | **15** | **true** | **null / SIGKILL** |

This reproduces the report verbatim on the shipped package: the helper returns at ~100 ms with every stream still connected, and the worker survives until the harness `SIGKILL`s it.

### Built dist: the same reproducer, base vs head

The same `repro.mjs` then runs against **built `dist` trees**. Each side is a full `scripts/build-all.mts` build of one tree, differing only in the two changed source files; the worker imports the shipped `mcp-http-fetch-*.mjs` and follows its own `provider-transport-dispatcher-pool-*.mjs` import, exactly as the report describes. (One substitution: the build minifies imports to `from"./..."`, so the pool-import regex is `from\s*"`; the lookup and everything downstream are unchanged.)

```sh
OPENCLAW_RUN_NODE_SKIP_DTS_BUILD=1 OPENCLAW_BUILD_WORKER_DEPLOY_BUNDLE=0 \
OPENCLAW_TSDOWN_MAX_OLD_SPACE_MB=5120 node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs scripts/build-all.mts
DIST_DIR=<dist>/ node repro.mjs <count>     # Node 24.22.1, containerized, loopback only
```

| Streams | Side | mode | `helperReturned` | `streamsAtReturn` | `timedOut` | `exitCode` / `signal` |
|---:|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | BASE | abort-first | true (5 ms) | 0 | false | 0 / null |
| 1 | BASE | fallback | true (101 ms) | **1** | **true** | **null / SIGKILL** |
| 1 | HEAD | abort-first | true (5 ms) | 0 | false | 0 / null |
| 1 | HEAD | fallback | true (102 ms) | **0** | false | **0 / null** |
| 3 | BASE | fallback | true (101 ms) | **3** | **true** | **null / SIGKILL** |
| 3 | HEAD | fallback | true (102 ms) | **0** | false | **0 / null** |
| 15 | BASE | fallback | true (101 ms) | **15** | **true** | **null / SIGKILL** |
| 15 | HEAD | fallback | true (104 ms) | **0** | false | **0 / null** |

BASE reproduces the report exactly at every stream count. HEAD returns on the same ~100 ms bound, leaves zero streams open, and the worker exits naturally with status 0. The `abort-first` positive control is unchanged on both sides, so the fixture still permits prompt natural exit when requests are cancelled. The published-package column above is the pre-fix behaviour, and HEAD's dist is the same tree plus this PR's two source changes.

### Source-level probe and regression test

Real undici, real `PinnedDispatcherPool` teardown, and an unfinished streaming response, run as a child process that is **not** given `process.exit()`. The parent watches for natural exit and only falls back to `SIGKILL` after a 3 s timeout, exactly as the report's reproducer does. The worker imports the unmodified source entry points.

Command (from a source checkout at the printed SHA, Node 24.22.1):

```sh
node --import ./scripts/tsx.mjs /tmp/probe-exit.mjs .
```

| Observation | BASE `217bb899f09` | HEAD `5319f987fe9` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `helperReturned` | true (102 ms) | true (110 ms) |
| `streamsAtReturn` | **1** (stream still open) | **0** |
| `timedOut` (forced kill) | **true** | false |
| `exitCode` / `signal` | **null / SIGKILL** | **0 / null** |

BASE reproduces the report exactly: the shutdown helper returns while the stream is still open, and the process only stops when the parent kills it. HEAD exits naturally (`exitCode 0`, no signal) because shutdown closed the socket.

New regression test in `src/agents/provider-transport-dispatcher-pool.test.ts`:

- `closes the sockets of unfinished streaming responses at host shutdown` — opens a real `fetchWithProviderHttpGuard` stream against a loopback SSE server, reads one chunk, keeps the reader open, calls the real `closeProviderTransportDispatcherPool()`, and asserts the server-side socket count drops to `0`. Red on BASE (the socket stays open and the assertion times out), green on HEAD.

Test run:

```sh
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/agents/provider-transport-dispatcher-pool.test.ts src/infra/net/pinned-dispatcher-pool.test.ts src/agents/mcp-http-fetch.test.ts
```

HEAD: 2 passed / 4 passed / 7 passed. The existing credential-reuse and pool-lifecycle tests stay green, so connection reuse and the graceful path are unaffected.

The factory normalization is covered by two new discriminant tests in `src/infra/net/undici-runtime.test.ts`: `keeps a callable origin factory when an explicit factory is undefined` (red on the pre-fix commit: the wrapper invoked `undefined`; green here) and `keeps an explicit custom origin factory when one is provided` (custom factory wins).

Re-verified at HEAD `e66d01fec5d` on Node 24.22.1 in a container against a pristine-base tree whose `undici-runtime.ts`, `undici-dispatcher-options.ts`, `ssrf.ts` and both test files matched BASE `217bb899f09` byte for byte before the sync:

```sh
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/infra/net/undici-runtime.test.ts \
  src/agents/provider-transport-dispatcher-pool.test.ts \
  src/infra/net/pinned-dispatcher-pool.test.ts --maxWorkers=1
node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json
```

`undici-runtime.test.ts` 7 passed, `pinned-dispatcher-pool.test.ts` 4 passed, `provider-transport-dispatcher-pool.test.ts` 2 passed; `run-tsgo` exit 0 (the strict-TypeScript finding is closed).

`src/infra/net/fetch-guard.ssrf.test.ts` has 4 failing cases in this environment; they fail identically on BASE `217bb899f09` (they exercise env-proxy routing and are unrelated to this change).

## Not tested

- The published tarball was installed from **pre-fetched local tarballs** rather than over the registry, because this test host's TLS-intercepting proxy fails registry certificate verification. Versions are exactly the report's (`openclaw@2026.11.6`, `undici@8.12.3`, `@openclaw/fs-safe@0.26.13`, `chalk@6.0.1`, `tslog@5.4.4`) and the resulting `node_modules` and `app/dist` are what `setup.sh` produces; only the download path differs.
- Both sides ran on **Node 24.22.1**, not the report's Node 26.12.1. The teardown path under test (`closeProviderTransportDispatcherPool` → `closeDispatcher` → undici `Agent`) is identical, and BASE reproduces the reported failure at the same ~100 ms helper bound, but a Node 26 run was not performed.
- A **real Gateway shutdown does not reproduce this** and is not claimed as a red/green. Measured: `chat.send` against a never-finishing SSE provider leaves one stream open, but Gateway stop aborts the agent run first (`model fallback chain stopped: reason=caller_signal_aborted`), which cancels the request before the destroy fallback is reached — BASE shut down cleanly in 4178 ms. This matches the report's own scoping: the defect needs an unfinished response that reaches the fallback "without an effective earlier abort".
- The `EnvHttpProxyAgent` path (`createHttp1EnvHttpProxyAgent`) has its own owned-set wrapper and was not changed; a proxy-routed live stream was not exercised end to end.
- Frequency in normal Gateway shutdown/restart/update workflows remains unestablished, as the report notes.

## Cleanup

Every run used a loopback-only synthetic SSE server and a disposable container with no OpenClaw state, credentials, provider account or production config mounted. The only killed process is the isolated test worker (by the harness, as the report's reproducer intends) and the disposable Gateway container used to establish the non-reproduction above. Both `dist` trees and all scratch directories on the test host were removed afterwards; the base tree's two changed files were restored and hash-verified against the pre-fix commit.

prs.title: fix(openai): stop sending a version header; identify OpenClaw by originator and User-Agent
prs.body:
## Problem

OpenClaw sent a `version` header on ChatGPT/OpenAI requests (Responses turns, realtime, TTS, embeddings, usage probes and device-code login). ChatGPT uses `version` as a Codex client gate on `/responses`, so the value had to be kept in step with model listing (#202380, #202427). No other ChatGPT-subscription client does this: Zed, Crush, opencode, Kilo, Cline, Roo Code, Hermes and pi send only `originator` and `User-Agent: <app>/<version>` on turns. Only omp sends `version`, and it sends a real Codex version.

## Solution

Identify OpenClaw the way other clients do:

- `originator: openclaw`, a fixed client name with no version (like Codex's `codex_cli_rs`).
- `User-Agent: openclaw/<build>`, which carries the version.
- No `version` header anywhere.

Changes:

- `src/agents/provider-attribution.ts`: the OpenAI/xAI attribution policy returns only `originator` and `User-Agent`.
- `extensions/openai/base-url.ts`: `/models?client_version=` now derives the numeric release (`YYYY.M.P`, year ≥ 2026, else `99.0.0`) from the policy's version. Before, it read the removed header.
- These producers built their own `version` header and now drop it: `src/infra/provider-usage.fetch.codex.ts`, `src/agents/auth-profiles/usage.ts`, `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/embeddings-remote-client.ts` and `extensions/openai/openai-chatgpt-device-code.ts`.
- Dead `version` entries are removed from the realtime browser-header filter and the embedding cache-key exclusion list.
- Docs (`model-discovery.md`) and `src/plugins/AGENTS.md` are updated.

## Impact

- **Turns:** ChatGPT applies no client-version gate to OpenClaw turns.
- **Model listing:** unchanged; it still sends the numeric release as `client_version`.
- **`User-Agent`:** still carries the full build.
- **Size:** net −17 lines.

## Evidence

- **Red on base, green on head:**
  - `provider-attribution.test.ts`: 2 cases fail on base.
  - `tts.test.ts`: 1 case fails on base.
  - `provider-live-listing.contract.test.ts`: 1 case fails on base.
- **Consumers green:** `extensions/openai` (95 files), the transport stream, prefix stability, embeddings client, usage probes, auth-profiles and the realtime webrtc UI test.
- **Gates:** `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:extensions`, `check:test-types`, `ocx build --dts` and the release-check packed smoke pass.
- **Live wire behavior:**
  - 2026-11-18 probe: gpt-6.2-sol on `/responses` returned HTTP 200 with no `version` header.
  - Scratch-Gateway E2E: the device-code request ran without `version` and ChatGPT accepted it.
  - The listing and turn proof is added below when complete.

## Merge risk

Low. The change only removes a header. The model list keeps its own `client_version`.

prs.title: fix: enable Perplexity Search through ClawRouter
prs.body:
## What Problem This Solves

ClawRouter catalogs can offer Perplexity Search, but OpenClaw rejects its declared search format. This prevents `web_search` from using an otherwise eligible native or manifest offer.

## User Impact

Users selecting ClawRouter can search through eligible Perplexity Search offers with their selected Router credential. Results keep the existing untrusted-content and unsafe-URL handling. This does not change the default search provider or enable the Perplexity Agent API.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing search codec registry now encodes the model-less `{query,max_results}` request and reads ordered Perplexity results. Queries must fit both the existing string limit and 8192 UTF-8 bytes. Malformed or unsafe rows consume their original result slots; later rows do not refill the requested window.

## Evidence

- Both actual registered-tool native/manifest cases failed on the unchanged base and pass with the codec.
- All 17 new registered-tool HTTP controls pass: selected credential/path/body, query/count bounds, rotation, denial, stale offers, cancellation, 30-second deadline, malformed/oversized responses and response closure.
- Timing for the new 17-case file: 63.05 seconds wall time (59.24 seconds reported by Vitest), including 30.006 seconds for the unfinished-body deadline case. The >30-second case keeps a real HTTP body open and proves the production deadline aborts it and releases the connection; a fake clock or isolated codec test cannot establish that timer/transport/closure interaction. Hosted run 44738834457: 17/17 passed; deadline case 30.009 seconds, Vitest 95.89 seconds, test shard 97.20 seconds (exit 0), tested merge `b26fd77846970350656dd4c8caa7f58a5fd925a3`. The hosted build-artifacts job was skipped; the local 160.874-second build remains separate proof. Actual SDK-to-Worker parity remains pending.
- All 14 existing ClawRouter search-provider controls pass.
- Core, extension and agents-tools test typechecks; focused typed lint/format; extension SDK boundary guard; and `pnpm build:ci-artifacts` pass.
- Scoped source review found no actionable regression. The subsequent braces-only lint correction was reversed in memory to verify the reviewed test source exactly.

These are local registered-plugin and loopback HTTP proofs. Shipping ClawRouter Worker/SQLite parity and live provider execution are not claimed; that downstream qualification remains separate. No deployment or release is included.

prs.title: fix(cron): recover script runs after a Docker sandbox stops
prs.body:
Closes #202460

## What Problem This Solves

Cron scripts can keep failing after their Docker sandbox container is stopped outside OpenClaw.

## User Impact

The next cron script or condition evaluation starts the existing stopped sandbox before it runs. A running sandbox keeps its prepared runtime.

## Why This Change Was Made

Each evaluation checks the cached container once before running. OpenClaw uses Docker's Inspect API on the captured Unix socket, or the Docker CLI on other transports. A confirmed stop sends the evaluation through the existing sandbox provisioner. The scheduler serializes evaluations of the same job and the runtime lease holds the sandbox through each evaluation.

## Evidence

I tested main `f7558cc8ff82` against this PR head on Docker Desktop 4.98.0 with separate Gateway profiles and Docker sandboxes set to mode `all`, scope `agent`. I stopped each sandbox by its exact Docker ID. Both post-stop script runs on main failed with `container … is not running`. Both PR-head runs succeeded after Docker restarted the same container. A scheduled condition evaluation also restarted its existing container on the next tick.

![Redacted Gateway run-history and Docker Inspect evidence for main script failure, PR-head script recovery, and scheduled condition recovery](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/daniel-lxs/screenshots/81360e8bff296f2c080128e5572f30554b5fa2eb/images/2026/11/0b34df0a-b653-493b-a2d6-fc1b5b2a5886.png)

I alternated 16 warm runs per build. These are Gateway run-history durations.

| Build | Median | p95 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Main `f7558cc8ff82` | 629.5 ms | 639 ms |
| PR head `bae29cb29d44` | 630.5 ms | 693 ms |

Docker recorded one workload exec per warm run and zero warm mount probes on either build.

The stopped-container regression failed on main at the first run after the stop. All 110 focused tests in seven files passed on the PR head. The regression took 13.7 seconds locally. Targeted lint, core typecheck, and formatting passed.

The live check used `docker stop`. A Docker Desktop restart and other Docker transports were outside the live check.
